The Proprietors of the MANCHESTER TAILORING AND CLOTHING DEPOT are convinced that the inhabitants of War- rington and the surrounding Districts see that it is to their interests to support them in their endeavour to supply GOOD FASHIONABLE WELL-MADE CLOTHING FOR MEN, YOUTHS, AND BOYS, at prices so much lower than other houses.

Their increasing trade each season is positive proof that the goods give satisfaction, and they are determined to sustain their reputation by sparing no expense in producing the most FASHIONABLE STYLES from the MOST DURABLE C LOT H 8 at the most moderate prices. From the encouragement they have received, their prepara tions for the coming season are far more extensive than any previous year, careful attention having been given to the selection of such high art designs and styles in all the best makes of Woollen Cloths as will ,satisfy the various tastes of their numerous customers.

They think it almost needless to remind their customers that they make up all their own goods at their extensive factory in Manchester by experienced workpeople only—the greatest attention being given to combine the most fashionable styles with elegance, neatness, and durability, at exceedingly low prices.

IN ME NEM,' All, LORD FREDERICK C&VENDISH. FOULLY :NII:RDEagt. IN IRIMAND, MY 6TEt, 1852. I loved thee, Cavendish! In cloistered halls Our youthful steps consorted; afterward Our ways were parted, but my heart kept guard Over thee, friend, hearing thy firm footfalls, Expectant till the hour tiny country calls To arduous honour, even to watch and ward, Beside her sacred person; nor too hard The post, for whom stroug-souleAl no fear appil3. Ah leal and gentle, unvaunting. kindly, pun ! A later Perceval! ah ! lovely spirit, A white ensign of amity thy hand Bore to the poor mad gurderess ! no cure For frenzy fire, a very goad to stir it! In thy true heart she plunged the treacherous brand! Cold in thy coffin! and the spring is here! Blasted in all the promise of thy prime! With healthful sinews patient braced to climb The 1, ftiest heights of service! on the bier Thy brow shows tranquil, as thy soul is clear! Renaembrance holds thee in thy youthful time, Crowned patriot martyr by infernal crime! Wnere thou hast fallen is a field of honour! Justice and Peace to you distracted isle Lave proffered, and she struck the felon blow; Yet there is hope; Saul's demon mood was on her; But sobered, shocked to find herself so vile, Kneeling she weeps o'er whom she bath laid low. The olive brai:ch may rise a sheltering wood, Baptised, dear hero, in thy sacred blood! . . . .
While arm-in-arm the sister isles may move, Wearing twin roses, sunned in thy warm love. —The Academy. RODEN Nov.L.

He'e armed without that's innocent within.—Pope. feleness is the key of beggary and the root of all evil. One soweth and, another reepeth," is a verity that ap- piiee to evil as well as good.—George Ellot. The reporter of a New York daily paper went to see the panorama of " Banyan'is Pilgrim's Progress." On being refused adieitrance without paying, he said, "Let me see Mr. lianyao, tnen ; he will let me in." "Here's a fly in my soup, waiter." "Yes, sir; very eerie., sir; hut you can throw away the fly and. eat the soup, can't you ?" Of course I can; you didn't expect me to throw away the soup and eat the fly, did you ?" Putting young hopeful through an oral examination in botany: Waere do the apples come from?" "The apple e' tree." "And the pears ?" "From the pear tree." "And I Coe figs?" "From the fig tree." "And the. dates ?" I "From the almanac." A h incisome lady entered a dry goods store and inquired for a "bow." The polite clerk threw himself back and re- marked that be was, at her service. "Yes, but I want a bog, not a green one," was the reply. The young man went on measuring goods immediately. Walsh, the publisher, was said to have gained £1,500 ate:ling from the publication of "Rinaldo," which drew from Handel this complaint—" My dear sir, as it is only right that we should be upon an equal footing, you shall comoorie the next opera and I will sell it." A watchinaker is sitting in his shop, surrounded by clocks and watchee, aed all going, and no two alike. He perceives that it is getting late in the afternoon, and anxiety rashes upen him. He rushes-tint of his shop and stops the first pasear-hy, "Sir, what o'clock is it, please ?" Lord Lorne, in mentioning the mixture of races in Canada, says that when ha first expressed a wish to see a real f ull- blooded Indian he was rather astonished when the Canadian, who at once undertook to gratify the wish, summoned the reqeired real specimen of the aboriginal race by shouting— " Come here, M`Donald !" "1 dare not ask a kites. I dare not beg a smile, Lest having that or this, I might grow proud the while." "No, no; the utmost share Of my desire shall be Onelv to kisse that mire That lately kissed thee."—Herrick. A gentleman was riding on the outside of a North Devon welch, from Barnstaple to Ilfracombe, when the driver said to him, "I've had a coin guy' use to-day 200 year old. Did you ever pee a coin 200 year old?" "Oh, yes, I have one myself 2,000 years old." " Ah," said the driver, "have ye ?" and spoke no more during the met of the journey. When the coach arrived at its destination, the driver came up to my friend with an intensely satisfied air, and said, "I told you as we druv' along I had a coin 200 year old." "Yes." "And you said to me as you had one 2,000 year old." "Yes, so I have." "Now it's a lie." "What do you mean by that ?" "What do I mean? Why it's only 1867 now." In a very scarce book—" Hal's Parochial History of Corn- wall—published at Exeter in 1750, mention is made of Kiilierew,the celebrated Master of the Revels, temp. Charles 11., though he never was formally installed Court Jester. The following anecdote will show, at all events, that he deserved the appointment, even though he did not get it:— When Louis XIV. sheaved him his pictures at Paris the King pointed out to him a picture of the Crucifixion be- tween two portraits. "That on the right," added his Majesty, "is the Pope, and that on the left is myself." "I humbly shank your Majesty," replied. the wit, "for the infermation ; for though I have often heard that our Lord was crucified between two thieves, I never knew who they W.r2Tt till now."—Erarper's Monthly. ItvetiaNterroN.—Doctor M— was for many years Vice- President of P— College, the worthy President of which sole the Rev. Dr. F—. The former was evidently very willing, not to say impatient, that the latter should resign, and so make way for him to take on himself the I ullhonours of the Presidency. One day a friend was speaking to him of the good old President, and of his excellent qualides, when he replied—" Yee, yes; Dr. F— is a most excellent old ruin; he has every one of the virtues except RESIGNA- TION 1" Now that the good old man, has for many years been dead and gone, one of the students asks whether the former Vice-President, hut now President, is not lacking in the some virtue he thought so desirable in his predecessor ! Harper's 3fonthly, Trne " PREIIIER MAN.—It is a good thing to be loyal; gold to teach little youngsters and voungstreeses to be loyal; not bad to think of the Union Jack in all sorts of places, among all sores and conditions of men. As they say at Epsom a good send off at life's outset is four to one better than a false start. A sad case of irregular start comes to us Iro-n a town in the north, which has one of the best Sunday echools in England. In the juvenile department of that echeol taught Mrs. Smith, who had picked up a class of tirctina not old enough to read, whom she taught by "rote." On a recent Sunday good Mrs. Smith propounded to the dm the following historical interrogatory—" Who was the first man ?" A little fellow straightened up. feeling that he was competent to answer that question, and not half try. With eyes flashing with brightness and in a shrill little voice he confidently sung out—" Mr. Gladstone I "—Har- per's Monthly. How TO MAKE MEN FOND or HOME.—It is a great mlenaae for man, in his early married life, to be overdone with domesticity. A few, perhaps, have lived with their reletives ; but, as a rule, a husband's most recent experi- ence are of club and chamber life, and much society, which talls off often when he merles, unless his wife has a large circle of aequaintancee. She, probably, is quite content with his company alone while the man is apt to weary of the toujours percirix. To enjoy home life, therefore, culti- vate your friends, lest the woman dwindle down into a mare hon-iekeeper and bead nurse, with a spice of the dressmaker. Shut out from family life before marriage, many men have experienced bat little family affection, and affect to dis- believe in it, and to give themselves up to excitement and money-winning. But deep in the heart of each one is a yearning for the love of some good woman, who, to keep his love, should also he a wise one. Club life and the world may have set a hardening crust over the husband's heart, brit this is most easily broken through in those early days of -love and marriage by tenderness, sympathy, and tact. Do eat, however, make the sympathy futile by over-talking—a kindly pressure tithe husband's hand, a little forethought, waiting until he wishes to unburden his mind, without fore- ing confidence, will beat establish your claim to be a worthy friend and help-meet. Men are apt to consider women more or loss playthings—mi-,trusting their power of keeping a sai:rer. If, puffed up with the importance of his confidence, the if confides in her dearest friend only once in her mar- ried, life, she has irrevocably confirmed the impression.— Ca?sll's Magazine. Born , in the Seagate of Dundee in 1782, she was the daughter of --Stirling of Pittendreigh, Forfarshire, and of Amelia, daughter of Alexander Graham, of Duntrune, who died in 18'4, and was thus the last lineal representative of Clever- house. In addition to her accomplishments, she possessed tot and inventien in a high degree, and was always lively, atlnd, and hspitable. Sh 2 had a keen perception of the humorous, and was well known in Edinburgh society in the loahny days of Jeffrey. Gifted with great powers of mississY, her persouifications at private parties were so sta;que that even those who knew her best were deceived. Oee of the most amusing of these took place in 1821, at the hone, of Jeffrey. He apked her to give a personification of an old ledy, to which he consented; but, in order to have a little amusement at his expense, she called upon him in the character of a " Lady Pitlyal," to ask his professional opinion npon an imaginary law plea, which she alleged her agent was misconductlog. Oa this occasion she drove up to his house in the carriage of Lord Gillies, accompanied by a young lady as her danghter, and so complete was the pereonification that the smite Jeffrey did not discover till text day that he had been duped! ,orkiftptltrl -.Om; . SCIENTIFIC NOTES. .. ELECTRIC Flex lenerceeva.—The following arrangement has been proposed by M. Ledieu for a simple and cheap pyroscope, or " preventer" of fire (as he calls it). A oylinder of strong insulating matter is interposed in a circuit. It is filled" with a liquid which resists electrolysation, and has good conductivity, increasing considerably with the temper- ature. (Absolute alcohol is found to serve very well.) At either end a tight packing is penetrated by a platinum rheophore, connected with the end of the divided circuit. The effect of increased temperature on the liquid is indi- cated by a galvanometer, the needle of which, at a certain point, sets a bell ringing. AN AERONAUTICAL EXHIBITION. The A6ronautical Society proposes that an exhibition of apparatus for aerial navigation shall be held next year. Fourteen years have elapsed since an exhibition of this kind was witnessed in England, and censiderable advance has since been made in the knowledge and application of the principles of flight. Substantial prizes, it is understood, will be offered for the lightest engine in proportion to its power; for the beet form of aerial apparatus of dimensions reasonably considered ' equal to the conveyance of a man and any appliance for effecting aerial transport, whether by muscular or other power; and for the best mechanical model which shall be made to fly sufficiently in point of time to enable a decision to be formed as to its weight-carrying capacity and duration of flight with a continuous power. THE RECENT SOLAR ECLIPSE.—M. Janssen took mag- nificent photographs of the recent eclipse at the Meudon Observatory, Paris, where his revolver was set into opera- tion to determine the first and the last contact. He also took two series of photographs ninety cent. diameter, one negative, and the other positive, by direct exposure, with two large refractors. This is the first time that the whole photographic power of the Meudon Observatory has been set into ,operation. In the sitting of May 22 of the Academy of Sciences, M. Janesen presented the photographs of the last contact obtkined with his revolver during the eclipse, on Daguerreotype plates. He stated that the inspection of the several images proved the contact to have taken place at a later time than that calculated. He presented also a large Image, ninety cent. in diameter, obtained with his large re- fractor, and stated that he was unable to detect any differ- ence in the immediate vicinity of the moon in the repre- sentation of faculre and the minute details of the sun's structure. He considered the fact to be opposed to the ex- istence of a sensible lunar atmosphere, as inferred from the spectroscopic observations of the French astrbnomers in Egypt. A NEW Drszesz AMONG WORKBIEN.—It has been observed that the manufacture of bichromate of potash has a singular effect upon the nose, manifesting itself in a carious manner. A little hole is formed on the septum or partition of the nose dividing the nostrils, and increases gradually until the partition entirely disappears with the exception of its lower part, so that to a superficial observer there is nothing the matter with the nose, except a little outward depression. It is noticed that as soon as the parti- tion is destroyed the process appears to stop there, neither the lungs, air-tubes, nor throat being in the least degree affected. Some workmen at the chrome factory in Russia, where the disease has been chiefly watched, have been em- ployed for ten years and remained unaffected, while with others the hole in the nose begins to be formed after one molth's work. But that the disease is something more than an individual peculiarity is evident from the fact that an inspection of all the hands proved that more than 50 per cent, of the men had diseased noses. The early symptoms are a slight tickling of the part affected, followed by bleed- ing, but with no uncomfortable feelings, and, in fact, the destructive process is painless. The COMET.--Dr. Wentworth Erck lecturing lately at the Royal Dublin Society, said the distance of the comet from the surface of the sun at perihelion will not exceed five millions of miles. At this period it is calculated, having regard solely to the distance of the comet from the surface of the sun and from the earth, that the brightness of the comet will be 3.600 times greater than at the time of its discovery, when it was equal to an eighth magnitude

the estimated annual produce would be levied, which revenue instead of going in the pockets of a class, would be expended in the interests of the country. He would grant compensation to the landlords as a matter of "conventional justice." He reckoned the landlords' share of the property in the land at 20 years' purchase of half the present annual rental-140,000,000, which sum he would raise by a public loan at 3 per cent, the interest to be chargeable to Ireland's contribution to the Imperial revenue. Ireland would thus get rid of landlordism without touching the pockets of the English ratepayer. The present was the most opportune time since the passing of the Act of Union for the only remedy, in his opinion, was self-government for Ireland and the nationalisation of the land under the administration of an Irish Parliament. THE IRISH JUDGES AND THE ABOLITION OF TRIAL BY JURY. The Premier having stated in the House of Commons on Monday that he had received no memorial from the Irish judges relative to the new jurisdiction to be imposed upon them by the Repression of Crime Bill, a Dublin telegram says the judges again met on Wednesday. The proceedings were private; but it is understood their lordships passed a resolution reiterating the remonstrances already expressed by them and embodied in resolutions, a copy of which was forwarded to Mr. Gladstone. To prevent further mistake, the Lord Chancellor was requested and undertook to com- municate the decision arrived at to the Lord Lieutenant. A SPECIAL TRIBUNAL FOR AGRARIAN OFFENCES. It is stated that the Crown intend removing all prisoners charged with agrarian offences against whom indictments ' are found at the forthcoming assizes into the Queen's Bench Division for hearing by special tribunal. On Thursday, on the application of Mr. Peter O'Brien, Q.C., for the Crown, five prisoners charged with "Moonlighting" offences were thus removed from Kerry Assizes to the Queen's Bench Division on the fiat of the Attorney-General.

div.head: FATAL BOAT ACCIDENTS. SERIOUS LOSS OF LIFE.
div.p: FATAL BOAT ACCIDENTS. SERIOUS LOSS OF LIFE.

A distressing boating accident occurred late on Friday evening at Kent's Bank, near Grange, on the west side of Morecambe 'Bay, by which two young gentlemen lost their lives and another had a very narrow escape. It appears that Norman Chandler, son of Mr. H. Chandler, of Boarbank Mansion, Allithwaite, purchased a sailing yacht a few days ago at Preston, and had it stationed at Kent's Bank, that he and his friends might enjoy themselves in the bay during the holidays. During Whit-week young Mr. Chandler, along with Edward YOung, soa of the late Mr. J. S. Young, Abbott Hall, and Herbert Elliott, eldest son of Dr. Elliott, a retired medical gentleman living at Kent's Bank, made several excursions, and on Thursday sailed from Arnside, anchoring close to the shore at Kent's Bank. They deter- mined that on the tide rising on Friday evening they would have a trip round Humphrey Head, and anchor in a creek near Holywell. On Friday night the three young men proceeded to the yacht about ten o'clock, when there was a strong current running, accompanied by a high wind. All went well for about a mile. When making a tick the yacht collided against the bank of the channel, capsizing itself and throwing the occupants into the water. Chandler and Elliott endeavoured to make for the shore, and young took hold of the main mast. The former two were capital swim- mers, bat Elliott was rendered almost powerless by being struck with some portion of the vessel. Chandler, however, nobly assisted Elliott until- a strong wave separated them, and Elliott was lost. Chandler swam to a shallow .part of the bay where he regained his feet, and shouted to Young, who feebly responded. It is thought that as the tide rose Young crept higher up the mast, but when he was four feet from the top the mast unfortunately broke, and nothing more was heard of him. Chandler succeeded in swimming about a mile and a half, and he roused the occupants of a farmhouse, who administered stimulants to the half-drowned man. On recovering, Chandler set out with others in search of his friends. The yacht was found buried in the sand. Young's body was found on the west side of the channel, and Elliott's a mile lower down on the Morecambe side. Both bodies showed signs of a desperate struggle for life. Elliott had just completed his term of apprtnticeship as a surgeon dentist, and Young held a post on board a mer- chant vessel. Each was twenty years of age. The boat- men of the district hardly considered the craft suitable for that coast.

A Ramsgate correspondent reports that on Monday after- noon, as the harbour tug was towing a smack out to sea she came into violent collision with the Deal galley punt Knoctae, overturning her, and immersing her crew of three men in the water. Two of them were drowned, but the third was fortunately rescued. A Torquay correspondent reports that a sad boating fatality occurred in Torbay on Sunday morning. Two young men, Fred. Edwards, son of a Torquay coachbuilder, and Henry Parker, of Bromley, Kent, an assistant in a Torquay clothing establishment, went out in the bay ir, a small sail- ing boat to fish. When off Paignton the boat capsized, and both occupants were drowned. Neither the boat nor the bodies have yet been recovered. At six o'clock on Sunday evening, a number of men, residing in the neighbourhood of Southwark, were sailing down the Thames from Bankside to Erith in a barge, when the sail suddenly "jibbed," sweeping two of them into the stream. A boat was hastily lowered, but without any result, the men having disappeared. Their names are Thomas Howard, of Bear Gardens, Southwark, and W. James, a hatter, residing in Park-street, Southwark, the latter leaving a wife and family. Howard's mother, on receiving the news of her son's death, fainted, and without recovering conscious- ness died within an hour.

On Saturday evening, Mr. Benjamin Dutlin, of 41, Regency Place, Kennington, a clerk in the Post-office, St. Martin's-le-Grand, was drowned in the river Lea. The de- ceased gentleman, with two others, engaged a boat, and whilst rowing towards Tottenham, round a point, came into violent collision with another boat, the shock of which overturned their craft and threw all three occupants into the water. There were large crowds of persons on either bank, and the rescue of two of the gentlemen was effected, but although a very gallant .attempt was made to save Mr. Duffin, the effort failed. The drags were therefore pro- cured, and in a short time the body was brought to the surface.

div.head: DEATII OF GENERAL GARIBALDI.
div.p: DEATII OF GENERAL GARIBALDI.

General Garibaldi died at his island home, at Caprera, on Friday last. The deceased general, whose career has been eventful and romantic, was born at Nice, of poor parents, July 22, 1807. Having, in 1832, been implicated with Mazzini in a conspiracy against Charles Albert, King of Sardinia, he was compelled to quit his country, was again in trouble in 1834, and was condemned to death in his absence for a similar attempt. He escaped to France, and landed at Marseilles, whence he sailed in an Egyptian corvette, and offeted his services to the Bey of Tunis; but the life was not stirring enough for him, and in 1836 he fought for the Republic of Rio Grande, then at war with Brazil. He com- mended a vessel of thirty tons, with sixteen men, and having I been taken prisoner at Gualeguay, on trying to escape was cruelly treated., After being set at liberty, he again fought for Rio Grande, and, attended by his wife Anita, passed through a variety of stirring adventures. He commanded an Italian legion of 800 men against the Dictator Roses, and fought the battle of Salto Sant' Antonio. In 1847, on hear- ing of the elevation of Pius XI. to the Papacy, he offered his services, transferred in 1848 to the provisional govern- ment of Rome, Charles Albert declining them. Received with great emthusiasin at Rome, he was in the thick of the struggle which ensued when the French troops attacked that city. On the entry of the French, Garibaldi fled, the , French and Austrians. pursuing him. During the'terrible time which followed, his wife sank from exhaustion and dread. Garibaldi became a manufacturer of soap and candles on Staten Island, went to Valparaiso, and returned , to the United States. In 1854, on visiting the Tyne, he was presented by the people of Newcastle with a sword. Afterwards he settled in the island of Caprera, where he commenced farming with great success. On offering his services to the Sardinian generals he was much opposed, but was allowed to organise a bedy of Volunteer', called Alpine Chasseurs, consisting of 17,000 men; and with this force he engaged at Varese, Cainerlata, Como, Brescia, Magenta, Montebello, Soiferino, Sze. He landed at 'Marsala in May, 1860, took Palermo, marched on the mainland, and the struggle was carried from Reggio to Pizzo, to San Geevanni, Mileto, and finally to Naples, which King Francis 11. abandoned. On his march to Gaeta he met Victori Emanuel, and saluted him "King of Italy." Capna and Gaeta afterwards capitulated The cession of his native city Nice to France caused him deep sorrow. He published at Palermo, July 26th 1862, a revolutionary address to the Hungarians, inciting them to revolt,.possibly with the hope that such a movement would divert a large body of the Austrian troops from Venetia. But the effect of this proclamation was neutralised by a public letter fron General Klapka, addressed to Garibaldi, in which he demonstrated that any rising of the Hungarian people at that juncture would be ruinous to their cause. Garibaldi, who was not to be easily thwarted, joined a body of Volunteers at Ficuzza, a forest district, about twenty miles from Palermo, August Ist. General Cialdini was sent by the government at Turin to check this hasty and ill ad- vised movement; but before he arrived, Garibaldi and his followers had crossed in two French steamers from Catania to Melita, a small port on the Calabrian coast. They were followed by a strong body of the Royal troops under Colonel Pallavacino, and were attacked on the mountain plateau of Aspromonte, when they surrendered, Garibaldi himself being severely wounded bya rifle bullet in the ankle. On account of his services in the cause of Italian In- dependence in 1860, he was pardoned, and he returned to Caprera. In the spring of 1864 Garibaldi visited England. During the campaign of 1866 Garibildi again took tbe field, was engaged in operations in the Tyrol, sustained a severe repulse from the Austrains, July 22, and retired upon the Sow. This reverse he retrieved July 23, and was preparing to advance, when the war was brought to a close, and Gari- baldi retired to Caprera. The year 1867 was a still more disastrous one for Garibaldi. In spite of the reserve main- tained by the Italian Government, he determined to complete if possible, the unification of Italy. Accordingly he revived the agitation on the Roman question, and openly organised invasion of the States of the Church. The Government re- solved to suppress this movement, and accordingly its leader was arrested at Asinalunga, by order of the Minister Ratazzi, on Sept. 24. Garibaldi was taken in the first instance to ' Alessandria, but was afterwards permitted to return home to Caprera, in the neighbourhood of which island a man-of-war was stationed in order to prevent the escape of the revolu- tionary chief. This vigilence was, however, unavailing, as Garibaldi escaped on the 14th October, and proceeding to Florence, harangued the populace and started on the 22nd, to join the insurgent bands on the Roman frontier, M the

head of four battalions of Volunteers he defeated the Pon- tifical troops at Monte Rotondo (Oct. 26;; bat on the 4th November the Garibaldians again encountered, at Mentana, the Pontifical troops, who had been reinforced by a portion of the French Expeditionary Corps, and suffered a speedy and crushing defeat, thanks mainly, according to the official re port of General de Failly, to the suneriority of the Chasse- pot rifle, which "did wonders" on this memorable occasion. Garibaldi was arrested at Figliene, on his journey to Caprera, and carried to the fortress of Verignano, near Spezzia. The General protested against this act, and claimed the protection due to an Italian Deputy and an American citizen. He was set at liberty on the 26th, and retired to his island home, which he again left on hearing of the downfall of the French Empire and the establishment of the Republic, when, hastening to France, he placed his sword at the disposal of the Government of the National Defence. He landed at Marseilles October 7, 1870, arrived at Tours, the seat of the Government Delegation, two days later, and on the 16th was nominated to the command of the irregular forces in the VOges. In February, 1871, Garibaldi was returned a deputy to the National Assembly for Paris and several of the departments, but at the preliminary sitting of that body at Bordeaux, on the 12th, the General, "loving the Republic, but hating the priesthood," ungraciously gave in his resignation. He also resigned the command of the army of the Vosges, and soon afterwards took his departure for Caprera. In the year 1874 the fact was made public that Garibaldi was in necessitous circumstances, whereupon offers of pecuniary assistance were made to him by several of his admirers in England, Scotland, and the United States. Some of these offers he accepted, but he declined, in not very respectful language, to accept a national gift which was voted to him in the Chamber of Deputies by 207 votes against 25 (December 19). Being elected a member of the Italian Parliament, he emerged from his island retreat and proceeded to Rome' where he took his seat amid much popular enthusiasm, January 25, 1875. Since then he has been engaged in promoting a project for the deviation of the Tiber, and for the improvement of the Roman Campagna. In April, 1876, he wrote a letter to Signor Depretis announcing his acceptance of the donation of 100,000 lire, presented to him by the nation and the king.

div.head: ILLUSTRIOUS iinsimN.
div.p: ILLUSTRIOUS iinsimN.
BY WILLIAM FRANCIS. No. XXIII.—DANIEL. O'CONNELL : TAKING HIS SEAT.

The history of Catholic Emancipation, to which we have from time 'to time directed the attention of our readers, is a very instructive one. The lessons are written in such bold type that the dullest historical student cannot fail to read them. We have seen, in the course of our studies, the pride of a great soldier and the strong conservatism of a great statesmen bending or breaking beneath the imperious neces- sity of an unseen power. What is the lesson of this? Clearly one of distrust and one of faith—of distrust in men, of faith in principles. Pitt pawned his honour for the accomplish- ment of Catholic Emancipation, and he lost it. Wellington took cffice to prevent Catholic Emancipation, and he accom- plished it. The reason for this is plain. It was not because these men were untruthful, false to their convictions and traitors to their cause, but because there was a power ;Wye and around them mightier than they were—a power break- ing the great heart, bending the strong will, taming the boastful tongue—a power that carried on the cause in spite of its enemies and in spite of its friends. That power has been variously described. Politicians call it "the growth of public opinion." Moralists describe it as "the inherent force of a just cause." Religionlets designate it "The Providence of God." Well, all are right. It is God who. has established the law by virtue of which the right is ever tending to realisation, and who teaches by the stern logic of events the blindest and stabbornest of men. "I have nothing to fall back upon," was the wail of the miserable king. "The sari of Eaglani has set for ever," was the less selfish lament of his old adviser, Lord Eldon. Poor men The royal George could not see that there is ever the en- circling atmosphere of the Divine care to fall back upon, and the Lord Chancellor that Legislative Acts could as easily prevent the rising of to-morrow's sun as lessen, towards the next generation, the Divine love which is shed on all the I ages with impartial beneficence. And unless history gene- I rally, and this intricate and humiliating story in particular, ' has taught us this lesson, we have studied it to little pur- pose, and history is to us, to use the memorable phrase of Plankett, "no better than an old almanac." The "Catholic Relief Bill," though not a perfect measure, was considered a great legislative achievement. Its liberality and completeness won great praise from the Whigs, who were then in Opposition; but it had one serious flaw, an unworthy contrivance which, by a certain turn of phrase, excluded O'Connell until re-elected. No second opinion existed among the Whigs on this point. It was re- garded by them as sheer infatuation abortively to endeavour thus to shut out the man by whom confessedly the door had been broken in. Spring Rice, who loved him not, said truly "that instead of excluding him they should pay him to come into Parliament, and rather buy a seat for him than let him remain oat." Daring the present Parliament, when Charles Bradlaugh, the elected of Northampton, claimed his seat, we witnessed the not very edifying performance of a "Comedy of Esters." Let us see how the same comedy was performed in 1829, when Peel and Harcourt were the prin- cipal actors, and not Sir Stafford Northcote, Mr. Newdegate, Mr. Gorst, and such like staunch and consistent champions of Christianity. Gazing upon this. picture and then on that, we are forced to the melancholy conclusion that religions intolerance and bigotry have not as yet disappeared before the growth of intelligence and national advancement. When O'Connell was returned for Clare, Parliament was still in session, but he did not seem in any hurry to cross the Channel for the purpose of calming his seat. He con- tented himself with franking letters, and delighting the multitude by allowing them to call him "The Member." All daring the autumn lively debates arose at every dinner table as to whether he would attempt to take his seat. In one of these convivial discussions Plunkett asked Chief Baron O'Grady what he thought. His learned brother re- plied, "I think he will, although he said he would." It was not, however, until the 15th of May that he pro- ceeded to the House to assert his right. It was well known that on this particular day the " Man of the People" would go down to the House, and great crowds filled the public ways from Chaning Cross to St. Stephens, anxious to see the great Irish Agitator. The House of Commons itself was crowded in every part. The galleries were full of spec- tators. A great number of Peers were present. The excite- ment was unprecedented. At the proper time O'Connell presented himself to be sworn at the table of the House, by Lords 'Ebrington and Duncannon. He was not after all the first Catholic member who so presented himself, for Lord Surrey, the son of the Duke of Norfolk had been elected for Horsham during the Easter recess, and had taken his seat, but the strongest interest of course was attached to the appearance of O'Connell. The Clerk offered the oaths, which had been repealed by the late Act—one the oath of supremacy to the effect that "the King is head of the Church," the other that "the sacrifice of the Mass is impi- ous and abominable." Mr. Peel, apparently to gratify his spite against his old antagonist, had cunningly and dexter- ously inserted a clause in the Relief Bill admitting only such Catholics as should after the commencement of the Act be returned as members to the House of Commons. O'Connell objected to take the oaths as presented, and waving away the pasteboards on which they were fixed said to the Clerk, "You will be pleased to inform the Speaker that Ido not think lam bound to take these oaths.' The Clerk communicated the objection to the Speaker, who had, of course, made up his mind what to do and say. He ad- dressed the Hbuse, declaring his opinion "that the election having taken place under the old law, the oaths imposed by the old law must be taken to entitle any member to sit in that House. The House might be appealed to by petition from without, or by the question being raised within the House itself. Meantime Mr. O'Connell must withdraw." As soon as O'Connell had withdrawn, Mr. Brougham moved "that he should be recalled in order t 3 be heard in regard to his claim." Everyone was aware that he must be heard. As it required some consideration whether he should be heard at the table or at the bar, the debate was adjourned from the present Friday to Monday, the 18th. On that day Mr. O'Connell spoke at length at the bar, and astonished some of his hearers, as much by the gentlemanly moderation of his tone and manner as by the strength of his pleas. When he finished opinion was very much divided as to his construction .of the case, and some proposed that as there appeared even to the lawyers to be doubt, Mr. O'Connell should have the benefit of the doubt, and be at once ad- mitted on taking the oath. But the Solicitor-General moved that Mr. O'Connell was not entitled to sit without first taking the oath of supremacy. The question was pressed to a division, when the numbers were 190 to 160 in !avow of O'Connell's exclusion. When Mr. O'Connell appeared at the bar the next day to hear the decision of the House, he was asked whether he was ready to take the oath of su- p r emacy. He requested permission to look at the oath, and

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

About 50 writs of ejectment were about to be served on Saturday on Colonel Purefoy's estate, county Tipperary. By the intervention of some of the Roman Catholic clergy a friendly settlement was effected, the tenants agreeing to pay one year's rent and half the costs at once, so that none of the ejectments were carried out. Several of the Tipperary electors whose names are attached to the requisition calling upon Mr. P. J. Smyth to resign his seat in Parliament deny that they either signed the document or authorised any one else to sign on their behalf. _ _

A telegram from Athlone says • that a few nights ago a Roman Catholic priest, the Rev. Martha Davies, of Bally- foran, was subjected to insult and assault by a party of Moonlighters, whom he had fallen ist with on his way home and had ordered to disperse. A Boyle correspondent telegraphs that in consequence of private information received by the authorities that attacks were contemplated on the residences of several landlords in the neighbourhood, small detachments of military have been sent to occupy Rockingham Castle, the property of Colonel King-Harman; Kilronan Castle, the property of Lady Tenison ; and Kingsborough House, the property of Captain Gethins. A special correspondent in Ireland, in describing the con- dition of the Labour League movement, says that harvest prospects in Longford and in the adjoining counties of West- meath, Roscommon, aud King's County, are excellent. The open winter has t een followed by an equally favourable spring. Grass lands present a most luxuriant appearance, and both cereals and potatoes., although late, are remarkably healthy. Rents are being paid everywhere, a reduction about equivalent to that made in the Land Courts being almost universally granted. Mr. P. J. Smyth, M.P., in a letter to the Dublin papers respecting the Kihrtainham Treaty, says :—" 'Treaty' is a misnomer; surrender is the proper word. The cotnmunica- tion came from Mr. Parnell uninvited." Mr. Smyth refers to Robert Emmet, Smith O'Brien, and O'Leary, and Kick- ham, and says "that if they had made promises to refrain from rebellion and that they would use their organisation in support of the Government, Emmet would never have been executed; a vessel of war would have been despatched to convey him back to home and liberty. O'Leary and Kick- ham would have been unconditionally released. The public have a right to know all about this transaction, for which the annals of Irish patriotism furnish no parallel." The Limerick Chronicle reports a most interesting scene at Adare Manor, the residence of Lord Dunraven. It revives a hope that amicable , relations tray alit be established be- tween landlords and tenants. Some time ago, his Lord- ship having expressed a desire to facilitate in any way the working of the Land Act, his agent, Mr. Horace Townsend, proposed that the new valuations of the h)ldings should be made at his expense. This generous offer was acceded to, and Mr. Hurst, a highly-qualified valuer, made a field- to-field val dation. In many instances the tenants were not only satisfied with the reductions which he I recommended, but expressed such a grateful pleasure that he made a further redaction of 31 per cent. This most gratifying arrangement was ratified and commemorated by a fote at the mansion, at which all the tenants were enter- tained, and showed the utmost joy. IRISH LAW APPOINTMENTS.—The Press Association Dublin correspondent says the Right Hon. the Attorney- General for Ireland has accepted the judgeship of the Queen's Bench Division, rendered vacant by the promotion of Lord Fitzgerald to the Court of Appeal in England. It is stated, however, that the right honourable gentleman will not quit his post in the House of Commons until the Pre- vention of Crime Bill has passed through committee. Mr. Andrew M. Porter, Solicitor-General, will succeed to ..the Attorney-Generalship, and Mr. John Naish, Q.C., the present law adviser to the Castle, will take the position of Solicitor- General. Mr. Naish will, it is stated, offer himself as a candidate for the representation of Mallow, vacant by the promotion of the Attorney-General. Mr. W. D. Andrews, QC., of the North-east bar, who on two occasions contested the County of Down in the Liberal interest, is named for the law advisership. TRIAL FOR MURDER IN DUBLIN.

The Dublin Commission Court was crowded on Wednes- day, when two young men named Brennan and Martin were indicted for murdering Joseph M`Mahon. They were to- gether in a public-house, and, a shot being heard, the de- ceased was found lying dead on the floor. The accused men in trying to escape were captured. They alleged it was a case of accidental shooting, but it is supposed to have been a Fenian outrage. The jury, after deliberating from half- past five until eleven o'clock, failed to agree upon a verdict.

div.head: MR. DAVITT AND HIS CRITICS
div.p: MR. DAVITT AND HIS CRITICS

Mr. Michael Davitt replying to a pamphlet entitled "The Truth about the Land League," by Mr. H. 0. Arnold Forster, says he can well understand what he is told of the evil effect which the pamphlet has had. At a time when the efforts of good men on both sides of the Irish Sea are directed to the allaying of passion, it comes to stimulate and embitter animosities. Its evident purpose—and what purpose can be more wicked? —is to pander to prejudice and to arouse hate. The pamphlet is an attempt to prove that the Land League and all who have been connected with it advocated outrage, mutilation, plunder, murder, and every other crime. Mr. Davitt emphatically denies this, and challenge Mr. Forster to put his finger on one single word he wrote or one single sentence he uttered in connection with the Land League movement in which he had, directly or indirectly, counselled outrage; and he defies him to name one single occasion on which he did otherwise than decry the resort to force, and protest against outrage and murder.
MR. DAVITT'S SCHEME FOR THE SETTLEMENT OF THE LAND QUESTION.

Mr. Davitt addressed a meeting in Liverpool on Tuesday night. There was, he said, an intelligent, resolute, and practical spirit abroad in Ireland, which could be arrested by just and timely concessions. The force that could guide that spirit to safe and moral action and shape its ends to beneficial work for Ireland consistel in the character of the men who were now the leaders of the Irish people. From Mr. Parnell downwards they were nearly all young men pledged to work out the social and political regeneration of their country. As to the difference between himself and Mr. Parnell it was only this, Mr. Parnell advocated peasant Proprietary, and he (the speaker) was in favour of land be- e 'ming the national property of Ireland. The State would under his plan simply be the steward of the national property, and for the use of the property. a taz of say 10 per cent upon

div.head: GARIBAuDI'S REMAINS:
div.p: GARIBAuDI'S REMAINS:

The following is a translation of the —.autograph letter written by Garibaldi from Caprera on the 27th September, 1877, to Dr. Prandina, regarding the cremation of his body: " Mio carisshno Prandina,—You kindly undertake the cre- mation of my body; lam grateful to you. On the road leading from this house northwards to the seashore there is' at a distance of 1,300 paces to the left, a depression in the ground, bounded by a vall. Upon that corner you will erect a pile of timber, two metres high, of acacia, linden, myrtle, and other aromatic woods. On the pile you will place an iron couch, and upon that the uncovered bier, with my remains upon it, dressed in the red shirt. A handful of ashes shall be preserved in an urn of any kind, and this is to be placed in the little sepulchere which contains the ashes of my daughters, Rosa and Annita.—Yours always, G. GARIBALDI."

div.head: GARIBALDI'S SWORD.
div.p: GARIBALDI'S SWORD.

The Press Association is authorised to state that Colonel Chambers, the English officer to whom Garibaldi gave the sword he wore in the Tyrolese war in 1867, has offered to return the weapon to Italy, with the flag which Garibaldi had at Monte Video.

POLITICAL ITEMS. The Committee of the House of Lords on the Irish Land Act will resume its sittings on the 13th inst. Lord Randolph Churchill has, it is stated, determined to take no part in the proceedings of the House of Commons during the remainder of the present session. Daily whips are being issued by the Conservatives re- questing the attendance of their supporters in the house during the discussion of the Prevention of Crime Bill. A series of public demonstr ttions is being organised in the principal provincial towns, under the auspices of the Demo- cratic Federation, to protest against the new Coercion Bill for Ireland. At a meeting of Conservatives of the Pembroke Boroughs, Mr. H. Harben, deputy-chairman of the Prudential Assur- ance Company, was unanimously adopted as the candidate of the party at the next election.
The -Irish party will renew on report, and, probably on the third reading of the Prevention of Crime Bill, the question of excluding treason and treason-felony from the first clause of the measure.

The Standard believes that when the Arrears Bill again comes under discussion an effort will be made to show that Mr. Gladstone has under-estimated the arrears of rent. It is computed by competent authorities that the amount of unpaid rents in Ireland which will have to be made good by the State is between three and four million pounds. petition is now in course of signature at the House of Commons, urging that as the opportunities of private mem- bers are being sacrificed to Irish business, and as the Minis- try are unable to introduce their promised measures on the subjects of licensing and local administration, the Govern- ment should introduce a suspensory licensing bill, to remain in force until they are enabled to deal with the subject. The following English and Scotch Liberals voted in the minority against the first clause of the Prevention of Crime (Ireland) Bill, "as amended," which includes treason and treason-felony in the list of offences to be tried without a jury :—W. E. Briggs, H. Broadhurst, J. Cowen, Dr. Web- ster Professor Rogers, J. C. Thompson, A. Arnold, H. Labouchere, Whalley, Bryce, Sir Wilfred Lawson, and Mr. Hopwood. Mr. Bradlaugh has consented to await the issue of Mr. Firth's resolution, which demands that the electors of Northampton may be heard at the bar. He has, however, taken into account the strong probability that, owing to the urgency of Irish business, the night secured by Mr. Firth may be appropriated for Government. In such case, we un- derstand, Mr. Baadlaugh is not further inclined to delay the active prosecution of his claim to take his seat.— Observer. Txm CARNA.RVON BOROUGHS ELECTION.—The election expenses of Mr. Sorton Parry, the independent candidate for the Carnarvon boroughs, were returned last night at £1,940, £5OO in excess of the return made by Mr. Jones Party, the successful Liberal candidate. Solicitors' charges absorb nearly £6OO, agents £2BO, messengers and bill posters £314, conveyances £l4, public meeting £lB. and telegrams 95. The candidate's share of returning officer's expenses was £75. MR. BRIGHT'S REPRESENTATION OF BIRMINGA.AM. —On Tuesday, a meeting took place of the executive committee of the 800 of Birmingham, under the presidency of Mr. George Dixon, "to take into consideration the question of celebrating the 25th anniversary of Mr. Bright's representa- tion of the town in Parliament.* It was unanimously re- solved that the event be celebrated, and that the celebration include two parts—the first to be a demonstration in recog- nition of the respect in which the right honourable gentle- man is held by the people' not only of Birmingham but of the nation: secondly, the erection of some memorial in the town which shall permanently record the feelings of gratitude and confidence which are felt for him in the borough. ' The general condition of public business in the House of Commons is such that 'private members make very little progress with their measures. The orders of the day in the last Parliamentary programme numbered 33, of which only a very small proportion could be reached the other evening, partly through the system of blocking, which causes some delay in the progress of legislation, and provokes retaliation among members. In some few cases, where a bill has been read a second time, recourse has been had to the often con- demned half-past twelve rule, in order to prevent it being considered in committee. A strong case in point is that of the Churchwardens Admissions Bill, introduced by Mr. Monk, M.P., which was read a second time as far back as February 16th. Mr. Beresford-Hope has adopted obstructive tactics to prevent the bill from going up to the House of Lords, where it originated. Last year this bill was blocled for practically the whole session. The present session has produced a crop of 146 public bills, of which only eight have yet received the royal assent. Thirty-four of them are Government bills.

div.head: FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.

A fire at Quebec has destroyed the Grand Trunk Railway buildings and a great quantity of merchandise. A journal in Posen states that the police have discovered a Nihilist " mine " under one of the streets in Moscow.

A telegram from Ttipoli states that defensive works are being carried on there with great activity and enthusiasm. An order has been issued by the Indian Government insisting on a stricter enforcement of the law against lotteries.

A body of Mexican cavalry have had a severe engagement with the Apache savages. Forty or 50 of the latter were killed or taken prisoners. Princess Louise has arrived at Quebec, where she has been received by the Marquis of Lorne. Enthusiastic crowds met to cheer her Royal Highness on her arrival. An official decree has been published in Mexico abolish- ing the export duties on gotd and silver coin, bars, and ore, and increasing the import duties on all foreign gold by two per cent.

Complaints have been made in the Spanish Chamber of Deputies that England has not fulfilled her promise to lower the alcoholic sale for Spanish wines in exchange fpr the abolition of differential duties.

The Japanese mission which will shortly visit St. Peters- burg will enter into negotiations with the Russian Govern- ment in regard to the opening of the Black Sea ports to Japanese trade, and the establishment of tea plantations in the Caucasus.

The Calcutta correspondent of the Times says the reports of cruelties inflicted on Armenians are confirmed by intelligence from Mandalay. Some Armenian and other ladies, inclusive of two nuns, are said to have been forced to take fresh oaths of allegiance to the Queen before an image of Guatama.

The iron strike in the Unitad States is reported to be un- changed, except that an attempt is to be made at Cleveland to start a rolling mill with non-union bands at the old rites. The police and militia are in readines3 to protect the men if the strikers interfere, but the strikers deny any intention to molest.

Notwithstanding the presence of Prince Bismark, tho Reichstag on Tuesday rejected all the proposed increases of the customs duties. The result of the voting is, however, attributed to an accidental predominance of Liberals amongst the members present, and it is believed that on the third reading the Government Bill will be restored to its original form.

cotting as advocated by the Land League.—Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT said he would state distinctly the positionof the Government with regard to this fourth clause. They would not accept any amendment which would be inconsistent with the putting down of boycotting, and that was the test he was going to apply to every amendment on this clause. Boycotting did exist, and must be put down. Their thcory was that a man should be relieved from boycotting, not by the plenary authority of Mr. Dillon and his colleagues, but by the law of the land.—Mr. GLADSTONE pointed out the inconvenience of discussing the whole clause on each amendment. The Government were not bound to the particular working of the clause, and would insist on the purport of it. He would say, without hesita- sion-, however, that the Government were prepared to deal with the question in regard to Ireland on the same principle as they bad dealt with intimidation in England.—Mr. HEALY warned the Government that boycotting in cases where land-grabbinc, took place would still be pursued by the Dish people, and, in fact, that a coach-and-four would be driven through the Act of Parliament.—Mr. PARNELL moved to report progress—Sir Was. HARCOURT said the Government could not assent to the motion, but, of course, he was aware that at that hour (20 minutes to 6) hon. members opposite had tile matter in their own hands.—The Committee divided on the question of reporting progress, when there voted—For reporting progress, 30 • against, 250.—As it was now live minutes to six, the Committee stood adjourned. HOUSE OF LOBDS.—THURSDAY.

JUSTICES JURISDICTION BILL.—Lord BRAMWELL moved the second reading of the Justices' Jurisdiction Bill, the ob- ject of which is to enlarge the jurisdiction of Courts of Quarter Session by empowering them to try certain cases of burglary and forgery.—The Lord CHANCELLOR approved of the principle of the bill, but suggested that time should be taken for its due consideration before going into Committee. Lord COLERIDGE urged that although many trumpery cases of burglary and forgery were sent to the assizes, some of them required the very best judicial talent and experience, and be thought the bill before the House was not surrounded with sufficient safeguards. The bill was read a second time. THE COMBINED FLUET AT ALEXANDRIA.—The Earl of RAVENSWORTH, who described the position of the combined fleet at Alexandria as critical, wished to know precisely where it was lying, whether the old forts were fully armed, and whether they commanded the whole of the harbour,— The Earl of NownrunooK, in reply, assured their Lordships that the Government had sufficient knowledge of the fortifl- -catioas of Alexandria and the position of the earthworks not to feel the slightest apprehension with regard to the safety of the fleet.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TIMRSDkY.

EGYPT.—Sir C. DILKE, in reply to Mr. Bourke, said he still adhered to the statement made by him on June 2nd that the earthworks in Alexandria harbour were not armed in any way, and he denied that at the time he spoke there were three 18-ton guns and 20 64-pounders in the earth- works. He would add that the Admiralty had sufficient in- formation with regard to the fortifications of Alexandria not to entertain the slightest apprehension with regard to the fleet. THE PROPOSED CONFERENCE.-Sir C. 'DILKE, in reply to Mr. A. Bartlett, said there was no foundation in the rumour that the Governments of England and France had presented a joint Note to the Porte insisting on the proposed Con- ference.

POSTCARDS.—Mr. FewcErr, replying to a question, said he could not assent to allowing other cards to be sent through the post with halfpenny stamps affixed as postcards. With respect to foreign postcards, any postcard with the proper stamps could be used for transmission abroad. PREVENTION OF CRIME (IRELAND) BILL.—Upon the House resuming the discussion of Mr. C. Russell's amend- ment to clause 4 of the Prevention of Crime Bill, the HOME SECRETARY stated that the Government had considered the suggestions made on the previous day as to a limitation of the intimidation section. The Government were willing to introduce the words "provided that the circumstances show that such words were spoken or acts done with a view to or in consequence of the matters mentioned in sub-sections A and B of the section."—Mr. PA,VNELL argued that the concession was intended to throw dust in the eyes of the Committee, and said it would be the duty of the Irish members to oppece the clause so long as open combination on the part of the tenant farmers was prevented.—Mr. LABOUCHERE suggested that the clause should be passed over for the cresent, but the PRIME MINISTER replied that the Government were determined to legislate against boycotting. They deemed it their first duty to see that the legislation should be sufficient and effec- tive; but they were anxious not to carry it beyond what was necessary.—Upon a division Mr.-Russell's amendment was rejected by 268 to 45.—Mr. PARlicimr, then moved an amend- ment the object of which was to limit the operation of the clause, but the Home Secretary refused to accept it, and it was eventually withdrawn.

div.head: REFORM BILL OF 1832.
div.p: THE REFORM BILL OF 1832.

Fifty years have now elapsed since the passing of the Reform Bill, and it has been suggested that the anniversary should be celebrated in some fitting.' maneer. Owing to the recent murder of Lord Frederick Cavendish, however, and the present condition of business in the House of Commons, it is understood that should any public celebration be decided upon it will be deferred until after the close of the session. It may be interesting to note the names of the surviving members of Parliament by which the Reform Bill of 1832 was enacted, with the constituencies they repreeeeiteel in June.lB32 :—The Dukes of Northumberland (Beeralston), Devonshire (Derbyshire), and Wellington (Aldeburgh); the Marquises of Cholmondeley (Castle Rising), and Donegal (Antrim County); the Earls of Shaftesbury (Dersetshire), Strafford (Milborne Port), Grey (Northumberland), Mansfield (Woodstock), Amherst (East Grinstead), Verulam (Newport, Cornwall), Harrowby (Liverpool), Mexborough (Galton), Meath (Dublin County), and Enniskillen (Fermanagh County); Viscounts Eversley (Hants), Halifax (Wareham), and Portman (Dorsetshire) ; Lords Ebury (Chester), Cottesloe (Buckinghain), Forester (Wenlock), Brougham (Southwark), Stafford (Pontefract), and Mostyn (Flintshire); Lord Edward Thynne (Weobley), Sir Hugh Owen (Pem- broke), Sir George Phillips (Steyning), Sir Edward Dering (New Romney), Sir Denham Norreys Mallow);( Messrs. P. H. Howard (Carlisle), W. L. Maberlv (Shaftesbury), F. Barnes (Dunwich), Joseph Yorke (-Reigate), W. Lyon (Seaford), A. Lefroy (Longford County), R. Etwall (Andover), and C. R. M. Talbot (Glamorganshire)-37 in all, of whom only the iast, Mr Talbot, is now a member of the House of Commons. If Mr. 11. Ross, of Rossie, M.P. for the Aberdeen Burghs in 1831-32, is not dead, his name should be added. The peers still living who were entitled to seats in the Upper House at the date of the passing of the Reform Bill were the present Dukes of Buccleuch and Abercorn, the Earls of Berkeley (who has never taken his seat), Chichester, Stradbroke, Sydney, Redesdale, Mount- cashell, and Selkirk (of whom the last two were, as they still are, representative peers for Ireland and Scotland respec- tively), Viscount Falkland, and Lord Gardner. The Earl of Sandwich, Viscount Torrington, and Lord de Tabley had uceeeded to their titles, but were minors.
