div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 10, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 10, 1882.
MISCEL LAN FOIJS.

The Res% W. Boyd Carpenter was on Wednesday installed , as canon of St. George's Chapel, Windsor. , The Marquis of Hartington, M.P. has definitely promised to visit Darwen on Wednesday, the 21st inst., for the pur- pose of opening the new Market Hall. On Saturday night, as seven boys were rowing in a boat on Penrhyn river, near Plymouth, it suddenly filled and sank. One of the lads was drowned, the others narrowly escaped. On Wednesday, at the James Watt Dock, at present under construction at Greenock, the jib of the steam crane broke, killing one man instantly in its fall. A boy and a man were also injured. A mass open-air meeting was held in the Bull Ring, Ply- mouth, on Wednesday night, to celebrate the jubilee of the passing of the Reform Bill. Resolutions were passed acknowledging the benefits conferred by the Act, and ad- , vocating the completion of the franchise. A VENERABLE MEMBER.-Mr. Isaac Holden, the new M.P. for the North West Riding is a hale and hearty man of seventy-five. He has recently built a palace at a cost of £lOO,OOO. On a recent birthday he gave a feast to his family, and when they came to the table his daughters found in each of their napkins a cheque for £50,000. Early on Tuesday morning, two fashionable houses in Kingston were partly destroyed by a most destructive fire, in which an old lady named Johnston was burnt to death. All the other inmates-were safely removed, but the flames pre- vented the rescuers from reaching Mrs. Johnston, who only arrived at the house from Dublin the previous night. The Bishop of Bath and Wells commenced his annual visitation at Bridgwater on Tuesday, and, alluding to the work of the Salvation Army, he remarked that it was an agency which should be dealt fairly and kindly with, and if its followers were met in that spirit by the Church of Eng- land they might be led to co-operate and ally themselves with It.

Writing in condemnation of pigeon matches, which he characterises as simply detestable, Lord Shaftesbury says no expressions of abhorrence on his part will be of any avail. When he was young such expressions would have been put down to impertinence; but now they would be called twaddle. On Wednesday a meeting of the Preston Watch Com- mittee was held to appoint to the office of claief constable of the borough, in place of Mr. Oglethorpe, resigned, one of the seven candidates selected a fortnight ago. It was agreed unanimously that Captain Gore Little, superintendent of the Cheshire Constabulary, be appointed. The new chief constable is 30 years of age. He will at once enter on his duties, at a salary of £350 per annum. Tne; PRINCESS OF WALES AND THE LEICESTER INCIDENT. —The Princess of Wales has written a letter declaring her annoyance at the published version of the disagreeable inci- dent which occurred on the occasion of the recent Royal visit to Leicester. The Princess was reported to have prodded an ill-mannered drunkard with her parasol, but Her Royal Highness says her purpose really was to protect the fellow, who was being roughly treated by the police and was in danger of being trodden down by the cavalry. THE CHANNEL TUNNEL.—The report of the Select Com- mittee on the Channel, Tunnel, now in the 'hands of the Duke of Cambridge, states that, in the opinion of the majority of the members, the tunnel may, with safety to this country from danger of invasion, be made. Also that means can be devisedlor either destroying or flooding it, so as to render it useless to any enemy. Several members Orthe cemmittee held that its safety will be best secured if the 'entrance or approach is at a point of considerable distanceinland ; whilst other members believe it would be better to have the entrance near the coast, where it might be defended by the fleet in case of danger. ALLEGED DOUBLE MURDER AT Bitrrose.—At Skipton, Yorkshire, OR Saturday, Matthew Jackson Hunter was charged with the murder of his wife and child, on April 25. Evidence was given to show that the prisoner went for a walk with the two children on the day named, and was afterwards found lying in a field with his troat cut and his wife and child dead beside him. The prisoner, who could not speak, was committed to the assines for trial. -TERRIBLE ACCIDENT IT A MARRIAGE.—Two BROTHERS KILLED.—A sad accident marred the rejoicings on Wednes- day at Brynmally, a few miles from 'Wrexham, on the occasion of the marriage of one of the daughters of Mr'. Clayton a large coal owner in North Wales. During the firing Clayton, cannon in honour of the event the cannon bnrst into several pieces, one of which struck two brothers named Ellis, dreadfully mutilating them, and killing them on the spot, one was single, but the other was married. A LONDON FIRM DEFRAUDED ,OF .£2,ooo.—The well known London firm of Dimecq and Co., extensive shippers of Spanish wines have been defrauded of £2,000 by two Spaniards of gentlemanly appearance, who presented to them 'what purported to be a letter of credit to that amount issued in the ordinary course of business by a firm in Cadiz. Believing the letter to be authentic, Messrs. Dimecq and Co. gave a cheque for the sum stated on their bankers, and they did not. discover it was a forgers until after the swindlers had cashed the cheque and returned to Spain, where it is doubtful if they can te reached by English 'justice for such an offence. ' ATTEMPTED MURDER AT Hnize—On Saturday a mechanic at Hull, named John Barnfather, who lived unhappily with his wife, and seems to have formed an impression that his wife's sister had some responsibility in the matter, went to the house where his sister-in-law, Ann Jane Jackson, lived as a domestic servant, and made a murderous attack upon her with a clasp knife. After inflicting several wounds he proceeded to the police station, and, charged himself with stabbing a woman. The police authorities refused to believe 'hie story; but as he was persistent he was locked up on a -charge of drunkenness, and in a shert time it was found that i the man's self-accusation was really well founded. 1 'THE ',ELMO& MURDER—The adjourned inquest on the body of John Carlisle retired chernict, who was fatally stabbed by Richard Wells at Fulham, was resumed on Tues- day. The evidence showed that deceased returned from Epsom races with the accused to a house in Moor-Park-road, the landlady of which was. Mrs. Sykes. They sent out for a bottle of whisky in the evening, and later on both men went •into the back garden, where a fight took place. Deceased was struck on the head with a whisky bottle, and afterwards stabbed. Mrs. Sykes said -she did not know the origin of the quarrel. After hearing medical and police evidence, the jury found a verdict of "Wilful Murder" againstaichard Wells. TERRIBLE WIFE MURDER IN LONDON.—A shocking murder was committed shortly before 'five o'clock on Wednesday afternoon in Waterloo Place, St. George's-in-the- East, London, the victim being Elizabeth Sullivan, wife of Timothy Sullivan, a waterside labourer. Sullivan went home the worse for drink, and on being appealed to by his wife to give up drinking, he picked up a bar of iron which did duty for a poker and threw it at her. The weapon struck her on the head, shattering the temple bones, and she fell to the ground. The police were summoned on the alarm being given by Sullivan's son, and medical assistance was pro- cured, but when the doctor arrived the unfortunate woman was dead. Sullivan left the house immediately after delivering the fatal blow, but was shortly afterwardscaptured and conveyed to Leman street Police Station. On being charged he said he did not do it intentionally. A LAD Tibl-GEDY : SUIC:DE BY A NEWS BOY.—A par- ticularly sad tragedy was investigated, at the Liverpool Coroner's Court, on Saturday, when an inquest was held on the remains of a lad sixteen years of are, who appears to have committed suicide in a fit of dispair. The deceased wac a vendor of newspapers, and had been doing badly of late, and this fact preyed upon his mind. Pollee-constabe Armitage, who wee one of the witnesses called, deposed that the unfortunate lad attended an evening class for destitute children, which he (the constable) was in the habit of teaching. One day last week the boy said he had not broken his fast all day, and the kindly constable gave him three- pence to get something to eat. The story has its bright side in the humane and compassionate conduct of Constable Armitage, who was highly complimented by the coroner for the manner in which he had acted. A STRANGE WEAPON IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.— Some comment has been made amongst certain members of Parliament and officials of the House of Commons by the discovery that a well known Irish member is in the habit of carrying, at Westminster, a walking stick which contains a ' dagger of extraordinary construction. Upon a spring being touched the dagger starts up from its place, and the effect of its appearance is increased by the fact that the middle of , the blade i 3 twisted in a spiral form, which would add to lits deadly effect if brought into use. The attention of the ISerjeant-at-Arms has been called to the matter, and in turn is said to have privately taken counsel with the Speaker. Sir Henry Brand, it is understood, replied that however unusual the practice may be of carrying such a swordstick , in the House, it is not in itself illegal, although no member ' would be allowed to introduce such a weapon within the bar. The Press Association belies-es that the stick is generally left by its owner in the cloakroom downstairs whilst he is in attendance upon his parliamentary duties. THE DALTON BROOK MURDER.—The Rotherham magis- trates had again before them on Monday Aaron Leedham, sheep shear forger, and Robert Siddall, labourer, both of Sheffield, charged with being concerned in the murder of Mr. John Whitaker, farmer, of Tbrybergh, on the lath October, 1856. Aaron Leelatn, the prisoner who made the confession, was called as a witness. His evidence was almost a repetition of the statement he made to the police, which has already been published. Mr. Parker-Rhodes, for the prosecution, then asked for a remand for another week, stating that Superintendent Hammond, of the Rotherham police, had that morning received further information which justified a renewed inquiry. Mr. Hickmott, who appeared for Siddall and objected to Leedham being called as a witness, postponed his cross-examination. The prisoners were both remanded in custody. The remand caused softie excitement, as it had been expected that the prisoners would be discharged for lack of corroborative evidence. AN ELECTRIC BURGLAR DETECTOR.—At the Liverpool Police Court, on Monday, two young men named Quinn and Dodd were charged with burglary on the premises of Messrs. Henochsburg and Ellis, clothiers, Ranelagh-street. Mr. Ellis, one of the prosecutors, was awakened about four o'clock on the morning °of Whit-Snnday by the barking of his dog. He got up and went to the window, when he saw the prisoners in the act of getting through another window which they had opened. They saw him and made off, turning their attention to the premises of Messrs. Humphrey, Roberts, and Co., timber merchants, in a neighbouring street. They entered the place over the roofs of some houses, and one of them, Qainn, passed through the door of the office. This, however, was furnished with an electric indicator, which, unheard by the thief, awakened the foreman who slept on the premises. That official at once informed the police, who found Quinn hiding under a desk. Dodd was captured outside. A number of burglars' implements were found upon them. The prisoners were committed to the assizes for trial.

1 The Princess of Wales on Monday 'unveiled, in Trinity Church, Windsor, a window memorialising the escape of her Majesty from assassination on the 2nd March last. .At Godlty, Hyde, on Monday, a platelayer named William Smith attempted to commit suicide by cutting his throat, and a letter found in his pocket attributes the act to domestic troubles. He may recover. A bill was submitted to the Manx House of Keys, on Tuesday, which purposes, amongst other changes, to abolish the law of primogeniture. It was referred to a committee to be reported upon. The abundant moisture so urgently required by the crops after the arid easterly winds and hot sunshine of last week has fallen, and the prospects of farmers have already con- siderably brightened. Sir Stafford NorthcoLe presided on Saturday at a dinner of the Commercial Travellers' Benevolent Institution at Exeter. He dwelt on the importance of the commercial travellers' position as the nerves, so to speak, of our home trade. . . _

It is stated that the Empress of Austria has made arrange- ments with Lord Combermere for the use of Combermere Abbey during the hunting season for the next three years. Several of Her Majesty's favourite hunters are now at the Abbey stables. The Primitive Methodist Conference was opened at Sheffield on Wednesday, when five candidates were nominated for the office of president. Three withdrew, and the Rev. Joseph Wood, of Leeds, was elected by 124 votes to 39 re- corded for the Rev. T. Southern, of Sunderland. The Queen, It is announced, will be represented at the christening of the young German Prince at Potsdam by one of her sons, probably the Prince of Wales. Invitations to the ceremony have been accepted by the King of Saxony, the Grand Dukes of Weimar and Schwerin, the Duke of Coburg, and others. On Tuesday a deputation of artisans had an interview with Mr. Chamberlain, to urge that the Board of Trade should take action on a bill of the South-Eastern Railway, now before Parliament, to compel them to run workmen's trains. Mr. Chamberlain said that he should lay their views before the oommittee, and endeavour to attain their object. On Tuesday, the Nottingham magistrates remanded a woman named Eliza Belton, upon whom suspicion has re- cently fallen in connection with neglecting her family. Five of seven of her children have died, and on Monday night, one of the remaining two, an infant four months old, was foundjn a dreadfully emaciated condition. A woman named Hannah Smith, who formerly lived at Birkenhead, has been committed for trial at Manchester, chatged with throwing vitriol in her husband's face. The man aroused her ire by running oft with another woman named Macdonald, who was, on the 27thu1t., stabbed by the wife just before the latter threw thevitriol on her husband. _ _ _

The Hanley magistrates, on Monday, fined John James, farmer, £4 and costs ,for not repnrting the existence of swine fever on his premises. The police authorities became aware of the existence of disease in defendant's neighbourhood, and traced it to nine pigs, three of which the defendant bought, and the others were sold at various markets, but all died except one, the old sow, which was killed and con- sumed before the police could interfere. A Parliamentary return shows the amount of poor rates levied and expended during the year ended at Lady Day, 1881, the total of which whs :80,302,800. the receipts in aid being £1,038,504. It is observed that £5,578,101, or con- siderably more than one-third of the poor rate now levied, is expended for "other purposes" than the relief of the poor. The Prince of Wales telegraphed from Great Yarmouth to the Mayor of Leicester is 'follows :—" Having seen in the newspaper that the maw who ran up to our carriage has been imprisoned with hard labour, I sincerely bone that you will remit the remaind4r of the sentence at my special wish, in which the Princess fully concurs." The man has been released. _

MARRIAGE UNDER DIFFICULTIES.—An extraordinary in- cident is reported from Little Halton. An engine-stoker, named James Collier, having been prevented from getting married through his 'father hiding his clothes, next morning stopped his engine on the line, climbed up the embankment, and entered St. John the Baptist Church, where he found his bride waiting. The ceremony having been performed, the bridegroom remounted his engine and proceeded on his journey. Mr. P. T. Barnum, Mr. J. A. Bailey, his manager, and Mr. J. R. Davies, who assisted in his behalf in the removal of Jumbo from London, arrived at Liverpool in the Inman steamer City of Rome, and proceeded to Southport, as the first town of a considerable number which are to be visited for the purpose of arranging for the exhibition of the cele- brated zoological collection to which attention has lately been drawn. At Tithebarn-street Railway Station Mr. Barnum was saluted with cries of "How's Jumbo ?" Ile replied that the famous elephant was "all right in his new quarters." A CLERGYMAN CHARGED WITH GAME TRESPIES.—At Pocklington, on -Saturday, the Rev. William Edward Remfrey, curate of Low Catton, and Alexander Wallace, medical assistant at Stamford Bridge, were charged with game trespass an land belongiug to Lord Halifax, on May 2. Evidence was given to show that while the defendants were driving from Garraby to Backthorpe on the day in question, Mr. 'Remfrey shot a hare, which he took away with him in the trap. They were followed by Lord Halifax's gamekeeper, who stated that Mr. Remfrey oflered him money to say nothing about it.—The defendants were fined £2 each and costs, or in default one month's imprison- ment. CHOKED ET -.A STRAWBERRY.—An inquest was held before the Manchester City Coroner (Mr. E. lierford) .on Monday, on the-body of Mary Craven, aged 13 months, the daughter of William Craven. galvaniser, living at 44, Brad- ford-road,,Manchester. It appeared that on Friday last the mother of the child was wheeling it in a perambulator through Shudehill Market, and bought some strawberries. One was given to the deceased, who after eating a part of it began to struggle and show signs of choking. The child was immediately taken to the surgery of a medical man near, where it was found that the child was already dead. A piece of strawberry was found to have become fixed in the child's windpipe. The jury returned a verdict of acci- dental death.

GREAT RIFE IN THE PRICE ,OF A PICa uRE.—On Satur- day, at the sale rooms of Messrs. Christie, Manson, and Woods, London, the picture of "Napoleon I. in the Cam- paign of Paris," which was painted in 1862 by Meissonier, and was sold a few years ago for 1,000 guineas to Mr. Rus- kin, was bought back again by the original vendor, Mr. Henry Wallis for £5,800 guineas (6'6,080), amid a scene of the utmost excitement. The bidding was watched through- out with breathless interest, and this feeling intensified as the original price of the work wan successively doubled, trebled, quadrupled, and quintupled. When at last the hammer fell at nearly six times the sum given for the gem- like masterpiece—which measures 12in. by 9in., and has therefoas cost £56 a square inch—at the time of its exhibi- tion in the French Gallery, the sound evoked a burst of ap- plause. NIHILISTS AND FENUNS : MEETING IV LONDON.—On Sunday afternoon a meeting of Nihilist and American Fenian plenipotentiary delegates took place in London. The object was to express zympathY with the Irish agita- tors, and to consider the advisability of an official union between the two parties, who were alike seeking the total and unconditional eradication of their respective Govern- ments. A Russian delegate from Moscow, narratirby, the history of the Nihilists. declared that one-half of the Rus- sians were members, and the other half sympathised with the movement. The Nihilists now influenced Russian foreign policy. A delegate of O'Donovan Rossa's party followed, and it was decided that an official union should be established between the Nihilists and the Fenians.

CELEBRATION OF THE QUEEN'S BIRTHDAY.—In honour of the Queen's birthday, which was officially celebrated on Saturday, the Admiralty and War Offices were closed and the bells in many London churches rang merry peals. Royal salutes were fired in St. James's Park and the Tower. All the troops at present in London took part in the trooping of the colours and were inspected by the Duke of Cambridge. At Windsor the 2nd Battalion of Scots Guards proceeded in full dress to the Long Walk, and, with the 2nd Life Guards, fired a feu de joie. At Chatham the day was observed as a holiday in all the Government establishments, and the troops were reviewed by Sir Evelyn Wood. The usual Ministerial dinners .were given on Saturday. The illuminations were tasteful beyond those of former years, and the popular in- terest in the celebration was considerably increased. In Dublin the whole of the troops in the garrison paraded in review order and marched past the Lord Lieutenant. At Belfast a parade of all the troops in the garrison was held.

CHILD MURDER BY I MOTHER:A dreadful child murder was committed on Friday afternoon at Hyde, near Manches- ter. The house, 48, Cross-street, was occupied by Mr. Frederick Shawcross, a very respectable man, who was en- gaged at a miW in the town. He has a wife and several children, two of whom are young. In tbe afternoon Mr. ShawcrosS, With s,everal of the family, went out to see the Sunday scholars' procession, leaving Mrs. Shawcross in the house with the two youngest children. On their return they found one of the children, three and a half years of age, lying in a pool of blood on the floor, with a dreadful wound in the throat, and quite dead. Mrs. Shawcross, on being taxed with having killed the child, admitted that she bad done so, and made a rambling statement to the effect that it would not want bread now.. The unfortunate woman, who was arrested immediately afterwarde, had shown no signs of mental derangement. She has been committed for trial.

DISASTER OIN: BOARD THE SWIFTSURE. - The Castle Company's steamer Warwick Castle; which. arrived .at Plymouth on Wednesday from Capetown, brings intelli- gence from Madeira of a disaster on board H.M.S. Swiftsure. It appears that after leaving Plymouth three weeks ago the Swiftsure put into Vigo owing to strong weather, and pro- ceeded when the gale abated to Madeira, arriving there on the 30th ult. She at once saluted the Portuguese flat, a French frigate being already in the roads of Funchal, and it was upon tha firing of the sixteenth gun that the lamentable casualty occurred. There are eight guns of similar construction on board the Swiftsure for saluting purposes and otherwise. The gunner's mate, it is stated, was apprisel of the fact that the breech of one of the star- board guns was insecure, but be that as it may, when the tube lanyard was pulled the breach flew out and, rebound- ing to the opposite gun, struck Charles James, gunner's mate in the side, killing him instantly. One of the men at the same gun had his right arm broken, and it was at once amputated by the ship's surgeon. Another man had his eye burnt, and it is thought be may lose its sight. Another man's face was disfigured with powder. The deceased was interred on Saturday last in Funchal Cemetery. Captain Aitcbeson, the officers, and most of the crew, and mmy of the officers and men of the French frigate, were present. A private official inquiry- was held, which terminated on Saturday.

Mr. George Howell has been adopted as the sec3nd Liberal candidate for Snifford. For the Cambridge University higher local exarninatior, which commences on Monday. June 19, there are Otil can- didates to be examined at the 21 centres appointed. A Conservative whip was sent round, on Thursday, to the Opposition Peers, earnestly requesting their attendance in the House of Lords, on Monday next, to support Lord Balfour's motion rejecting the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill.

The London correspondent of the Dublin Freeman, re- ferring to the significance attached to an interview between Mr. Parnell, Mr. Chamberlain, and Mr. Labouchere, explains that it was only a casual meeting, and that there was no lengthened conference. The iron manufacturers of the West have held a confer- ence at Pittsburg, at which they resolved not to start their mills under present circumstances, and to form a stronger alliance against the men on strike. The meeting was the largest ever held by the association. The trial of Martin, a compositor, the companion of Bren- nan, charged with shooting a man in Dublin, and in whose case the jury disagreed on Wednesday night, was to have commenced on Thursday morning, but the Crown decided not to proceed. The judge highly complimented a witness named Tracey, who, on the cry of murder, chased and cap- tured the prisoner. Such praiseworthy conduct was:unusual in Dublin, and d2served substantial recognition. Shortly before eight o'clock on Thursday morning an alarming fire broke out at the New Gilhow Mill, Bolton, belonging to Messrs. Crosses and Winkworth, Limited. It originated In the cotton mixing-room, in which was stored an immense quantity of cotton, and before the flames were extinguished some seventy bales were more or less damaged. The damage, which will amount to several hundred pounds, is covered by insurance. On Thursday evening a filthily-dressed person, evidently a tramp, was charged at Tarporley (Cheshire), with break- ing into the house of Mr. Joseph Jones, farmer, Peckforton. On Sunday night the house was broken into, and the drawers and chefronier-ransacked. Bread and cheese and beer had been largely partaken of, indeed so much of the latter had been drunk that next morning, on coming downstairs, Mr. Jones found the prisoner in an adjacent shed helplessly drunk. He was committed to the assizes. _

The Devon and Cornwall Chamber of Agriculture, after full discussion on Thursday, resolved :—" That this Cham- ber considers that an Arrears Bill is necessary in the preseat condition of Ireland, and approves of the proposal of the Government regarding the Surplus Church Fund, but ob- jects to the further proposal of meeting any deficiency by charging English taxpayers through the Consolidated Fund, as any such deficiency should in justice be borne by the landowners and occupiers concerned." ATTEMPTED SUICIDE IN A BARBER'S SIIOP.—Jane Lister, 37, single wsman, respectably connected, was charged, at Wolverhampton, on Thursday, with attempting to commit suicide. The evidence showed that whilst waiting for a male friend in a barber's shop she seized a razor and tried to cut her throat. The barber ran to her, and after a severe struggle, in which he was severely cut, wrested the razor from her. The prisoner now said she was merely in fun, but it was shown that she had made a similar attempt two years ago. She was remanded for a week. Intelligence received from Lloyd's pn Thursday morning states that the fine iron clipper ship Min-y-don, of London, 1,103 tons register, has foundered off the Australian coast, and her crew of 30 men all drowned. The vessel which had arrived out at New South Wales with a full cargo and a number of passengers from London, was on a voyage from her port of discharge to Lyttelton, New Zealand, to load a cargo of produce, when she was lost. The captain was a most experienced man. At Bolton. on Thursday, a domestic servant named Lucy Evans was charged with attempting to defraud the London and North-Western Railway Company. Some time ago the prisoner travelled from Llandudno to Bolton. On her arris al at Bolton she complained of having lost a box containing articles worth 12; inquiries, however, showed that the prisoner had ne box when she left Llandudno and she was apprehended. The prisoner, who wept bitterly in the box, was remanded.

PARLIAMENTARY OATHS. The Duke of Argyll has introduced into the House of Lords a bill relating to parlia- mentary oaths. The proposal is that, if a p ,er or member of Parliament writes_ that he has a conscientious objection to the form of the oath, or that the taking of an oath would have no binding effect on his conscience, he may, make and subscribe a solemn affirmation. This affirmation would be in the farm of the present oath, except that the words "solemnly, sincerely, and truly declare and affirm " would be substituted for the word "swear," and the words "so help me God" would be omitted. THE MURDER AT ROTHERHAM : ATTEMPTED SUICIDE OF •ONE OF THE PRISONERS.—One of the two prisoners in cus- tody at Rotherham on the charge of complicity in the Dalton Brook murder, which was committed in 1856, has sunk into such a melancholy condition that a separate watch has been placed over him. He has attempted to commit suicide by tightening a boot-lace round his throat, bnt he was detected in time to save his life. Notwithstand- ing the confession made by Leedham, Superintendent Ham- mond fears he will not be able to make the case sufficiently clear against the prisoners unless one or two doubts are cleared up. FATAL EXPLOSION OF DYNAMITE.—A correspondent at Irvine, N. 8., telegraphed on Thursday that the inhabitants of Irvine and surrounding districts were alarmed by an explosion which shook the houses to their foundation, besides causing material damage to many. The explosion occurred at Nobel's explosives factory at Ardeer, where one man at the sample magazine was blown to atoms. He was in the act of taking samples of dynamite and nitro-glycerine into the magazine, it is supposed, and, when about to change his boots, the vials which contained the material fell and exploded about 6 cwt. of dynamite, nitro-glycerine, dr.c. Deceased was Peter Hughes, foreman of the department. Several houses in the vicinity suetained damage, and the report was heard within a radius of many, miles. - -

EARL GREY ON PARTY POLITICS—At the anit meeting of the Edinburgh Conservative Working Men's °elation a letter was read from Earl Grey, dated Powderham Castle, May 21. Acknowledging a letter from the secretary, he -says :—"I have to inform you that I have for several years ceased to interfere with party polities. What is called the Liberal party I consider to have entirely departed -from the Whig principles in which I was brought up, and to which I still adhere, and to have adopted such dangerous views that I cannot give it my support. On the other hand, I am sorry to say that the conduct of the Conserva- tive party is also such as not to command my confidence. So that I can only stand altogether aloof from both parties. At the age to which I have now attained, this is, I conceive my most fitting course." Lord Cranbrook was re-elected patron, and Sir Stafford Narthcote lion, president, of the association.

The Brussels correspondent of the London contemporary writes :—The trial of Prince Camil'i De Loos Corswarem, for an attempt on the life of a bailiff, of Rochefort, has re- sulted in a verdict of not guilty. It was stated in evidence that the prince is a young man of gentlemanly manners, but subject to nervous attacks. The bailiff had come to present a bill for a thousand francs, which the prince, who is not well off, was not prepared at the moment to pay; but be expected funds to meet it by- that morning's post, and it was arranged that be should call at the inn before twelve o'cl3ck. This he did, but on the huissier claiming to be paid for the protest that he had in the meantime drawn up a discussion arose, in the course of which the bailiff used insulting language, and Prince Camilli, whom he seems to have tried to exasperate, forgot himself, drew a revolver which he always carried in his pocket and fired at the man, whom he wounded slightly. He immediately expressed his regret and gave himself up to the police. Damages were laid at 15,000 francs, but the court only allowed 6,000. _

GOVERNMENT ANNUITIES.—Mr. Fawcett's new bill per- mits annuities granted by the Government through the medium of savings banks to be as high as £2OO a year, the present limit being £5O ; and the minimum age for the grant of an annuity is fixed at five instead of ten. Provision is also made for contracts for the payment of sums on a cer- tain age being attained. Moreover, the maximum sum to be issued is advanced from £lOO to £2OO, and all restric- tinon the smallness of the amount is removed, the present minimum being £2O. The limits of the age at which savings-bank assurances may be granted are extended from CO to 65 as a maximum, and 16 to 14 as a minimum, or if the amount does not exceed £5, even to eight years. In empowering the Treasury to form new tables at once, and also at any future time, the bill directs that they shall be laid before Parliament for 30 days. If the fund formed by the receipt of sums in respect of insurances turns outto be so much in excess of the .liabilities that it is possible to re- duce the payments, the Treasury is empowered to give bonuses to persons previously insured. The time after which an insurer is to be entitled to surrender his policy is altered by the bill irom five years to two. Various other regulations are set forth in the bill for encouraging the grant of savings bank annuities and insurances. ACTION AGAINST A RAILWAY COMPANY 11Y A GrIARD.— On Thursday morning, in the High Court of Justice, Queen's Bench Division, Mr. Justice Manisty delivered judg- ment in the case of Crook v. the Great Northern Railway Company, which came before his Lordship and a special jury on Wednesday last. The action was brought by a railway guard, residing at Stockport-road, Manchester, who was employed on the trains between Manchester and Lon- don, to recover damages for personal injuries sustained by him by reason of some trucks being shunted against his train at King's Cross on the 6th September last, while he was fixing the tail lamps to it. The defence was that the plain- tiff at the time of the accident was in the joint employ of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway and the Great Northern Railway Companies, and therefore the acci- dent occurred through a risk incidental to his occupation, and he could not, it was contended, under the circumstances, recover against his employers. His lordship, it will be re- membered, left certain questions to the jury, who found in answer that there bad been negligence on the part of the defendants' and contributory negligence on the part of the plaintiff. They also found that the defendants might have prevented the accident by scotching the trucks, and that the plaintiff was at the time of the accident in the employ of both companies.—His Lordship said that as the jury had found that the plaintiff was in the employment of both companies at the time of the accident, the verdict must be for the defendants. He was very sorry for the plaintiff, but had no doubt he would be properly treated by the company. Judgment accordingly. STATE OF THE CROPS,
Through the courtesy of farmers. and others we are able to publish the following particulars as to the state of the crops in the districts under-mentioned :

CnoNToN.—Corn crops, with very few exceptions, are more promising than they have been for a considerable num- ber of years. As to hay prospects, our correspondent was of opinion there would not be heavy crops, as in Tarbock, Halewood, Speke, and Knowsley it was the exception and not the rule to see heavy clovers, and in many cases meadows are light. It is early to speak of the root crops, especially mangolds and turnips; but magnum bonum potatoes are not growing well, the sets having decayed. GRAPPENTIALL.—Wheat is looking well, and appears to be forward. The present weather will push it into ear earl ie than usual. Oats are growing very quickly just now, and look very promising, especially for an abundant crop of straw. Potatoes are not looking so well as in past years, particularly those planted very early, and some fields have been almost spoiled with frost. Late or winter potatoes are growing much stronger. Mangolds and turnips have not made much progress. KNOWSLEY.—Wheat is looking very fair, and is thicker on the ground than it has been of late, and promises to be an average crop. Oats are looking well in most places, and the rain has been very beneficial for all crops. Potatoes are not looking so well as they did last year at this time. The seed of many sorts rotted in cold heavy soil, which was bad to get in good order for planting. That was the cause of the rot, and a. fall of snow after planting made the land colder. Beans are looking ; rye grass and clover are first rate, in fact, grass of all sorts will be a good crop. Turnips and mangolds are coming up well, and the rain will do them good, but turnips in places have suffered from fly. LYMM AND Digrufar.—Never in our correspondent's ex- perience has land worked so unkindly as it has this spring. Strong soils have taken twice the amount of labour, with a very indifferent result. But with the genial rain of last week, and the sunshine of the succeeding one, turnips have braided remarkable well, and up to the present time there is no appearance of fly. Potatoes for early raising have been very much injured by frost, consequently they will be an indifferent crop, and a week or fortnight later than they ought to be. But late potatoes will be an average crop. With these few drawbacks the farmers' prospects are bright. Wheat and oats, the staple produce of the district, were never seen to better advantage. The very mild winter, with all its other drawbacks, has had a beneficial effect on the wheat crop; and in some places it is almost ready for sheot- ing, if length be any criterion, and, besides length, it pre- mises to be a full crop. The same may almost be said of oats. Sown pretty early, they braided well and have the prospect of making a full average crop with an early har- vest, and our correspondent adds that he has not seen one field that has suffered to any extent from the ravages of grub. Grass crops will be moderate. There is no prospect of their being heavy, unless allowed to stand until over ripe. Rye grass is fairly shot, and will be ripe in a fortnight or three weeks, whereas clover will be scarcely more than beddee, and it is to the clover more than anything else that farmers look for weight of crop. Meadow land, which is subject to flood—and there is a considerable quantity of that kind in this district—will cut a heavy crop, but upland will be light unless allowed to stand and mature. On the whole the pros- pects of the farmers around here are the brightest they have been for at least four years for good all-round crops. And stock of all kinds are making extraordinary good prices— prices which grazers will have some difficulty in making when selling time comes. PnEs.role Buoox.—Corn has the appearance of a very good crop, and clover an average one. Upland hay is light, and root crops are only average ones. SronE.—Crops are looking moderately well. Clover is generally good. Grass, second and third years, lies thin, is much in want of rain, and will not be above half a crop. On the other hand the crop of wheat is good, and the sime may be said of oats and barley, which however want rain very badly. Generally potatoes look well, though some seem as if they were "giving up " for want of rain. SUTTON—Wheat promises well on most farms in this neigh- bourhood. Oats are first class, generally speaking. A few fields have lost root from wire worms and poor land. Grass is an average crop. Early potatoes look well on light and well-managed farms ; but late planted potatoes on heavy clay soil are not over ground yet. Turnips,have been much benefited by the late rain.
TARBOCIL—Wheat looks very promising ; a good crop for straw. Oats promising for a fair crop. Roots arc back- ward, but look well. Good crops of clover; other grasses Hot so heavy.

WINDLE AND NEIGHEOURROOD.—A correspondent writes :--So far as my observations go I think the hay crop will not be very heavy, as I find in many places the clover does not seem to have stood very well, although the rain during the last few days will improve it a little. The wheat crop appears to be doing very well, although in some places it is rather thin of root. Oats are looking very well; I think they are looking better than any crop we have. Barley does not appear to be d, ing very well ; in some instances it has been ploughed up. Whether the fault is in the seed I don't know; but there were many very inferior samples of barley last year. It is rather early to give any account of the potato crop, as there are a great many that have aot made their appearance above ground; but so far as I have noticed Champions appear to be coming up very well indeed, and although there are some complaints about Magnum Bonums not coming up so well, I think it is only where the ground was very wet when set, or caused by the heavy rains which came immediately after being set. Upon the whole I think they are coming on very well.

div.head: WIGAN.
div.p: WIGAN.

LOCAL GOVERNMENT (WIGAN) PROVISIONAL ORDER.— This provisional order, which is one for altering and amend- ing certain local acts, came on Monday as an unopposed measure before Dr. Lyon Playfair, the Chairman of Ways and Means in the House of Commons, and ft e preamble ef the bill was passed.

WIGAN AND THE ST. JOHN AMBULANCE ASSOCIATION.--: The Earl of Crawford and Balcarres presided at a meeting on Monday of the Wigan Centre of the St. John Ambulance Association, the committee being called together to take steps for the formation of classes in the district. Lord Crawford explained the reasons of the delay since the resolution was passed to form a centre for Wigan. Means had been taken to test the feeling existing in the district with reference to the desirableness of the movement, and SO strong was it deemed to be that it was thought it ought to be set at work at once. He thought it was desirable that a commencement should be made in the town, and he under- stood that the Chief Constable of I% igen (Captain Kennion) had been se kind as to say that he would allow a class te be formed among the police. The volunteers, he might add, would join in the movement, and he trusted that classes would be formed at the principal collieries in the district, and he hoped that before long they would have one of the largest centres in connection with the association in the kingdom. Lord Crawford having to leave for London, Canon Fergie succeeded him as chairman, and stated that Lady Crawford had kindly prom;sed to give her assistance towards establishing a ladies' class in connection with the association.—Ultimately it was decided to form two classes at once amongst the members of the local police and volun- teers, and a small committee was appointed to carry out the arrangements.

div.head: ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.
div.p: ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.
THE EARL OF CHEB7ER'S YEOMANRY CAVALRY.—Sub- Lieut. Victor Alexander, Kiri Grosvenor, resigns his com- mission.
Application has been made by the Nantwich Rural Sanitary Authority to the Local Government Board for per- mission to borrow £7OO for the Sidney water extension scheme.

At Saturday's meeting of the Nantwich Guardians on the question that in future the election of Guardians take place triennially, it was resolved that the committee be appointed to go thoroughly into the matter, and report to the Board that day three months.

Captain Hildvard, Local Government Board inspector, will on the 30th inst. hold an inquiry at Tarporley as to whether the townships of Eaton, Rushton and Utkinton, are to continue to form part of the district of the Tarporhy Local Board. _ _

A petition for liquidation by arrangement has been filed in the Manchester County Court by Norman Barrow, Booth- street, Manchester, solicitor, and residing at Woodlands- road, Altrincham. The liabilities are set down at £5,000. SHOCKING COLLIERY ACCIDENT IN CHESHIRE: THREE MEN Buramo.—On Friday morning week the roof of the workings at Neston Colliery gave way, burying three brothers, named George, Edward, and Thomas Shone. Men were set to work to relieve them immediately. George and Edward Shone were dead when reached, and Thomas lies in a most dangerous condition. THE AUXILIARY FORCES.—The Ga:ette contains the following announcements :—Volunteer Rifles: Ist Cheshire, J. H. Crosby to be quartermaster. 2nd Cheshire, the under- mentioned lieutenants to be captains: E. Brassey and W. M. Lightfoot. sth Cheshire, J. Somerville, Esq. to be cap- tain; Lieutenant R. A. Thorp resigns. The undermentioned gentlemen to be lieutenants (supernumerary) ; A. J. Sally, H. C. Yates. and H. Brown. CATTLE DISEASE IN THE COUNTY.—The Chief Constable (Lieut.-Colonel Hamersley) reporis that four animals have been attacked during the week with pleuro-pneumonia and slaughtered, the disease having appeared on one fresh farm in the township of Manley. Eleven animals still remain under treatment from foot-and-mouth disease from last week. No fresh attacks. There have been no fresh cases of swine fever during the week. CUSTER FARMEIis' CLITB,—A general -meeting of the members of this club was held at Chester on Saturday, Mr. J. Roberts (vice-president) in the chair. With regard to the proposed farmers' deputation to the Premier, Mr. T. Wright (hon. sec.) reported that the Wirral and Liverpool Farmers' Club had intimated they would join, and, as there was no possibility of legislation on the subject this year, they had adjourned the date of seeing Mr. Gladstone in crder that the Cheshire and Central Chamb2rs of Agriculture might join.—Mr. H. E. Taylor (Hawarden) said he had been lately to London and saw several members of the Government, ' whose names he need not mention. From them he learned that they were quite alive to the farmers' grievances, and they felt it would be a kindness if for the present the deputation deferred their visit. There was no possible chance of the matter being brought before the Reuse of Commons this session, as Ministers had all their time taken up with other subjects. It was agreed "that the deputatien appointed to wait on the Premier be requested to defer their visit until a more fitting opportunity presents itself. Mr.

Taylor then gave an address called "Warning Notes," fa which he asked where were farmers going to find labourers to fill the place of the old ones, skilled in the school of practice. He was afraid that the education neces. sary for the future carrying (Ai of British agriculture wail being neglected. lie pointed out that a farmers income-tax was arrived at by estimaCrig his gains. .Some years farmers made nothing and yet kept on paying income-tax., while ft landlord, if he had a farm on his hands, got off paying:. The only way for a farmer to recoup himself was by showing hie loss; but that required the putting down of every halfpenny he spent, and the use of a large number of books. To MS up, he believed that the farmer had been depending too long on others to have the remedies supplied, and it was time he now looked to help himself. Re warned them, at the same time, as farmers, to be careful they were not too grasping' He also warned landlords that now was the time to look CI themselves and their tPnants.

SFORD. LIBERAL MEETING AT OVER.—A meeting of the Liberal A wiation of Over was held in the Board Schools, Over,' on Wednesday evening, to meet Captain Tomkinson. Mr. Slater occupied the chair. The early part of the evening was spent in ascertaining the extent of the Liberal gala likely at the next revision of the list, and after it was the chief event `of the evening. The Captain, in his speech ,oa this, the anniversary day of the great Reform Bill 50 years ago, to which he adverted, spoke of the Corrupt Practices Election Bill, and favourably alluded to the Tory candidate as the son of LibPrals and the inheritor of the estate of hie Liberal uncle. He was sorry he was on the opposite side. He also alluded to the want of policy on the Tory part, while the Liberals are carrying that with wLich they entered 1,1 office. Ireland received justice at their bands. A vote of unbounded confidence was moved in Mr. Tomkinsos. by

the Rev J. T. Maxwell, and carried. ANNUAL SUNDAY SCHOOL SERMONS, WINSFORD. Now that the period of holding anniversary services on behalf of Sunday schools has come round, the Free Methodists at Winsford opened the services. A former minister, the Rev. Joseph Jenkins, of London,preached twice, and the children sang hymns "sitting up" on a gallery erected for the par- pose. Formerly this was much more important than at pre- sent, for the elder children were trained to sing with the choir, in fact, made the choir of the day. Then they ren- dered (as often is the case in the North of England) on similar occasions some production of a great master, instead of only the ordinary hymns. This music, not the sermons alone, formed the great attraction of the auditory. On Sarday last the Sabbath school put forth the yonnges: boys and girls of the establishment, when the 'Happy land" and "Sweet story" were sung. But the choir supplemented this by two anthems, "Thou wilt keep him," by Perkins, and "The Lord reigneth," by IL A. Smith, which they rendered, as i the wont of the choir, with great taste and skill. Miss Buckley (the Academy) accompanied on the organ. The chapel was well attended on both occasions, and the collections amounted to £26 16s. ad. W INSFORD AND SANDBACH QUARTERLY MEETING—The etuarterly meeting of the Free Methodists of Winsford, ezc., held on Monday last, at Middlewich, was surptisingly attended for this season of the year. Business of the o; di- nary character, including the appaintmmt of a Plan Com- mittee. was transacted. The committee consists of 'Messrs. J. Hulse, T. Dodd, and W. Blagg, with Revs. W. J. Hopper and James Wright. The representative to the conference, called "annual assembly," is Mr. J. Slater, and alternative Mr. J. Hulse (to Bristol.) The financial state of the circuit was in some measure in advance of the previous quarter, and such as to call forth the satisfaction of the quarter board on the whole, and more especially when coupled with the port of last district meeting, at which it had the largest increase of any circuit in the district, viz., 47 members and 131 on trial. The discussion in reference to the appoint- ment of next superintendent by annual assembly was warm but good humoured, and the action of last December wan confirmed. The most cordial vote of thanks was unani- mously offered to the Rev. W. J. Hopper, who has been the full three years in the circuit, and who will leave it witb the character of being one of the best preachers and ministe- rial workers which the circuit has ever had. Indeed, it ha. all but the unanimous wish of the circuit that he should exceed the three years, but he would not yield to that Nvisix at the first.

CHESHIRE SALT TRADE. The salt chamber continues firm, and prices are maintained at annexed figures without variation. Scarcity of ships alone has prevented a ri.se to hieher figures for stocks are low, and the large stoppage 01 works ccntinues. Sooner or later these facts must produce the usual results, especially in the large markets of the Unit d States and Calcutta. The export list compiled frona Custom House returns, shows that. we have sent during May the following. qnantities:—to United States 8 734 tons, British America 10,826, West Indis and South America 1,429, Africa 4,010, Calcutta and Chittegong 20,926, Aus— tralia, &c. 1,170, P-ussian ports 3041, Russian ports 12,097, other Baltic ports, dz-e. 4 843. Francs and Mediter— ranean 9, Newcastle 1.362, rest of England 136, Sc,,llandl 3,574, Ireland 635, Holland 1,639, Belgium 2,920. The es- ports from Liverpool were 77,351, and Runcorn 30.537.. making a grand total from the Mersey of 107,883, which is !ewer than any previous May for years, if we except 18i8, when it only reached 95,342 tons. The prices have kept up at common salt lie, butter do. 12s 61, Calcutta do. 13s, elute stoved 14s,banded squares 17s, best fishery 14s.second best fishery 13s, factory filled (including, sack,) 26s 6:1; best Prussian rock 68,picked lump rock Os 61, ground rock ;first quality) 84. rough ditto 7s. rough iiddlings for ship saltirx, 63 6,1, soiled agricultural 7s. Now that the Tees valley has set up opposition to the manufacture of salt, even thougla on a moderate scale, some degree of competition may be ex— pected which my tell on the Weaver trade. That no great rivalry is to be feared just yet is hardly pertineftt. That Lt will come eventuality is certain, and this complicate existing arrangem,nts, unless the enterprising manufacturers will join the Salt Chamberand so keep up the prices by regulating the production to the consumption. The firm of Messrs. Bell, Bros., Limited, which has begun operations "near Middlesbornuerh, seems determined _ to go on with the work begun by Mr. T. Vaughan, for, during the last two years, a 'different policy prevailing, the firm has not only sunk a new small bore shaft, made brine, but also salt at the rate of nearly 300 tons weekly, and may go on to preduce 1.000 weekly. Thus Durham will enter with Cheshire and Wor- cester for teonoply of salt trade.

TRADE NarEs. A Cardiff correspondent. reports that after a long discus- sion on Tuesday night the Monmouthshire and S tuth Wales. Joint Slid'ng Scale Committee succeeded in establishing a new scale for the regulation of all the colliers' wages in the district. The employers agree to concede as front June let, an advance of 24 per cent. on the rate of standard Wage.. payable in December, 1879, in addition to the ,cn-, per accruing under the accountants' report of May 30, 1880. THE CLEVELAND IRON THAL/I.—The Cleveland iron- masters' returns have caused some disappointment. A I.lrge, addition to stocks for May, amounting to 26,170 tons, ap- peared, the first increase for nine months, a decline of 110,000 tons having previously taken place up to April. The increase in May appeared in makers' stocs, as a reduction of over 13,000 tous occurred in warrants, about one-third of the production for steel making purposes. The increase is due to the fortnight's strike of iTonworkers, and the Wltit- enntide holidays causing a great reduction in the consurnp- tion of iron.

ARBITRATION' IN THE POTTERIES.—The Executive of the Manufacturing Potters' Association on Monday met a depn- tation of operatives at Hanley, to receive suggestions for the reconstruction of the Potteries Board of Arbitration. Last year the Board was disolved throutzh the men, who - were dissatisfied with the award of Sir Thomas Brassey, the last arbitrator withdrawing, and the consequence of this step was a strike of six weeks' durati,m, in which over 50,000 hands were concerned. The men now say almost unani- mously that they prefer .arbitration and conciliatima to strdtes, but claim .advantat,es not allowed by the last Board. It is believed the Board will ba reconstructed.

TUE CORN Tnens.—The Mark-lane Express says— , " Down to Friday in the past week the weather was charac- terised by scorching suns during the day, with harsh, boisterous, withering easterly winds and frosty nights. Under such circumstances it is not surprising that wheats eho dd have made scarcely perceptible progress. The plant see us to lose bulk rather than gain it, and gets more staring 4 spindling, and foxy in appearance day by day; and unless some marvellous imprownent should be eAected during the next fortnight, the wheat crop must apparently he very much smaller than it looked likely to be at the end of March All the other crops want rain and warmer nights. On :Fri- claya very favourable change in the weather occurred,- but yesterday the wind was again colder, and this morning tiler° is drizzling rain at intervals, with a cool south-west wind. Trade for English wheats both in London and the provinces has maintained its holiday character generally speaking, and must be written Is. lower than cl,ring the previous week. Flour, too, has !e'en irregularly cheaper, and the trade closed dull and vreakor. En_rlish red wheats are now worth quite as much as whte sameles. Other descriptions of native produce are unchanged in value. The trade for foreign whif ats off stands in London has been quite of a re- tail character since the holidays." In order

to repeal the imports on corn Sir Robert Peel had to sacrifice the interests of his party; but, in his own words, he has left behind him a name " pronounced with expressions of goodwill by those whose lot in this world is to labour, who, in the sweat of their brow, eat their daily bread, and who may remember him," he added, "when they renew their strength with food at once abundant and tuntaxed, which will be better relished because no longer embittered by any feeling of injustice." The political enfranchise- ment of the Jews and their admission to Parliament has also been accomplished since the passing of the first Reform Bill, but not without much opposition, though there are few, if any, who will now:be found disposed to cavil at this advance. The army has been reformed, and the system of purchase, which militated so much against promotion, abolished; there has been a general re-arrangement of the licensing laws, the hours for the consumption and sale of drink on licensed premises having been reduced, and there is every pros- pect of a greater advance in the sametirection ; a local government act has b'een passed extending to small towns and village districts the advantages of municipal government; and local burdens have been to a great extent readjusted. The farmer, for instance, has already been relieved of some of the taxes which bore so heavily upon him, and he is promised a remission of others. Voters are now protected in the exercise of their privileges by the ballot, whereas previously they were subjected to intimidation and undue influensee ; and we may trust a Liberal Government to still further improve the electoral law. The education problem has been satisfactorily solved, and by the measure which bears Mr. Forster's name an educa- tion suitable to his circumstances is now placed with- in the reach of every boy in the land. The benefits of a uniform penny postage have been experienced by all sections of the community, and that same scheme is now being ably developed by Mr. Fawcett; whilst among other matters deserving of mention in this resume is the abolition of the stamp duty on news- papers, the repeal of the paper duty, and a great remission of taxation on the necessaries of life, which lead us to hope the time is not far distant when we shall enjoy the luxury of „,a, free breakfast table. The benefits accruing from the steady progress which has thus been made since 1832 are common to the United Kingdom, but Ireland has been, we may almost say, specially favoured. The Irish Church which only cumbered the ground, has been disestablished, and partially disendowed ; University Education in Ireland has been placed upon a sounder basis; and a Land Act which gives to the tenant a fair rent, free sale, and security of tenure has been passed into law. Such are a few of the reforms which have followed in the wake of the Reform Bill. For nearly all of them we are indebted to Liberal Governments ; those for which Conservative Governments may claim the credit, having been wrung from them. In the passing of many of the Acts conferring these benefits the Peers have, we regret to say, been a stumbling block, as they are to a certain extent now, and always have been to Liberal measures ; but it is to be hoped that even they may in time see it to be their duty to offer nothing more than a respectful protest to what they call the " revolutionary " schemes of the people's representatives. Rapid advances have been made since 1832, but we may be sure that when the work then begun is completed, the advance in the path of reform will be even more active.

Sr. MICHAEL'S, DITTON HALL.—On Sunday, there will be special celebrations in connection with the beautiful edifice belonging te the Catholic body at Ditton. LIVERPOOL BRANCH OF THE LAND LEAGITE.—The usual weekly meeting of the Liverpool Branch of the Land League was held on Sunday afternoon, at the Irish National Hall, Great Crosshall-street. Mr. J. Denvir presided, and amongst those present were Drs.J.Bligli and A. M. Bligh, and Messrs. P. de L. Garton, E. J. Welsh, J. Quinn (Widnes), Whelan (Widnes), Fitzpatrick ( Widnes), Milvaney (Widnes), B. Hughes, T. Evans (secretary of the Democratic Federa- tion), P. O'Brien (secretary), and a large number of Lady Land Leaguers. Mr. E. J. Welsh read a paper on "The Irish power in England and how to use it," in which he urged the necessity for every Irishman to have his name placed on the register of voters, and endeavoured to show by reference to previous elections the influence an augmented Irish vote would exercise in future elections. On the motion of Dr. A. M. Bligh, seconded by Mr-r. Evans, and supported by Dr. J. Bligh, the following resolution was carried unani- mously :—"That the terrible scenes lately witnessed by Mr. Davitt in Connemara call for the indignation of all humane men against the Government under which such a state of things is possible; and we pledge ourselves to assist our fellow countrymen in their distress, and to protect them from the insidious action of the so-called benevolent emigra- tion agents, whose real object is the extermination of the Irish people." The proceedings were brought tb a close by the usual vote of thanks.

WEDNES BRANCH OF THE CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY—The first annual report of the cone mittee of this society is as follows:—" In presenting their first annual report, your committee think that they have good reason to congratulate the members on the success which has attended their endeavours to promote the spread of temperance in this parish. The Widnes Branch of the Church of England Temperance Society was inaugurated on Thursday, 28th April, 1881, since which date its meetings have been held weekly without intermission, except on one occasion when the room was otherwise occupied. During the year eight public meetings have been held, of varied character, at all of which temperance truths have, in some form or other, been placed before the audiences, with—your committee are pleased to think—considerable success. The average attendance at these meeting has been about 250, and the aggregate pledges taken 43. The total number of pledges taken since the society commenced operations has been 192, 34 of which have been in the general section and 158 in the total abstinence section. Unfortunately, as may be expected in societies of this kind, the whole of the mem- bers have not kept their pledges, but your committee think that the number of members who have severed their con- nection with us from this cause will be found not to be in excess of the averages of other societies, if it be not even lower than them. The roll has been further reduced by a considerable number, who, from various causes other than that just named, have ceased to be members of our society. In the general section only two persons have been sus- pended for exceeding their pledge, whilst in the total abstinence section, 14 persons have broken their pledge, 4 have withdrawn, and 1 has gone the way of all flesh, making a total of 24. Of the 14 who in the total abstinence section have broken their pledge, only 5 were initiated mem- bers, the remaining 9 being probationers who had not been ! able to keep their pledge a sufficient length of time to con- stitute them full members of the society. This fact, the committee think, proves the wisdom of insisting on a month's probation. After deducting the suspensions, withdrawals, etc., the numbers remaining good en the books are :—general section 32, total abstinence section 134, together 186. Added to this the juvenile branch of the society numbers 184, making the total number of members of the Widnes Branch of the Church of England Temperauce Society 350. Your committee are desirous of bringing more prominently before the members and the outside public, the endeavours of this society- to promote thrift as well as temperance amongst our working classes, and, as a means to this end, are wishful to call attention to the "Sick and Burial Tontine Society" and the "Summer Excursion Fund," which form part of our society's operations. The former has a membership of 63, and an acccumulated fund of £3O, which, by reason of the small amount of sickness, prevalent amongst the mem- bers, is rapidly increasing, and at the present rate of pro- gress, will at the end of the year entitle each member to receive .£1 6s. id. as his share of the distribution. Whilst referring to this subject, your committee cannot refrain from urging all those who have not made provision for their wives and families during the trying period of sickness, when wants are multiplied, and incomes curtailed, to join this, or, if such can be found, a better society, having the same objects. The latter has a two-fold object: first, the promo- tion of thrift, and secondly, the increased health of members, by enabling its subscribers to enjoy a day's pleasure ie the country or at the sea-side, free from those anxieties and cares, incident to providing the necessary funds, where no previous preparation has been made. As a result of the peculiar constitution of the society.—no subscription being insisted on—the amount of money passing through the hands of the treasurer is not large. It is satisfactory to state, how- ever' that the balance is on the right side, there being a sum of £2 15s. remaining in hand after payment of all expenses. The income from all sources has been £l2 12s. 2P., and the 1 expenditure £9 17s. 2id., leaving a credit balance as already , stated. Believing that, to a great extent, the future sobriety ' or otherwise of our country, anl of our own town in particu- lar, depends upon the efforts put forth by this and similar societies, your committee earnestly urge all members to remain true to their pledge, to do all that they can to induce , others to take the pledge, and do likewise, and to ask God's ! blessing on all our efforts, so that the three-fold object of I the society—viz., the promotion of temperance, the reforma- tion of the intemperate, and the removal of the causes which lead to intemperance—may be pressed forward in such a manner tit-At we may at length be permitted to obtain the end ' at which we aim, a temperance reformation in our beloved , !and.—(Signed) W. CHADWICK, hon. sec., J. FARRANT, hen, assistant sec."
