div.head: 'THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, JUNE 10,1882
div.p: 'THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, JUNE 10,1882

THE Itgv. GEO. HACK AT ASTON.—The Rev. George Hack, of Runcorn, on Tuesday, delivered a lecture in the Wesleyan Chapel, Aston, on "St Paul's life and work," the Mayor of Crewe (Alderman McNeill) occupying the chair.

ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.—A few days ago a woman named Mary Furnival, whilst walking down the steps from the Runcorn railway footbridge, fell to the bottom of one the flights, and hurt her head and right hand, the latter seriously. 1.0.G.T. STAR OF WIDNES LODGE. - Bro. H. Hut- ton, W.C.T., presided at the weekly meeting, on Wednes- day evening, and an address was given by Bro. T. Warne, on "Precept, example, and influence." WIDNES ATHLETIC SPORTS.—It has been resolved to extend the time for sending in entries for these sports to the night of Saturday, June 10th. The prizes will be distrir• buted after the Saturday's sports by Mrs. Bond, of the Vicarage, Farnworth.

THE WIDNES SEWERAGE WORKS. - The dispute between the contractor for the sewerage works at Widnes and the Local Board has not been settled. The Board have placed the matter in the hands of their legal advisers. It is rumoured that great difficalty has been experienced by the contrahor in getting men to continue labouring on some parts of the work where the chemical liquid has penetrated through the ground, as the men say that the soil is of such a nature that it seriously damages their boots, clothes, and hands.

Runoss FREE LIBRAMY.—At the meeting of the committee on Thursday, Dr. McDougall presided, and there were also present Dr. Steele, Messrs. Simpson, Handley, Riley, Hazlehurst, Briscoe, and Brooks (secretary). The draft rules were adopted on the motion of Mr. Handley, seconded by Dr. Steele; and the f °lowing gentlemen were appointed a committee to make a selection of new bcoks The Rev. Canon Barclay, Dr. McDougall, J. Simpson, Dr. Steele, and W. Handley. It was considered that the opening of the library ought to be celebrated by some aapropriate ceremony, and Messrs. Frith, Hazlehurst, Briscoe, and Riley were appointed a committee to make suitable arrange- ments for opening the library on the Bth July.

RUNCORN BRANCH OF THE SALVATION ARMY.— IMPORTANT PROPOSAL. -It is stated that the Runcorn corps of the Salvation Army purpose erecting a hall capable of accommodating 2,000 people in the town. It is believed that some friend of the cause can be constrained to give the site, and the cost of erection is to be defrayed by public sub- scription.

WIDNES CHURCH SCHOOL EXTENSION.—The tenders for this important work have been let to Mr. Thos. Sadler, joiner, builder, and contractor, of Widnes-road ; and within the last few days the preliminary labour has been com- menced. Full details of the scheme have already been, placed before the readers of The Examiner. At the monthly meeting of the General Committee of the Royal Masonic Institution for Boys on Saturday a son of the late Mr. J. Bowes, schoolmaster, of Warrington, was placed on the list of candidates for election into the school in October next.

A 'VALUABLE HORSE DROWNED AT WESTON POINT. On Saturday, a valuable horse belonging to Mr. John Williams, ship chandler, Runcorn, was drowned at Weston Point dock. Mr. Williams's son was taking some goods to a vessel, and left his horse and cart on the dock side, and so fastened the reins that as an engine was passing on the branch line, the animal became frightened, and backed inta the dock, together with the cart. When the horse was taken out of the water, it was found to be quite dead. A NEW WELSH WESLEYAN CHAPEL FOR WIDNES.— The present Welsh Wesleyan Chapel in Widnes has become totally unsuited for the widening requirements of that part of the Wesleyan denomination in Widnes; and it has been determined to erect a new building, at a cost of about £1,200 The consent of the North Wales Building Committee will linti-e to be obtained, and it is anticipated that they will not make a grant until they are convinced that the object is taking a practical shape. Mr. R. W. Roberts, who has al- ways given the Cromwell-street congregation all the help in his power, has promised the scheme his support. CHANCERY or LANCASHIRE.—OfficiaI notice was given on Monday that on and after next Monday the sittings in Chambers in London of the Vice-Chancellor of the Chancery of the County Palatine of Lancaster will be ' discontinued, and that in future such sittings will be held alternately at St. George's Hall, Liverpool, and the Assize Courts, Manchester. Since Vice-Chancellor Briatowe's appointment the chancery business of the County Palatine has considerably increased. THE SUDDEN DEATH OF A CHILD AT WARRINGTON.— On Saturday the county coroner, Mr. Driffield, held an in- quest at the Higher Seven Stars, on the infant son of James McCabe, a street musician, living in Ship-yard. The mother I said the child was much discoloured about its mouth, when she found it dead. in bed on Thursday, and she thought it had died in a fit. Although she had ',dried five children previously, they had all died a natural death.—From the evidence adduced the jury appeared to think the child had been overlaid, and returned a virdect that the child died "accidentally, casually, and by misfortune." LANCASHIRE BANKRUPTS, &C. (From Friday night's Gazette) : Liquidations by arrangement : J. Buckley, Carrington Mess, near Dunham Massey, and Sale, farmer ind cattle dealer; W. T. Stagg, King-street and Brown- street, Manchester, wine and spirit merchant ; H. Harrison, Bolton, grocer and provision dealer; and J. B. Cornwall and J. Brown, junr., lately coal merchants, Seacombe, Liverpool. From Tuesday night's Gazette: Liquidations by arrange- ment :—Richard Edmundson. M'Donald's-lane, Corporation- street, Manchester, yarn and cloth agent and merchant ; William Crossley, residing at Whitehaven Villas, and Alfred Crossley, residing at Carr's View, both in Portsmouth, near Todmorden, Lancashire, carrying on business in co-partner- ship with Henry Crossley as cotton manufacturers at Carr Field Mill, at Portsmouth aforesaid, and trading as John Crossley and Sons; William Troug'aton, St. Mary's-road, Garston, near Liverpool, grocer and provision dealer; Thos. Thompson, Townhill-street, Blackburn, hatter; James Cooke Enamel-street, Whalley-range, Blackburn, glass, china, and earthenware dealer; Thomas Haigh and Frederick Henry Hobson, both of Fraser-street, Liverpool, joiners, builders, general contractors and surveyors; Thomas Haigh residing at the Slades, Speake, near Liverpool, and Frederick Henry- Hobson, residing at Ivanhoe-road, Sefton Park, near Liver- pool. Also separate estates of Thomas Haigh and of Frederick Henry Hobson.

°severe internal injuries. Her husband, who was accom- panying her, had one of his arms knocked through the window of Mr. Roach's shop, and it was feared that he would be trampled upon by the steeds dragging the car, but he happily escaped. Another woman, named Martha Taylor, the wife of Mr. George Taylor, Sutton Weaver, near Preston Brook, was knocked down and trodden under the hoofs of the horses, and very badly injured about the head. Both the women were removed to Mr. Roach's shop, and every possible assistance rendered them. Three persons named John Marsh, aged 19, Union-street; Frederick Harvey, Bold-street; and Mr. Cooper, Mason-street, were dragged from beneath the horses' feet, carried into the police station, and afterwards removed home. A.number of others including Alice Bailey, orAstley, near Manchester • and a person named Slitchmough, of Sutherland-street, also sus- tained injuries. The cause of the accident is, as far as we can gather, shrouded to a great entent in mystery. Some say that one of the ponies knocked down a ladder reared against Messrs. Handley and Beck's shop, and shied, which caused the rest of the members of the team to start off. Others state that a number of boys were annoying the ponies by pulling their tala. We are informed that it is three years since this re- nawned firm of circus proprietors have been the victims Of any accident. It appears that the procession was going through the streets of Middlesborough, when the 40 horses drawing the large car turned a corner too sharply, and it seemed certain that the conveyance would overturn. Two men, who were riding upon it, became so terrified that they jumped off. One of the men was killed and the other seriously hurt. The following is a list of the .injured, as far as we have been able to ascertain :

Mrs. George Taylor, Sutton Weaver, very serious wound on each temple, and also a rather bad scalp wour.d. George Hitchmough, a boy, son of Gilbert Hitchmough, Sutherland-street, both legs and face badly bruised, and suffering from shock to system. Mrs. Dutton, wife of Mr. Dutton, milk dealer, Brick-hill Houses (middle aged woman), badly crushed in the lower part of the body. John Marsh, single wan, 42, Union-street, aged 19, his right hand, right and left leg badly bruised. William Cooper, boy, Mason-street, slightly crushed and kicked. _ _
Frederick Harvey, boy, 16, Bold-street, both legs badly bruised.
Alice (aged ten), daughter of Peter railey, flatman, Marsley Green Astley, near Manchester, one toe cut off. A man named Williams, living in Canal-street, severe con- clusion of the knee.
Frederick Percival, boy, Bridgewater-street. Ellen Reynolds, daughter of Mr. William Reynolds, King- street. _ _ _

Wilflam Carzons, painter, Ellesmere-street, left thigh and leg bruised. The sufferers were immediately placed under the care of Drs. Robinson, McDougall, Bagnall, Williams, and Mr. F. Salkeld ; and the worst of them were taken home in cabs. Three of Messrs. Sangers' men were thrown down and bruised. One of them was engaged in fastening the reins belonging to the team of forty horses at the time when the accident occurred, and had a narrow escape of having the life crushed out of him.
The doctors report that all the sufferers are progressing favourably.
RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Monday. Dr. Steele presided, and there were also present Messrs. Norman, Williams, McDougall, Lake, Shaw, Handley, Briscoe, Whittaker, Meadowcroft, Hazlehurst, J. J. Speak- man, P. Speakman, Linaker (law clerk), Brookes (eecre- tary), and Barker t surveyor).
MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

This report, which was presented by Dr. Mouritz, stared that the number of deaths registered in Runcorn during the past month amotinted to 25, and there had been one 'death in Halton-within-Runcorn. Of the above deaths eight were due to pulmonary diseases, six to abdominal, four to brain diseases, three to senile decay, and two to scarletina. Pre- mature birth, scrofula, and syphilis accounted for one death. The death rate was about 20 per thousand per annum. Eight deaths had occurred amongst children of five years old and under, and four under one year. Two inquests had teen held. _ _ _ .
The CHAIRMAN said the death rate was a little higher this year than last, but on the whole it was satisfactory.
SANITARY MATTERS: THE FOUNTAIN WATER.

The minutes of the Highway and Sanitary Committee stated that a report had been received from the surveyor that the ecavenging contract was being carried out in an unsatisfactory manner. The committee had passed a reso- lution instructing the law clerk to serve Mr. Cliff with a notice in regard to the manner in which he was performing his part of the agreement for cleansing and watering the streets. The surveyor had been instructed to present a report on the construction of the Bridgewater Navigation Company's streets in Duke's-field, and to attach a plan of the said streets. The surveyor had been instructed to get the ventilating shaft in Moughland-road completed without delay, and to remove the ventilating grids. The same official had also been instructed to call the attention of the railway company to a nuisance caused by the defective condition of the railway bridge in the Holloway. The committee recom- mended that the Law Clerk should apply for a magistrate's order to close the fountain for two months ; and also that a complete analysis of the water be obtained. Mr. NORMAN moved, and Mr. BRISCOE seconded, the adop- thai of the minutes. Dr. MCDOUGALL referred to the fact that a report which bad been preseated by Mr. Barker, the surveyor, as to new streets in Cooper's fields, showed that they were not trapped. A more fatal policy than this could not be adopted by the Board, as the fact of no traps being provided, would simply carry the poisonous g tses from the sewers into the houses of people living in such a neighbourhood. Was it not a fact that the nuisance caused from the smells in Moughland's- lane was such as to be almost intolerable? So long as there was poison escaping into the air, even in its most attenuated form, the risk was great, for there were no gases more deadly than those which came from sewers. Mr. NORMAN referred the speaker to the fact that the sewers in Ithyl were not trapped. It was agreed to refer the report to the committee for con- sideration. _ . . _

Dr. McDonaLL next spoke of the proposal of the cr)m- mittee as to the public fountain. For fourteen or fifteen years the place had been a splendid source of water supply for the town, having been presented to the ratepayers by one of the Countesses of Ellesmere. He considered that they certainly ought not to let this matter drop so easily. He certainly could not congratulate the Board on the course they had taken hitherto, as it looked very much like asking a particular ind:vidual to put his nose into a halter. The matter was right enough up to a certain date, and what they had to settle WWI how the pollution had been caused. Personally, he considered that it had first resulted from saline matter getting into it, and then decomposition of a very serious character taking place. To close the fountain because they could not find out the source of pollution was a singular reflection upon a public body. Mr. HezLEHunwr thought the Board had been very idle in dealing with the pollution of the Fonntain. If the culvert which the water passed through was in a reasonable good condition, the Commissioners were not responsible for the fouling of the water, and they could stop any one putting anything upon the top of the culvert which would cause the water to be polluted. The proposed analysis would show what it was which fouled the water. Mr. HANDLEY remarked that the old Board of surveyors would not have permitted the fouling of the Fountain water without taking stringent legal action. He gave several in- stances of the energy which the old body had displayed under similar circumstances.

Mr. &taw was of opinion that it would be found the Commissioners had no control over the culvert; and this point ought to he settled before they decided to spend any considerable sum of money. After a little further discussion, Mr. MEADOWCROFT spoke strongly in favour of some action being taken for protecting the interests of the ratepayers. It was ultimately agreed that the fountain should be closed for one month ; and the minutes of the committee, with this and the other alterations, were then adopted.

THE GAS MANAGER ON THE PRICE OF GAS. The minutes of the Finance Committee were passed, on the proposition of Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN, seconded by Mr. NORMAN.—The following letter was contained in the minutes with xespect to the price charged for gas by the Runcorn Gas Company:—" Gas works, Runcorn, 26th May, 1882. Dear sir,—Yours of the Bth March has been laid before my directors, and lam instructed to say that they have taken the subject of the same fully into their consideration. They find from enquiries they have instituted the results of which are tabulated at foot, that the price charged for the public lamps in Runcorn is singularly favourabAo to the ratepayers. In these circumstances, it will be obvious to your Board that the time has not yet arrived for a further reluction, but my directors are anxious to call the attention of the Commissioners to the fact that they have erected and main- tained, free of cost, four Bray's lamps, entailing an extra annual outlay of £3O to the company. For this extra ex- pense, the Commissioners have hitherto been charged nothing.—l am, yours very truly, J. R. Frith, secretary and manager. Mr. W. Brookes, secretary to the Runcorn Board of Commissioners."

div.head: STAMPEDE OF CIRCUS HORSES AT RUNCORN.
div.p: STAMPEDE OF CIRCUS HORSES AT RUNCORN.

TERRIBLE SCENE: SEVERAL PEOPLE INJURED About one o'clock on Monday afternoon, an accident of a vory serious and alarming nature happened at the point where Bridge-street and Hi gh-street, Runcorn, intersect, by which about ten people were injured, some of them very dangerously. At the time named the men connected with Messrs. Sanger and Son's gigantic circus, which had entered the town that morning, were arranging the immense chariots and triumphal cars, for which the establishment is so famous, in the order of procession, previously to parading the chief streets. This task was being carried out imme- diately below the Market, and whilst it was going on a very large crowd of people assembled opposite the offices occupied by the Board of Commissioners, with the object of getting a view of the procession, as it passed in all its pageantry of scarlet and gold. The immense car, to which it is customary to harness forty horses, was ready for a start, and the last lady had mounted her dangerous pedes- tal on the top of the various "chariots," when the assembled. crowd were stricken with terror on perceiving that twelve beautiful pones attached to one of the cars had broken loose from the control of the drivers, and were coming down Bridge.street at a break-neck pace. "Save himself who can" became the order of the momenta and the fright of the mul- titude was increased to a dreadful extent when they ob- served that the forty horses attached to the " Brobdigna- gian " car, which always attracts so great an amount of attention in the public thoroughfares, had joined in the panic, and were following the ponies at a frightful speed. On came the horses, with the towering car at their rear, and as the car went thundering along it looked like some huge monster threatening to crush beneath its weight the poor and almost helpless victims at the front of it. The rough and physically strong men composing the vast crowd, paid very little attention to the weak women and little children in their path, but knocked numbers of them down in the roadway as they ran, with all the activity born of intense fear, into the various shops and other places of business in the immediate vicinity. These openings were soon packed, and numbers of those who were unable to force an entrance were trampled upon by the furious horses. For a moment the entire scene was one of inextricable confusion. Men who are usually known as remarkably quiet individuals gave vent to the strongest language, and it would not have surprised those who were on the spot if the circus people present had been very roughly handled, as the feeling of indignation against them was exceedingly bitter. Sergeant McMichael and P.C's Bossons and Clarke happmed to be at the front of the court house, in which the Petty Sessions was being held at the time, and they rushed to the help of the drivers belonging to Messrs. Sane.bers, and succeeded in stopping most of the horses near the Royal Hotel. Many lads were rescued from under the feet of the animals. A considerable number of people ran up the narrow thoroughfare known as Penketh- street, and remained at the corner, probably through curiosity to see what would happen. Whilst they were standing there, four horses, drawing a small but heavy car, turned round the corner, and drew the van across the para- pet. The swingle tree of the car knocked down a middle aged woman named Dutton, the wife of a milk dealer, living at Brick-kiln Houses, against the wall of Mr. Roach's shop, squeezing her against it with great violence. She sustained

Also asking for the sum of £3O to be placed to the credit of the Committee's Fund to meet current expenditure." div.head: SUNDAY CLOSING MEETING AT W.IDNES.
div.p: SUNDAY CLOSING MEETING AT W.IDNES.

On Tuesday night, a public meeting was held in the I.acev-street Wesleyan School-room, under the auspices of the Central Association for Sunday Closing. The Rev. J. Wright-Williams presided, and amongst those present were the Revs. George Bond, vicar of Farnworth ; S. A. Spooner, curate of Farnworth ; Wm. Young, deputation from Manctiester ; J. Tesseyman, Wesleyan ; T. Peters, Congregationalist; Mr. Thomas. Snape, pf Liverpool, and Mr. S. Owens, of Widnes. There was a fair audience. After devotional exercises, the CHAIRMAN first spoke of the benefits which would accrue from the proposals of the society being carried out. He 'adverted to the fact that many people employed in public-houses, would be very glad indeed if they had only to work six says instead of seven, as so many other people did. He referred to the Sunday Closing Bill which had been passed for Ireland, and re- marked that he was himself able to testify to the good which it had been the means of working in Queen's County. , He also spoke of the five towns, such as Dublin and Bel- fast, which were excluded from the scope of the Act, and , observed that now in those towns ten to one of the inhabi- tants were in favour of their being included. Then there was a Sunday Closing Bill for Wales, which by some un- happy accident, had not come into operation. What did they require to deepen their convictions as to the necessity of a Sunday Closing measure for England, when they saw so many instances around them of evils caused by the traffic. The opponents of the proposal said it was an inter- ference with the liberty of the subject. This was the old cry which they had heard so often ; aed lie asked if a man were to jump from the landing-stage at Liverpool into the river, and a policeman interfering with him for doing so, would that be interfering with the liberty of the subject? If a man came to his (the speaker's) house, broke into it as a burglar, and met with due punishment for his act, would that be interfering with the liberty of the subject? In fact they /ound that our laws continually interfered with that liberty, when it was not found to be consistent with the general good. He concluded by expressing a hope that the law which had been passed on this questions in regard to our sister countries, would soon be placed upon the statute book of England. The Rev. W. YOUNG remarked that it was rather humiliat- ing when they remembered that it had taken 15 years of continued labour in order to induce England to accept a Sunday Closing Bill. Still they must not forget that the Welsh Sunday Closing movement, which had resulted in the passing of a measure for that country, had really been the offspring of the Central Asseciation in Manchester ; and the bill of a similar character which had been passed for Ireland owed its origin, to a great extent, to their efforts. Wales was ripe first, and the Central Association said to it "God . speed." He hoped that England would %Try soon he ready to follow in the same path, and that the bill brought in by Mr. Stevenson would be c trried by a large majority. He went on to show that this movement was a political one, since its object was to influence our legislators, bat though it was such, tt was not is party movement. It was not a Liberal or Conservative questive though lie supposed there were representatives of both political sections at that meet- ing. The fact was that no Government would give them what they wanted unless they made their voice heard on the subject with no uncertain sound. As to Sunday drinking, it was like a narrow isthmus connecting the two large weeks, one behind and one before; and he believed theta great deal of the Saturday drinking was connected with Monday, Tuesday, and, perhaps, with the whole of the next week's drinking by this narrow isthmus of Sunday. If they could do away with this Sunday isthmus of drinking, the drunken- ness of the country would be very much diminished, and their general comfort and prosperity greatly advanced. The speaker went on to speak of the canvass which had been made. in various parts of the country, under the auspices of the Central Association for Promoting Sunday closing. In Abedare, a colliery town, there were 210 opposed to the , movement, and 4,659 in its favour; and of the publicans 28 against it and 48 in its favour. At Barrow-in-Furness, which was a representative wakingman's town, whilst 91 householders were against the movement, 1,272 were in its favour. In Birkenhead, the city of the future, there were only 188 againt it and 3,201 in its favour. In Birmingham there were rather more than 4,000 against the movement and 16,000 in its favour. In Crewe 357 against and 2,036 in favour. The totals showed that whilst 679,000 were in favour of Sunday closing, only 78,000 were aginst it. The Rev. T. PurEns moved a!resolution to the effect that whereas intemperance occasioned so much crime and other • miseries, it was desirable that the principle of Sunday clos- ing should be adopted for England. He said that he very well remembered some of the first flights of the promoters of the society, in the good old city of Chester. They were now able to say that the whole country was almost ripe for the crowning triumph of the movement in the passing of a legis- lative measure en the subject. Mr. Peters next referred to the success which had attended Sunday closing in Ireland and Wales; and concluded by expressing a hope that Widnes would not be found lacking, or dilatory in the good work. Mr.T. SNARE seconded the motio:e, and remarked that he could not plead that he was in the same difficulty as to the questions which had brought them together as the deputation had confessed himself to be, for he had been ac- quainted with Widnes for the last half century. He considered that Widnes assumed a peculiar position in regard to the Sunday closing movement, for they could not in that town complain that the publican kept his house open on Sundays whilst all other trades suspended their operations, since the peculiar nature of the alkali trade necessitated a certain amount of Sunday work being done. At this point, how- ever, the analogy ceased, for no one would pretend that the result achieved by labour in the alkali trades was of a like character to that which the publicans' traffic brought about. We were governed by majorities, and it was satisfactory to think that from the least favourable point of view, the canvass which had been made in Widnes showed a majority of five-sixths, and from the most favourable point a majority of nine-tenths throughout the country, for Mr. Young's statistics proved that they had no fewer than nine to one, whilst if they counted those who were neutral along with their opponents, they would still have a majority of five to one. The speaker went on to say that if the Sunday Closing Bill for England passed, it would, he hoped, prove but the thin edge of the wedge, and they might ultimately succeed in getting public-houses closed every day in the week. He next described the scene in the House of Commons the other week, when the measure was introduced by Mr. Stevenson. He next referred to the operation of the Sunday Closing Act in Scotland, and remarked that in Ireland it had proved equally beneficial with the Forbes Mackenzie Act. One of the charges brought against the principle of Sunday closing, was that it encouraged illicit drinking, but the police superintendents in Scotland would tell them that such was not the case. He proceeded to argue that if such had been the fact, it would have been shown by the increased disorder. He doubted whether in the present state of legis- lation, there would be very much chance, of the Lill becoming law. In conclusion, he contrasted Sunday as it pwaaist noofwth we isttha t uSt eu nbdoaoYk aosf iEt nwgolauld nd.bevillenththe Bill became would dambae able to describe the day in the beautiful words of George Herbert- -0 day most bright! The fruit of this, the next world's bud, The endorsement of supreme delight. The world were dark but for thy light, TWhrei cot by e of t 1 ne de acnd bay ; Thy torch doth show the way! ' (Applause.) The resolution was then put and carried unanimously.

The Rev. Gro. BOND moved a proposition, to the effect that considering the success of the Welsh, Scotch, and Irish Sunday Closing Bills, a memorial should be forwarded to Parliament, petitioning for the passing of Mr. btevenson's X ill.

_ The resolution was seconded by Mr. J. WILLIAMS, and ' passed without dissent. The Rev. J. TESSEYMAN proposed that the memorial should be signed by the chairman, and Mr. SAMUEL OWENS seconded the resolution, which was also supported by the Rev. S. A. SPOONER, and passed. The CHAIRMAN said that the result of the householders' canvass in Widnes, showed that those who wished the houses to remain open numbered 112 ; those who were in- different 36, ana those in favour 1,032. On the motion of the Rev. GEORGE BOND, seconded by the Rev. T. PETERS, a vote of thanks was passed to the Chairman, after which the proceedings terminated.
THE SAD AFFAIR AT FARNWORTH.

On Saturday, Mr. C. E. Driffield, county coroner, held an inquest at the Black Horse Inn, Farnworth, touching the death of Joseph Abbott, who died on the previous Thurs- day, under circumstances previously reported in The Examimee.

John Abbott deposed that he was brother of deceased, who was 56 years of age, and .a shoemaker, of Church-street, Farnworth. He last saw deceased on Wednesday, when they were at Widnes together. On the following evening, he heard that deceased had been drowned, and on going to the pit where the occurrence took place, he sa-s- a policeman get the body out. Deceased was undressed, as if for bathing, and his clothes were at the side of the water. The body was taken to the Black Horse Inn.

Cross-examined by the Coroner: How long had he been in the water? More than an hour any way.—What is the meaning of it,. now? I don't know.—Has he been on the spree for the last few days I). When we went_to Widnes he was not on the spree, and not even drunk ;..but Ido not know how he went on the next day.—Do you- know whether he was working on Thursday? He has not been working for the past fire or six months; he has not been well.—He took the wrong medicine, did he not? I have no opinion to offer upon that.—ln reply to further questions, witness said his brother was a good swimmer. He once knew deceased swim across the river Mersey opposite Runcorn. He had not known deceased swim across the pit where he met his death before. Deceased was rather short-winded, and soon became exhausted. He had neglected himself for a long time.

John Cross, labourer, at Mr. E. Sulliyan's.chernicaworks, said that between 8 and 9 o'clock on the previous Thurs- day night, he was with some companions, when they met two. men. They walked back with the two other men, and then saw deceased taking off his clothes at the side of 'the pit. Abbott observed that he had swam across many a tirbe before. He shouted to deceased, "You old fool, come away from there." The man took no notice, on which he again called out, "You old fool, put your clothes on, and come away from the pit." Deceased, took no notice, but pulled off the rest of his clothes, went round to the other side of the pit, jumped in, and swam three-parts across. At first the man appeared to be swimming well, and then he appeared to fall bickwards in the water, and he saw him no more. Deceased afterwards came to the surface, went down again, and then rose a second time, after wLich he finally sunk at a point where it was deep. A man named Preston jumped in, but he did not get bold of deceased, as he could not swim.. Preston went overhead, and then called out, "Get hold of me, or else I shall drown ;" after which he was rescued with difficulty. In reply to the Coroner, the witness said deceased did not seem tipsy, but on the contrary, sober enough. He did not attempt to keep the man out of the pit, as he never imagined he would go in. P.C. Ross deposed that he was sent for to the scene of the accident, and, after dredging for the body, they obtained a boat from Birchfield House, the residence of Mr. Young, and launched it on the pit. They recovered the dead body of Abbott at about ten o'clock.

A man named Dalton said he knew deceased, and had heard him talking about his swimming. A few nights before Abbott said he should like to swim across the pit, on which he reminded him that he was very weak, and was not able to swim across any stretch of water. He knew that de- ceased had lately been in the habit of sleeping out. The man had slept many times in his (witness's) greenhouse, and at other times in neighbourning barns and hay sheds. Sergeant Coutts said he could produce further evidence, if necessary. The reason why be bad called all the wit- nesses who had been examined that day, was that the brother of deceased had been at Widnes police station, and said that deceased had met with foul play. The Coroner, in reply to a juryman, said there were any number of witnesses to prove that deceased went to the pit by himself. A verdict of "Accidental death " was returned.
RUNCORN WE'LIYANS AND THE
SALVATION ARMY.

Mr. B. Kniveton read a paper on" The evangelization of the masses and the Salvation army," at the weekly meeting of the Brunswick Wesleyan Methodist Mutual Improvement Class, Runcorn, on Wednesday evening. There was a good attendance. The speaker first reviewed the efforts of the various branches of the Christian church to reach the masses of late years, by agencies such as mission rooms. Observa- tion led them to believe that, notwithstanding all that had been done, there was a very large portion of the population living in a state of spiritual darkness and ignorance which was a disgrace to our common Christianity ; and he was not of opinion that this state of things could be attributed to infidelity. Their minds naturally turned to the mots modern phase of the question, viz, the salvation army. As an evangelistic agency there was sufficient testimony from independent sources to justify them in believing that the movement had been productive of good. There could be no doubt but that through its agency many a drunkard had become a sober man, and that in many lives and many homes there had been a great reformation effected. If conversions had taken place through the instrumentality of the army, and if the work of conversion was the work of the Holy Spirit, then so far the Holy Spirit had put his seal upon the movement. As an awakening agency it seemed to have been the means of picking up many out of the gutter, and giving them a start in a new life; but this seemed to them to be the , limit and measure of work. It did not appear to them to have within it the means of sustaining the work it might be instrumental in commencing, and consequently must in , time collapse, unless remodelled and wonderfully improved. They knew that a movement of that kind depended for suc- cess to a large extent on the judgement, tact, and ability of its leaders, and here one of the greatest weaknesses of the army was seen. Many of those in charge of the different corps were sadly deficient in these qualities. Many of them were persons they feared whose religious ideas and knowledge had scarcely attained the elementary stage, and the result was, that in order to keep up an interest in the movement the sensational side of human nature was pandered to a frightful extent. But granted that a new life had been begun in many instances, it could only be sus- tained by the sincere milk of the Word, and by the other duly constituted means of grace; and if instead of these means of spiritual nourishment they applied sensationalism in the hope of satisfying the cravings of a new man, they made a fatal mistake, for of sensationalism it might be said that "increase of appetite doth grow with that it feeds upon." The thing will first deaden and ultimately kill every holy aspiration that may have been awakened in the man, and the last state of such an individual would be worse than the first. The excessive, and they must add the disgusting sensationalism that characterised the movement in their own town at least, was its greatest drawback, and they were con- vinced from observation that the thing grew worse. It must have struck every careful observer that the degenerating process had been going on for a long time, and what had occurred recently would lead them to believe that the end was not far distant. The sensationalipm and extravagance in- dulged in were bearing their natural fruit already. Relapses from the ranks were constant and numerous, and where this took place, the individual would be less disposed to religious impressions than ever, while at the same time, his expe- riences of a religious character being of such a grotesque description, would have given him altogether a distorted conception of what religion really was. If the doings of the Army in Runcorn were anything like what the Army generally was, they failed to see how the cause of religion among the masses could be advanced by such an organisa- tion, and by such methods. To witness such things as they had witnessed lately,and to read the literature that was so exten- sively circulated among the Army, was enough to bring a ' blush on tne cheek of every religiously-minded man. Much as they valued the welfare of those around them, they de- clined-to seek it by dragging the fair and noble form of religion in the mire and the dirt. The object could be accomplished by other and more seemly means, and the best way for the churches to look at the matter was zea- lously to carry on their eyangelastic work on the lines that had been so successful in the places alluded to, and to ab- stain from countenancing so excitable and sensational a movement as the Salvation Army. Their respect for reli- 'glen and Methodism led them to hope and pray, and at the approaching Conference, the Methodist community would not be committed to a movement of this character. (Applause.) A discussion followed the reading of the paper. Mr. COVENTRY strongly supported the Salvation Army. Mr. LITTLER spoke in favour of the religious work done by the army, but did not approve the methods they adopted out of doors. The Rev. G. ElecK wished the Army God speed in the work they did, which was eeally good, but some of their modes of action were of a highl-y objectionable character. When he read the Whit-Monday placard he felt very ! indignant. Mr. letca gave almost unqualified approval of the. Army and their methods. As a soldier's son, he took no exception even to the drum, but one of the placards lately issued he must describe as little short of blasphemous. Mr. F. J. NORMLN opposed the essayist, and defended the Salvation Army from the attacks that had been brought against it. Be considered that the large masses now outside the pale of every denomination demonstrated the necessity of a special organisation, and until the churches showed themselves qualified to undertake the work, his voice should never be raised against the Salvation Army; and in the face of positive good, which personally he knew they had been instrumental in accomplishing, charity compelled him to view even their excesses with the greatest toleration. Mr. J. D. JONES had only one good word to say for the Army, and • that was, that its members were perforce teeto- tallers. As a body of religionists, they were, in his opinion, + an unmitigated evil:

After Mr. Kniveton bad briefly replied, The CHAIRMAN stated that he had not given expression, ' to his opinion of the Salvation Army, though often asked to do so. He had now to say that he heartily disapproved of the plans they adopted to carry on their work. • Processions were not enough; they should go to the men and take them by the hand and talk to them. Methodism was- reaching the masses, and never more successfully than at the present day. He advised his hearers to let the Salvation Army alone, and do the work of evaigelization of the peoule in the best way they could. The proceedings were concluded by the Rev. G. Hack pronouncing the Benediction.
WARRINGTON COUNTY SESSIONS.

-- WEDNESDIY.—Before Messrs. G. Artingstall, S. Rigby, and It. Houghton. THE ArrEmPTED SUICIDE.—James Baxter, a young man, was brought up on remand charged with attempting to com- mit suicide by hanging himself.—The particulars of the ocruasey, Th which have already appeared in e Examiner, re h these. On the Ist inst. the prisoner went borne drunk, and, after having a few angry words with his wife, he went into the back yard. When he did not return his wife became suspicious something was wrong, and went into the yard, discovering' her husband hanging by the neck in the closet. She ran for a neighbour, who cut the prisoner down. His "eyes were then stanling out from bk head," and his face was going black. He had suspended himself by a small leather strap.—The prisoner said he had no remembrance of the occurrence, and if the Bench would discharge him be would never take drink any more.—He was bound over for his good behaviour for twelve months. ABSCONDING FROM AN INDUSTRILL SCHOOL.—Theodore Williams, a youth, was charged %%Rh absconding from the Newton Reformatory School, and the charge having been proved by the governor of the school, he was sentenced to a month's imprisonment, with hard labour. INEBRIATES.—Tbomas Houghton was charged with being drunk at Sankey, on the 30th ult., and he was fined ss. and costs.—A.similar penalty was imposed upon Emma Harris, for being drunk and disorderly at Orford on the 23rd ult.— For being drunk at Houghton, on the 21st ult., Jas. Fleming was fined ss. and costs.

PITCH AND Toss.—James Hoon, James Morgan, and John. Quinn, youths, were summoned fortlavin, pitch and toss at Poulton, on the 28:1 of last month.—Evidence having been given by RC. Macfarlane, each defendant was ordered to pay es. ed. costs. _

- -CRUELTY TO A DONCEY.—Jobn Thomas Walmsley was charged with having, on the 10th ult., at Poulton, cruelly illtreated an ats by working it in an unfit state; and Win. Crank was charged with cruelly illtreating and abusing the animal by beating it with a whip stock.—Mr. Harper, 1.5.P.C.A., said on the day in question he was, driving through Padgate when he saw the prisoners in a cart laden with sand, rags, &c. With the thick end cf a whip stock Crank was beating the donkey on the right leg andback with all the force he could. Witness alighted.and examined the donkey, and on the place where the blows had struck it was much swollen, and blood was oozing through the skin. It had also another wound which made the ass unfit to work. Walmslev, in answer to his enquiries, said he had entire charge of the donkey.—The boys promised not to again illtreat the 'donkey, and they were each fined ss. including costs. POACHING AT CUERDLEY.—Thorras Cooper, beerseller,. Warrington, Alfred, John, and Wm. Henry Monks, and James Moss were charged with searching for and killing game at Cuerdley, on land in the occupation of Matthew Taylor and James Edgerlev.—Mr. Thurnam defended.— Richard Welding, the gamekeeper, said on the 16th May htt saw Cooper and eight, other men' with five dogs, going across Mr. Moorcroft's land. He watched them, and after a short time he saw eight men commence hunting in a field with four dogs, whilst Cooper stood in the road with a greyhound. A bare went across the road with the four dogs in chase, and Cooper put his dog also in chase. It captured the hare and killed it, when Cooper put up his hand to inform the men of that fact, running to take the hare from the dogs. Witness also ran, and Cooper seeing lie should be outrun returned. On securing the hare, witness and the head gamekeeper went in chase of the men in a dog cart, and succeeded in overtaking the defendants.—George Holding, head game- keeper, stated that when he overtook defendants he asked them their names, acd they all with the exception of Alfred Monks refused to tell him. He then told them to come with him, and he got them into the dog cart. As he was driving them to the Sankey Police Station, the defendant Cooper acknowledged that he had been hunting his dogs.— William Dunbobin, a rope maker, said that on the day in cplestion he went with the defendants for a walk along Liveipool road, turning down a lane which led to Cuerdley. Wheu they arrived there they saw some men in a field with dogs which were running about. When Cooper's dog saw these other dogs it went into the field, and although de- fendant (Cooper) called it back it. would not return to him. They then went down the lane for a short distance and sat themselves down thinking that the dog would come back to them. Witness then proceeded ahead of (Mendants walking homewards and had not gone far before he was met by Air. Holding who ar,ked him if he was one of the men who had been trespassing in pursuit of game. Whereupon he replied "No." Mr. Holding went up to his (witness's) friends, got them into the dog cart, and ran off with them.—Thomas Clare, of the Packet House, Bridge Foot, then gave evidence which went to prove that the defendants were all respectable tradesmen and strictly honest men.—The Bench had no doubt that the case had been clearly proved, and fined them 20s. and costs each. Mr. Artingstall, in imposing the fine, said that the full penalty was .£5 and costs each, and if they were brought up again the full penalty would be inflicted. USING ABUSIVE LANGUAGE AT PADGATE.—Kate Pritchard was charged with using language, on the 25th May last, towards Ellen Monks, which was calculated to provoke a breach of the peace. It appeared from the evidence of com- plainant that she had many years past been subject to abuse from defendant.—Defendant was bound over in her own recognizances of £lO to keep the peace for six months. THEFT OF A SIIEET AT ORFORD.—A married woman named Ann Salt, aged 53 years, was charged with unlawfully stealing from a clothes line in Warburton-street, Orford, a sheet belonging to Mrs. Rose Silver, on the 31st of last month.—lt appeared that prosecutor, on the day named, had occasion to go to town. Before going she hung the sheet on the line to dry. When she returned in about in hour's time she found that the sheet was missing, Further on in the week prosecutor went to a neighbour's house, named Mrs. Baxter, to look for a hen which she had lost, when she was told by Mrs. Baxter that she bad bought a sheet from de- fendant for 9d. Prosecutor at once recognised the sheet as her property, and Mrs. Baxter forthwith handed it to her.— Defendant stated that she was drunk when she took the sheet. —She was fined 225. including costs, or in default one month's imprisonment.

A CHILD SCALDED TO DEATH.—OH Friday, Mr. C. E. Driffield, the district csroner, held an inquest at Haydock on the body of Margaret Ashton, aged on year and seven months, who resided with her parents in lienyon's-lane, Haydock, and who met with her death under very painful circumstances. It appears, on Saturday evening, the 27th ult., the grandmother of deceased was preparing to wash the children, and had partly filled a large mug with boiling water, when the child came in from the street, and whilst the grandmother's attention was diverted, sat on the edge of the mug, and upset it, completely submersing the deceased, and badly scalding her, from the effects of which she died on Tuesday, the 30th May. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." ITAYDOCK WESLEYAN BAND OF HONE SOCIETY.—The annual demonstration and gala in connection with this society took place at Haydock, on Saturday. A procession of about 350 members and visitors was formed at the Wes- leyan Schoolroom, and headed by the Haydock Colliery brass band, promenaded the principal streets of the village. A visit was afterwards paid to the residence of Mrs. Evans, "The Heyes ;" and through the kindness of that lady an inspection of the beautiful gardens attached to the house was made, and was an evident source of enjoyment. After reviewing the gardens the processionists made their way to the schoolroom, where tea was partaken of. This society had so far been favoured with fair weather, hut on the con- clusion of tea rain commenced to descend. Notwithstanding this, a move was made to the field kindly lent by Mrs. Evans for the purpose of holding the gala' which consisted in contests in reciting, singing, speaking, Sze. A portion of the recitations were gone ihrough in excellent style, but the rain having increased it was thought desirable to complete the programme as far as practicable in the schoolroom. Mr. J. Fairhurtt took the chair and conducted the proceedings. In the recitation contest there were three grades, the first grade being open to members under 12 years, five entries; second grade, four entries, for members between the age of 12 and. 16; third grade, two entries for adults ; singing contest, two grades, first grade, no entries; second grade, five entries for. adults; speaking contest, four entries, no speaker to exceed, ten minutes. The judges in the recitations and speaking contests were the Rev. J. C. Taylor and Mr. T. Newman, of Earlestown, and in the singing contest Messrs. Thomas. Clare and Parr, and the prizes were awarded as follows : Recitations, first grade—lst, Mary Fairhurst, subject, " Thc, dying child's app-al to a drunken father ; " 2nd, Thomas Rigby, subject, "I'm but a little soldier." Secon&grade- -Ist, Benjamin Fairhurst, subject, "Tile fire Brigade; " 2nd, W. Blackey, subject, "The Pump's Lecture." Thirdgrarle,„ one prize awarded by the n-embers of the sccietf:—Miss 11l Goldstraw, subject,'" The lips that touch liquor shall never touch mine." Singing contest, second grada—lst, .lanies Blackey' "Save the Drunkard ; " 2nd, Mre. A, Harris"• "Touch not, taste not." Speaking contest, one prize, Mr. James Blackey, subject, "The evils of intemperance." IIEALTIL AND FOOD. Sir,—Writing to Prufessor Newman, Lady Mount Temple lately said. "It is now proved that we can live and be healthy without animal food." The statement has, no doubt, excited considerable attention. 'Permit me to mention for the convenienip of any of your readers who may be inquir- ing upon the subject that papers giving information upon it have been placed at my disposal, and at the service of any reader who may like to ask for them.—l am, &e. R. BAILEY WALKER, F.S.S. 56. Peter-street, Manchester.

NEW MEMBER. The TOWN CLERIC : I have to report to the Council that Mr. John Edward Wright has been elected as representative for the South-West Ward. The MAYOR: From what I know of Mr. Wright's ante- cedents, I think we shall find him a very useful member of the Corporation. (Hear, hear.) LONDON MUNICIPAL REFORM. The MAYOR: I have to inform you that I have received a communication from a society calling itself the London Municipal Reform League, for voting a representative municipal government for the whole of London. I will get the Town Clerk to read the letter, and any gentleman can make his comments on it afterwards: The TOWN CLERK then read as follows: "To the worshipful the Mayor, aldermen, and burgesses of the borough of Warrington.—Mr. Mayor and Gentlemen.—On behalf of the London Municipal Reform League, we beg to draw your attention to the questions now agitating the public mind as to the reform of the loctl government of London. After many disappointments, and many long years of waiting, a responsible administration has at last undertaken to promote a measure for the establishment of a uniform system of loco.l government in London, and there is good reason to believe that such measure is alrrady prepared and will shortly be submitted to the consideration of Parliament. In this crisis of the muni- cipal history of the Capital, Lt is of the most importance that the great principle of complete popular control over adminis- tration and over expenditure shou'd he insisted upon, and sup- ported as the essential basis of all reform. In your Corpora- tion this principle, has received full illustration and develop- ment, and we therefore venture to ask your sympathy and influence in favour of the effort to obtain for London the same municipal privileges which have proved of such untold benefit to other corporations in the kingdom. The same body of Com- missioners, upon whose report the Munthipal Corporations Act, 1835, was framed, afterwards reported in favour of similar prineiples being applied to and a similar measure prepared for London; and its delay at that time was due to other difficul- ties of the administration of the day, and not to any doubt as to the wisdom of the report. From that day to the present time, the recommendations of the Commissioners have for various reasons remained in abeyance, 'out a vigorous effort is now being made to have them carried into effect. Men of every shade of political opinion are now united on the neces- sity for reform, and the only diffe:ence which is likely to arise is as to the manner in which such reform may be most usefully carried out. The London Municipal Reform League contains upon its council more than 50 members of Parliament, and many hundreds of influential and representative men from all parts of London; it has branches in each of the Metropolitan boroughs, and has held a very large number of meetings all over the metropolis. The judgment of the League and the Immense ma's of London opinion so ascertained, is in favour of the constitution of a single representative municipal authority with final control over all administrations and all expenditure, together with such adequate guarantees for local representation and assistance as may be found most effective. The only other method of reform which has been proposed is the establishment of separate municipalities for the various London boroughs. , The relative advantages of these proposals involve questions of much difficulty, and a trustworthy judgment upon the matter can only be formed by aid of much local knowledge and full public discussion. We do not, therefore, suggest that your influnce should be exercisod in favour of any parti- cular scheme of reform' but we may hope that upon the simple Issue of the grant to London of representative self-goVerning Institutions, we may rely upon the sympathies an I support of those great municipal organisations of the country, whose splendid public service, and whose vigorous municipal life form the most forcible illustration of the advantages which such in- stitutions are calculated to confer. The accompanying state- ment will convey to you in a succinct form some idea of the present condition of local administration in London, an i from such statement it may be understood how far removed the Capital now is frem the possession of adequate control over its own affairs. Many independent, and often conflicting authorities discharge various municipal functions over different areas; and whilst the Board of Works, as the chief central authority, is not a directly representative body. it will be secn that over our police (except in the City araa), and even over so small a matter as our own Mos' we:possess none of that control to which weare justly'entitled. It has been-sometimes assumed that municipal reform in London necessarily involves hostility to the Corpora- tion which now controls the one hundredth part of its area In answer to this, it is only needful to say, that we have every reason to expect that the proposals of the admini•trations will proceed upon the line extending the Corporation so that its history, its form of government, and its ancient renown may become the heritage of the whole Capital. We do not venture to indicate to you the direction in which your influence may be most usefully exerted. In that matter we can simply rely upon your judgment, but if your Corporation think it fit to assist us, and the great public work of Lond -n municipal reform, by signing the enclosed petition, we shall highly value such sup- port, and if desired shall be glad to ensure the presentation of such petition to Parliament. We have the honour to be, Mr. Mayor, and gentlemen, &c.—JOSEPH F. B FIRTH, WILLIAM PHILIPP, and JOHN CLARK (signers on behalf of the London Municipal Reform League)." The petition was as follows:— "To the honourable the Commons of the United Kingdom in Parliament, assembled.—The humble petition of the Mayor, Aldermen. and Burgesses of the Borough of Warrington, sheweth that the various Municipal 03rporation Acts under which the local affairs of this bmough are administered, have been proeuctive of great public advaul age. That your peti- tioners are informed that it is proposed to adopt the principles of the same Acts. so far as may be practicable, to the govern- ment of the metropolis; wherefore your petitioners humbly pray that in any measure for the reform of the Local Govern- ment of London, which may receive the sanction of your honourable house, there may be given to the inhabitants of the Capital that full representative control over all administration and over all expenditure which has been found e'sewhere of such great public advantage. And your petitioners as iu duty bound will for ever pray. The TOWN CLERK said there was another letter from the opposite point of view. It was as follows : "To the Mayor and Town Councillors of Warrington. Gentlemen,—You in all probability have received an address issued by the London Municipal Reform League. In that ad- dress it is stated that an immense mass of public opinon is in favour of single representative municipal authority for the Metropolis. As we are enabled to speak on good authority with relation to this immense mass of public opinion said to have been evoked on behalf of one municipality we now unhesitatingly give our unqualified contradiction to the accuracy of this state- ment. At a meeting held at Kensington Town Hall a short time ago there were present only some 250 people. The hall is capable of holding about 1,000 people. This meeting was fully advertised, and the hall is situated in the borough of Chelsea, which borough is represented in Parliament by the promoter and chief of the Municipal Reform League. Not only is such the case with regard to Chelsea, but ha every other metropolitan borough the public are conspicuons by their ab- sence at the meetings convened by the Municipal Reform , League. Considerable difference of opinion is manifes'ed at these meetings. The prevailing opieion is that one Municipal Council for tile whole of this vast metropolis would be too gigantic and impracticable. The whole City of London alone , pays one-seventh of the rates of London, and, seeing that such is the case, it is fully entitled to that municipal lire which has so long existed within its boundaries. Abuse and ignorance have each played their part with reference to the City authorities, and it is wonderful what a large amount of the latter prevails. The book published by Mr. Firth, 'Municipal London,' is entirely misleading. In one article relating to sewers he said the construction per mile was £ll,OOO, whereas, upon enquiry, it was only £1,142 per mile. He also stated that one company spent a certain amount upon dinners—the Goldsmiths'—and it actually transpired that the sum he mentioned was in excoss of their total income. These sort of instances might be multiplied ad libitum. The largest vestries in London have passed resolutions condemnatory of the proposal to establish one Municipal Council for London. In fact many of these vestries represent a population equal to some of the great provincial towns. As you would resent in- terference on the part of the Lendon vestries or the City of London authorities with respect to your local affairs, may we ask you to pursue a policy of non-intervention regarding Lon- , don municipal matters, and refuse to sign the petition of the London Municipal Reform League. which is toe ked upon in London as being a missive framed in the spirit of undue inter- ference with municipal life, the chief essence at which is the control and conducting, as far as local affairs are concerned, by each respective locality. We, therefore, appeal to you to adopt the course of non-interference.—We remain, yours re-pectfully, - -vr pality League, 73, Farringdon-street, London, E. 0." _ AGRARIAN MURDERS IN GALWAI. "THE TIMID ANIMAL." Sir,—An old friend resident in Newton-le-Willows has sent me a copy of your paper for the 27th of May, and my attention is drawn to a paragraph with reference to a "com- pany, limited," which purposes to acquire a lease of pro- perty in Newton, and "to lay out the same for preserving and coarsing hares, rabbits, akc.;" and out of the "first shareholders" I see that two hail from Liverpool. I sincerely hope the preject will be abandoned. The circum- stance reminds one of the fact that it is recorded that the passed away "luxurious living of Liverpool "sprang from the profits of the slave trade, a traffic th,at had its warmest sup- porters in the then local historians. And there is something exquisitely sardonic in the complacent remark of one of these writers, who, even after the traffic was declared to be illegal, said of it, evidently with a lingering love of the abominable thing, that "however repugnant it may have been to the feelings of humanity, it was productive of opulence." And so, I presume, that " however repugnant it may be te the feelings of humanity " in the present day to breed and preserve hares and rabbits, that they may afterwards be subjected to the most torturing and cruel of deaths, it will now, as the Liverpool slave trade did, be pro- ductive of profit. lam told that the "rail and the press" have helped to make Newton (which I have not visited since 1851) "one of the prettiest and most prosperous vil- lages in the north of England ;" that being so, I should think the last thing the inhabitants would desire would be that the " rail "—the so-called second agent in civilisation —should periodically deposit in their midst the rowdy camp-following that too often hangs upon what in the present day is terrnd" sport," especially when it takes the form of hunting such animals as the soft-haired timid rodent and its congeners to death. If in their natural style the mischievous yet useful hare anl rabbit breed too fast or take tao much tithe of the farmer, let the latter mercifully ex- terminate them as enemies of the survival of the fittes` theory; and Shakespeare's sentiment, put into the mouth a Hotspur, that

"The blood more stirs To rouse a lion than to start a hare," is one that should ever be present to the mind of a healthy- minded Briton. This is a subject I should have expected the worthy clerical whom "vos give credit for "using his pen so deftly," would have taken up instead of gi.ding at school board officers, neglecting figure facts, and ignoring the contagiousness of scarlet fever. I would remind the "promoters" that the individual, whose name it is to be hoped will always live in history in connection with nobility of mind and purpose, the destruction of rodents when they be- come pests, but not in cruelty, hailed from Lancashire. It is recorded of Whittington, though thrice Lord Mayor of Lon- don :--

But of poor parentage Born was he, as we heare, And in his tender age Bred up in Lancashire. I would also remind the worthy "father "it is in connection with charity and Education recorded of Whittington that— God did then make him great, So would he dey see Poor people fed with meat, To show his charity. Priioners poore cherish'd were, Widowes sweet comfort found, Good deeds both far and neare, _Oi him do stdi resound. Whittington Colbaga is One of his chari.ie4 ; Accords reporteth this Ti la.ting memories, In cOnclusion, I hope the press, the rail, and Newton will continue to flourish, that obstinate priests and positive school board officers will unite in a common effort to spread more light and so dispel the taste or love for gambling in conn ec- tion with cruel and debasing so called sport. —I am, sir, tkc. ANGLO-SCOTUS. Newington, London, May sth, 1882. •

WANTED, AN IRISH POLICY. LETTER 11. Sir,—ln my last I drew attention to the increasing pro- minence of the Land Question as a •subject of interest with Englishmen as well as Irishmen. And I ventured to infer a doubt as to the freedom of the Government to pursue a pure policy so far as Ireland is concerned, There are ample grounds for the inference. It, however, mainly rests upon the fact that Mr. Gladstone's party is not strong enough to legislate impartially on the Land Question, even if disposed to view it with the intention of subsequently remedying the laws, whose defects are responsible for the agitation now vigorously proceeding in Ireland. Mr. Gladstone himself, much as he may long for improvements that will make the people of both England and Ireland feel they are less strangers to the blessings of a truly free soil than they are at present, is conscious that he cannot depend upon having a "cast iron majority" should he introduce any policy more than fAintly Radical ; while he is equally well aware that a' Ritpullacan cast of opinion would lead to his fall from the Premiership. This is easily accounted for. It is a yfeaken- in.g feature of the Gladstonian majority,that its elements are too diversified to repres,nt a reliable framework for advanced legislation. Were the Liberal party purely composed of men thoroughly true to the principle of Liberalism, men pre- pared to advocate and uphold measures righteous to the in- terests of the people, we should soon observe an inclination in the Government to deal with laws that are a blot upon our national honour. Unfortunately, such an ideal concre- tion does not exist. Too many of Mr. Gladstone's colleagues are irreliable where prejudice offers a doubt or private in- terests are involved. They are not all Bright's. We need only refer to the Bradlaugh episode in the history of the current Government as an illustration of the restraints which handicap it in its effort to deal justly with public questions and popular interests. We should hail with pleasure the ascension to power of a party so sympathetic in its love for justice all round, that such blots upon our "fair fame" as a civilised nation as our opium traffic with China, and our licensed drink traffic in Britain, w ould disappear in the past, with other abortive drags upon the people. Now, as ever, interference in prevailing laws is predicted more upon its propriety than justice, its sagacity than equity, as a stepby the Government in the march of progress. There is a Mammoth revenue attached to the drink traffic, a smaller one with the opium traffic; and, as a Government must have an income, the traffics are tolerated, even pushed, although there is a terri- ble emphasis of crime attaching to them. Public morals may suffer; but the expensive machinery of the police courts is feron the acme food which, it is no metaphor to say, poisons millions of martyrs to " political economy " Is it unreasonable to assert that if these reproachful things can exist under a Liberal regime, that other and not much inferior influences may prevent the same Government from being faithful to the interests of the public. On this Land Question are there not men, ostensibly Liberals, who dread the,approach of a day when the land shall be for the people? Men who are animated by selfish projects of personal advancement; men who are affiliating the very society which vegetates upon the soil morally the people's, for the sake of the "good things" prospectively theirs? Undoubtedly there are. And it is these who foster penrility where they ought to promote strength, who hinder instead of helping the Government to give impetus to broad and popular measures. Let us hope each constituency will intelligently discern what kind of representative it has got in Parliament, and improve where necessary. In my next, I shall deal directly with the Land Question.—Yours truly, Warrington, June 6. BENJ. SAWDON.
