div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 10, 1882.

present at the commencement of the proceedings. He thought they would have been surprised, even in Warrington, if London had gone out of its way to enquire as to how the municipal government of Warrington was carried on ; and that was exactly their position as regarded interference. There would be about as much pro- priety in London investigating anything that took place in Warrington, as in little Warrington beginning to investigate what was done in London. It had been pointed out that there were certain evils. But they could not suppose it possible, by making London into a leviathan corporation, that those evils would be swept away. On the contrary, he thought the evils would be greater with a leviathan corporation than they were now with bodies looking with suspioion upon each other. He had heard gentlemen in that room speak of manufacturing concerns which had actually extended beyond the possibility of management, and so it would be with London if it were made into the leviathan corporation suggested. Supposing itwere to be accomplished it would be suicidal in corporations to invite any interfer- ence with the Corporation of Londonlif that interference was to be brought about by a central authority of this country. They ought to be jealous of the interference of the Govern- ment. As an authority of the Local Government Board said to him the other day, it was a remarkable circumstance that the Local Government Board were in the habit of acting— indeed they were entitled by Act of Parliament to act—as auditors of the various Local Boards in the country. It happened that the Local Government Board and the Government itself were not liable to audit by independent parties, and the authority said it was high time the Local Government Board should be subject to independent audit, ' so that they would be amenable. There was another reason why he would prevent interference, because any corporation that did take action, whether London, Liverpool, or any other town, would have power to go the Local Government Board as a stepping stone to that cenatralisation to which they all objected. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR took it that the feeling of the meeting was that the petition should not be bigned. If Londoners wanted to interfere with their own Corporations let •them do it themselves, and not invite a corporation like Warrington to assist them. He did not think the Council had any interest in the matter, as it did not affect the ratepayers of Warring- ton at all. .
.. —... . The proposition that no action be taken was then carried.
PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE,

At a meeting of the above committee, held on the Bth May, it was recommended that the sewer in Palenyra square (south side) be continued to the junction of Thynne street and that the apportionment of the cost of paving Cartwright, street be approved. At a meeting held on the 22nd May, ii was recommended that Councillor Wright be appointed a member of this committee, and that the apportionments of the cost of forming and paving Howard and Catherine streets be approved. It was recommended that the tender of the Bessbrook Granite Company, Limited, for 800 tons of granite cubes, the tender of Messrs. John Nunnerley and Co. for 1.500 tons of red sandstone bur, and the tender of Messrs. John Pendlebury and Co. 50,000 chequered tiles, be accepted. Alderman KEAN moved, and Councillor WOOLFALL seconded the adoption of the minutes. Councillor MACKIE asked whether the recommendations for the three or four tenders amounting to some £l,OOO or £1,200 were in the position of recommendations at the pre- sent moment, or whether they had been absolutely passed and orders given. He had no fault to find, but wished to know whether it was any exception to the plan pursued by some committees. Councillor FAIRCLOUGH asked whether it was intended to give a greater fall to the sewer in Palmyra-square. Councillor BARKER enquired if the Chairman could give any information respecting the pavingof Arpley-street. The street had been made for a long time, and he believed the land was let for building upon, and he should be glad if Alderman Kean could give any information about it. At present the street was in a very unsettled state; and was not fit for persons to walk along in the evening, especially in such weather as there had been lately. Councillor BROADBENT : Perhaps the Chairman will also tell us when the Latchford drainage scheme will be carried out. (Laughter). The MAYOR: Does any other gentleman wish to know anything? (Laughter). Councillor Mcmcs hoped the Borough Surveyor would see that there were such gradients in Latchford as would obviate the everlasting cleansing of the sewers that there was in Warrington. The MAvon : That is provided for. Alderman KEAN, replying to Councillor Mackie, said that as soon as the recommendations were confirmed the materials mentioned would be purchased. [Councillor Mackie: That is satisfactory.] The committee had a lot of streets under order, and they would be proceeded with as quickly as possible. The work of paving many of the streets had been held back because of what they considered the in- ability of the owners to pay for the paving of the streets. In answer to Councillor Fairelough, he said the intended sewer had nothing to do with the sewer in Palmyra-square. It was an independent sewer, and consequently they would not interfere with the present fall in Palmyra-square, about which they had had no complaint. He thought Councillor Barker was old enough to know that the question of Arpley- street had been in the bench of the committee for a long time, but the committee had had what they considered a bona fide promise from Lord Winmarleigh that he would make the street after a certain period. That, however, seemed to have fallen through, and the matter had been 'referred to the Town Clerk to make some arrangement for having the street formed, and if that was not done, the com- mittee would make the street and fall upon Lord %Vintner- leigh for the cost thereof. It was quite time the work was done, as the committee were aware. The contract for the sewerage of Latchford was in the hands of the patentee, and the committee expected very shortly he would carry out his arrangement. Replying to Councillor Monks, he said there was no gradient which could stand against the force with which the sewage was ejected by the injector, and the com- mittee had taken every precaution that the fall should be as great as possible. Alderman DATIES said perhaps Councillor Monks would be pleased to hear that the matter was the subject of discus- sion the previous night. The BOROUGH SURVEYOR, in reply to enquiries, said he expected to have everything connected with the drainage of Latchford completed about the latter end of August. Alderman KEAN: That is all right. You can go shooting then. Alderman HARRISON: What, in the sewers! (Laughter.) 1 Alderman KEAN: No.—The minutes were adopted. i THE PAYMENT OF SCHOOL FEES.

The minutes of the School Attendance Committee con- tained the report of the inspector that 50 cases had been en- quired into by the Board of Guardians, and school fees al- lowed in 40 cases for 52 children. 48 cases were brought be- fore the magistrates, and a fine inflicted in 45 cases, two ad- journed, and one warrant ordered. 43 cases were brought before the Committee and dealt with. Recommendation, that Councillor Dr. Mackie be appointed a member of this corn- mittee. Alderman WEBSTER, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, referred be the question asked at the last meeting by the Deputy Mayor as to the payment of school fees by the Board of Guardians for poor children. He said he did not know that the matter at all affected the Council or the School Attendance Committee. It was simply a matter affecting them as ratepayers, and, therefore, with that impression he thought it would perhaps be as well to explain how the matter really stood. It seemed that at the end of each quarter a sheet was sent from each of the various ' schools to the Clerk to the Board of Guardians which showed the attendance of each child for each week in the quarter. Now, it had been laid down he believed by the judges that if a child went to school on Monday morning without its school fees and was sent back this was not an attendance within the mean' ing I f the Education Act; and, therefore that showed that th" payment of fees was requisite for even a single attendance in the course of a week. It appeared if the child went one Monday morning and only attended once the whale week's fee was paid; but if he did not attend at all then the fee was not paid—(hear, hear),—and each quarter a sheet was sent in which showed how the weeks were paid for. The committee's enquiry officers examined all these papers, and they saw, of course, which child had not been attending regularly. A note was made of such cases, enquiry was in- stituted, and if there was no reasonable excuse the parents were summoned before the committee. The Council would thus see that really no more was paid for the attendance of poor children at school than would be paid by the parents of other children under similar circumstances. He men- tioned thatithere were some parents who were so short- sighted in regard to their children that when they were summoned before the committee and the magistrates they actually removed their children from the school at which complaint had been made of their attendance to some other school, and entered them there as a kind of revenge to the teachers of the school. He wished it to be known that such conduct made no difference at all in respect to the child. If the child did not attend the parent would be summoned be- fore the magistrates, whatever the feelings of the school- master might be. The master had n3thing to do with it. If the enquiry officers examined the registers and found a child had not been attending school, or had been attending irregularly,if there was no reasonable ground of excuse for it, the parent was then summoned before the committee and he was told the child must attend school. If he was still re- calcitrant then he was summoned before the magistrates. Alderman HARRISON seconded, and said things were not quite what they seemed. There were not so discouraging. He was told when children went late to school, altliougu they attended, they were not marked as being present, and therefore the Council would see that it was not after all so discouraging as it appeared. Alderman Webster had explained that if a child went to school one day, the first day of the week, the fee for that week could be enforced, and it was only reasonable. But it was very rarely that a boy only went to school one day during the week. Frequently he went during the week, but went late and did not get marked down as being present. Councillor MACKIE expressed his high appreciation of the appointment as regarded himself, but said it was absolutely impossible for him to attend any Thursday at half past two. Therefore he would be glad if they would appoint some other gentleman. Alderman DAVIES remarked that there was a Board of Guardians that had come to the determination to ply the school fees to the parents of the children. [Alderman WEBSTER : That is illegal.] It was being done. The Guardians were in the habit of paying fees to the parents, and if the children did not attend school then their relief was stopped altogether. Alderman HARRISON: But that is impossible. Aldetman DAVIES : Wait a moment. lam stating what has appeared in print.

Alderman Hertarsox : Whatever statement has appeared in the papers, the Guardians certainly do not pay the school fees into the hands of the parents of the children. Alderman DAVIES :If gentleman would just listen—l say there is a Board of Guardians that is now paying the fees to the parents of the children._
Alderman HARRISON: You don't mean to say the War- rington Board of Guardians?
Alderman DAVIES : I did not say the Warrington Board of Guardians.
Alderman HARRISON: I beg your pardon. Alderman DAVIES : They are not clever enough for that. (Laughter.) Alderman HARRISON: It is a most illegal proceeding. That is all.

Councillor FAIRCLOL Gli was pleased to hear the chairman's explanation. He was certainly under the impression the fees were paid whether the children went to school or not. As to children not going to school, he thought in some cases, that arose from the complaints the children made to their parents of being illused, and the latter took them to another school in the hope that the children would attend better.
Alderman HOL3IES proposed that the minutes be confirmed with the exception of the recommendation, and this having been seconded by Councillor Monks, was accepted by Alderman WEBSTER, and carried.
MUSEUM, LIBRARY, AND ARTS COMMITTEE. THE LATE DR. HENDRICK.

The minutes of the Museum, Library and Arts Com- mittee, comprised besides the curator's usual report, recommendations that applications be made to the trustees of the British Museum for electrotype copies of Greek coins which have been made for distribution to the local institu- tions for educational purposes; that the chairman and Mr. Madeley be authorized to examine the library of the late Mr. John Fitchett Marsh, about to be sold in London, and make arrangements for purchase of such books, &c., as they may consider of value and importance to this institution; and that the tender of Messrs. Hesketh and Son for the painting and papering of the Librarian's house, be accepted. The minutes also contained a letter from Mr. B. Kendrick (given in our last issue) acknowledging the resolution of the com- mittee expressing sympathy with the family of the late Dr. Kendrick in their bereavement,and announcing that by the terms of his father's will the Museum and Library Commit- tee were to have the choice of 100 volumes from his library. It was recommended that the Chairman and Mr. T. G. Ry- lands, together with the Librarian, be appointed to make the selection of 100 volumes referred to; that Alderman Harri- son be appointed a member of this committee, to supply the vacancy occasioned by the resignation of Councillor Wil- liams, and that the best thanks of the committee be given to Mr. T. Glazebrook Rylands, F.S.A., for his valuable and interesting gift of forty-two 17th century Lancashire tokens.

Councillor GREENING moved the adoption of the minutes. Alderman WEBSTER seconded, and stated the committee had received the 100 vols. referred to as having been so kindly and affectionately left them by the late Dr. Kendrick, and they were now in their possessionr. They had been selected by the Librarian, and appeared to be a very valuable collection of books.
The MAYOR : Has arything been done with "reference.to Mr. Marsh's collection of books? Alderman WEBSTER said the works that were of interest
to Warrington consisted mostly of small pamphlets. They were so mixed up with other things that a good many would have to be re-purchased from those who had bought the bundles.
The minutes were passed. THE SANITARY COMMITTEE'S EXPENDITURE.

Councillor MONKS moved, and Councillor WHITTLE seconded, the confirmation of the minutes, which contained nothing of public interest. Alderman WEBSTER enquired whether anything had been heard about the working of the new sanitary apparatus at Birmingham. Councillor PLITT saw there were items "orders for pay- ment of accounts" amounting to £1,007. They were con- stantly having entries of that kind upon the minutes, but the Council was left entirely in the dark as to what the money was wanted for. (Hear' hear.) He had long been of opinion that the items should be printed on the Council summons. At all events they ought to have the accounts read out as they formerly were. He did not say that auy abuses had cropped up, but it was possible that large amounts might be passed without the Council knowing what they were passing. Alderman Hannesoet observed that some time ago he moved a resolution dealing with the question. He thought then, as he did now, that the Council were in the habit of voting large sums of money without having the least idea what it was for, and he thought that on the Council sum- mons should be inserted in detail all sums above £5, ex- clusive of salaries. If that were done, it would -give them fuller information, and be did not think it would involve very much additional printing. It did not seem satisfactory that they should be called upon to vote away sums like £l,OOO or £1,200 without knowing what they were for. He might be answered by the remark, "But you can get all that information by referring to the minute books ;" but that involved trouble and thought, and when the members of the Council came there to dispose of the monthly busi- ness of the Corporation, it did not at all times occur to them to obtain such information. It would also involve a con- siderable amount of confusion, if, during the reading of the minutes of the various committees, one member and then ,another called for the minute book to peruse what the items were. He was induced to withdraw the resolution he made on the subject at a former meeting of the Council on the understanding that some means would be devised to meet the difficulty, and by which fuller information would be given; but he did not see that anything had been done. The MAYOR: That might easily be done, because the principal items in these accounts are for wages. Alderman HARRISON would give one instance—he did not make the remark peevishly—namely, the question of depu- tations.. (Laughter). During the past twelve months they had had several very interesting deputations to various places. He did not suppose any member of the Council, ex- cept the members of the committees from which the deputa- tions were selected, knew anything about the cost. If there was any branch of municipal government likely to degene- rate into abuse, his opinion was it was the branch spending money on deputations. He did not for a moment say that money had been improperly spent, but they were liable to that sort of thing unless the matter was watched; and when they found their rates increasing to an extent that was becoming alarming, he thought a vigilant eye should be kept over the expenditure. (Hear, bear). The MAYOR : I fancy there must be the cost of a depu- tation ineluded in this £1,007. (Laughter). Alderman KEAN: It will be the old £7 then. Alderman WEBSTER said the matter was in a degree met in this way: the members received their Council summonses several days before the meeting of the Council--(The Mayor: Five days.)—and in the event of any large item appearing a member could easily go to the Town Hall and make en- quiry, or he might go a little earlier on the meeting Alderman HOLMES sympathised with the expressions of the previous speakers, but pointed out that the right time for the surveillance of the eNpenditure was when the orders were given. Councillor WALLINGTON thought it important that the accounts should be looked after and more detailed infor- mation given, as from the 3rd to the 31st May the ex- penditure had amounted to £3,000. Councillor JEANS agreed with the remarks that had been made, and said he had often thought that more detailed in- formation should be given. Two or three months since he took the trouble to go through the different items passed for two years previously in connection with the sanitary depart- ment, and he was very much surprised to find the monthly dribblets amounted during that period to the very small sum of nearly £30,000, upwards of £25,000. He had roughly added up the sums they were passing that evening, and they amounted to nearly £8,000; while for the sanitary department alone they were asked to pass £2,000 in round figures. He thought the mem- bers of the Council ought to know more of what they were asked to pass than they aid, and that the details might very concisely be given in the summons. It was not only im- portant that the Council should know, but that the rate- payers should know also. (Hear, hear.) Very great com- plaints were being made, and they knew that the rates bad gone up tremendously during the last few years. The Maxon : The rates have gone down, Mr. Jeans. (Laughter.) Alderman KEAN was glad to hear Councillor Jeans had gone to the trouble to investigate the payments made by the Sanitary Committee, but said they should place against the expenditure the income, so that they could arrive at a right conclusion as to the expenditure. Alderman CIIANDLBY agreed with the desire for further details, and said be believed every committee in the Council wished to exercise every economy. Deputations might be extravagant—(laughter)—but he had never been upon mere than one, and he then had the pleasure of travelling with the Mayor and several other members in a third-class car- riage. (Laughter.) Third-class fares were charged, and that was not a very extravagant transaction. The MAYOR: I think I travelled first-class, did I not? (Laughter.) Alderman DAVIES pointed out that all information respect- ing the accounts was given in the Corporation Year Boot:, and that if it was given in the summons it would simply be repeating what would be given afterwards. Councillor MONKS did not see what the cost of deputations had to do with the subject. Alderman KEAN: That was only a slip. Alderman HARRISON: It was not a slip at all. Councillor MONKS: It is perhaps some disappointed Alderman. Alderman HARRISON (lenehing): It is not, indeed. Councillor MONKS was satisfied that deputations were worth all the money they cost. (Hear, hear.)- As to the accounts of the Sanitary Committee, he had made no secret of his belief that it was an expensive com- mittee. But it was so with the sanction of the Council. When the Council deputed to certain members the spending of their money, he presumed they did it with their eyes open, and that they gave them credit for care and watchfulness. The expenses of the Sanitary Committee were necessarily heavy. Most of the accounts were for provender for horses, for wages for carters and men em- ployed at Longford, for scavenging, and for food for patients at the Infectious Diseases Hospital, and other expenses. The accounts almost entirely consisted of such items as those Ile had named. He was sure that it would needlessly add to the length of the minutes if what was suggested was carried out, and there would be no advantage. Alderman Webster had suggested a very sensible course, namely, that if any member of the Council saw a large expenditure it was not too much trouble for him to apply to Mr. Chorley. The

experience of every member of the Council was that Mr. 4 Chorley would be able to afford the most complete informa- tion anyone might desire. (Hear, hear.) They had made a new departure. The members of the committee had made up their minds that they would work within their estimates, and they had instituted such a system of accounts that they , would be able to keep a check over their expenditure, and ascertain whether it had exceeded the income. (Hear, hear.) Referring to the item of £1,007, he said £B2B of that amount was a balance of account owing to Messrs. Manlove, All iott and Company, which Mr. Chorley had refused to pay without the authority of the Council. Councillor PIERPOINT : That is what we want to get at. It ought to be put on the minutes. Councillor MONKS thought it would be well if the deputy town clerk would see in future that particulars of any exceptionally heavy amount were put on the minutes. Replying to Alderman Webster with reference to the Bir- mingham machine, he said he had expected some com- munication from Birmingham that day. The machine, how- ever, had been got to work, but like many other new machines it required some little alteration, At present the machine had done its work satisfactorily, and a much larger amount than would be required from it in Warrington. (Hear, hear.) The difficulty which kad arisen was, he believed, in the engine. The Birmingham people found that the machine being so large required more power than was expected, but this Was simply a question of the engine power, and could be remedied simply by putting a larger cylinder in. He thought the Birmingham Corporation were in a f+ir way to solve the difficult problem of dealing with sewage, not only for themselves, but for other towns as well. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were then agreed to. THE ' OF THE GAS WORKS.

div.head: ASSESSMENT
div.p: ASSESSMENT
Alderman HOLMES moved the adoption of the minutes of the Gas Committee.

Alderman DATIES, in seconding the resolution, took the opportunity to inform the Council that the overseers very properly sent their representative (Mr. Tunstall) to go through the accounts, which the committee had submitted to the Assessment Committee, for the purpose of determining the assessment of the gas works; and he did not hesitate a moment in saying that in Mr. Tunstall the overseers had a very able representative. (Hear, hear.) He examined the accounts most thoroughly and with a masterly mind, with a thorough knowledge of the technical character of the under- taking, in which he did not know his like. The Gas Com- mittee had stated they ought to be assessed at .£4,800, while the Assessment Committee required the assessment to be placed at £4,500, or the gross assessment at £5,294. After going into these figures, and considering the various objec- tions, Mr. Tunstall came to the conclusion that the require- ment of the Assessment Committee was about the proper thing to do, his figures, within a few pounds, being similar to the committee's. He could not help repeating that Mr. Tunstall was the ablest man that had ever been in the over- seers' department in Warrington.
GAS FOR COOKING PURPOSES. INTERESTING DISCUSSION.

Councillor MACKIE inquired whether the recommendation "that with the view to encqurage the sale of gas for cook- ing purposes, the Committee purchase and hire out gas cooking stoves" was one which came within the powers of the Town Council.
The TOWN CLERK: It is. Alderman KEAN : They have the same power as with gas meters.

Councillor AIacKTE said he had great faith in Alderman Kean in an overseer's meeting, but he had not much faith there. (A Voice: "This is absurd.") He now wished to ask as one interested in seeing the gas works turn out as great a volume of gas as possible could be,—which, he was sure would delight the heart of the gas manager—and seeing that they hap an enormous amount of plant erected at a cost of only £40,000 or £so,ooo,whether the Council had also the power to purchase small gas engines and put them out to hire to such ratepayers as had to make their living by driv- ing mangles. (A laugh.) He was not doing this in a joke. There were small gas engines which could be got for about £l5; he did not know whether cooking stoves cost less or more than that. (Alderman Holmes: They are a deal less.) In Warrington there was a large number of small manufacturers, and people usinc, small machines, to whom a gas engine would be of home benefit. There was no doubt that cooking by gas referred to the better class in Warrington; no working man was likely to hire a stove, and he wished to know whether the Council could not extend the area of the thoroughly ex- perimental—boldly, wisely, experimental plan of assisting in the consumption of gas. At the same time they shodtd take care they were not burdened with an enormous number of gas-cooking stores. He hoped they were not going to com- pete with the shopkeepers of the town, and he hoped they would supply gas to the stoves as cheaply for an ironmonger as they would for the stoves from the gasworks. (Several voices: Certainly.) Councillor PIERPOINT thought it scarcely necessary for the Gas Committee to take upon themselves to be vendors of gas apparatus; it would be sufficient to prove to the rate- payers of Warrington that they were in a positioi to supply them gas for cooking purposes at a certain rate, which should be at so low a figure tO become an inducement to customers. If the committee went in for purchasing a quan- tity of stovesand a fewgas engines, it was quite possible they might have on their hands £l,OOO or £5,000 worth of goods which may not be turned into capital so very easily. He did not know why the committee should turn ironmongers in any shape or way, as they had sufficient dealers in iron- mongery and small engines to supply all necessary demands —(hear, hear); and if the Corporation could prove satisfac- torily to the inhabitants, that there would be a saving of cost by using gas instead of -coal for cooking purposes, that would be sufficient. He moved an amendment that the minutes pass with the exception of the one relating to gas stoves.

Councillor Dlxore seconded the amendment. The Gas Committee, he thought, had quite sufficient on their hands at present, for he came to that meeting expecting they were going to have such a large reduction in the price of gas announced as would astonish them. (Laughter.) There was a report abroad in the town that the new gas works had to be closed for four or 'five months, and he should like to know if it were true. After remarking on the dirty state of the street lamps, he said it had been suggested to him by a gentleman whom he had lately met, that the committee should fix 10 candles as the standard illuminating power of the gas and charge about is. 91 per 1,000 feet, and keep an account of the power above that standard. Councillor Monks, he believed, had stated that one candle was equiva- lent to 3d., and thus if the illuminating power of the gas was 19 candles the charge would he about 2s. 6d. per 1,000 feet. He told the gentleman that the gentlemen connected with the gas works were rather dull of hearing—(laughter)—and not at all disposed to give a reduction. Councillor JEANS said with the exception of tlio gas works, the business of the Corporation was not carried on to make a profit, and he thought they were travelling out of their course in becoming traders of things not strictly neces- sary for carrying on the gas works. It was his opinion that many people would not go in for cooking stoves of-the char- acter ramed, and it should he understood that a large number should not be purchased. Trading ought to be confined to the tradespeople of the town, and he should support the amendment. Councillor WALLINGTOI•7 remarked that it was a very good maxim, that we should be just before we were generous, and he thought the debts on the gas works should be removed or brought within a manegable amount before they spoke of a reduction in the price of gas. (Hear, hear.) The purchase of gas stoves he regarded a very wise procedure. (Hear, hear.) The Committee did not confine themselves to pur- chase stoves from townspeople, but they might, and perhaps would do so. He did not believe they were going to pur- chase very many,-:-{Alderman HOLMES : Hear, hear.]—but would extend their operations as the demand for the apparatus increased. (Hear, bear.) The object of the Committee was to show that the use of gas stoves was more economical and more effectual for cooking and domestic purposes than the ordinary fire place. He had much pleasure in support- ing the Committee, but he would not advocate a reduction in the price of gas. (Loud laughter.) Alderman KEAN was confident the Gas Committee would not involve the Corporation in any large debt in purchasing ' stoves ; and they were aware that those persons using them stated they effected a great saving, and the cooking was more satisfactory; for they could so arrange these stoves that they could put a herring in one chamber—(laughter)- 1 a leg of mutton in another—(renewed laughter)—and a round of beef in another, commence to cook them at the same time, and the heat was so regulated that all would be finished at once. Councillor Motes said he recognised the fact that there I was a tendency to treat many subjects in connection with the Council rather from, he was almost saying, a childish 1 point of view—(hear, hear)—and he thought if they treated each other a little bit more gentlemanly, and took it for granted that they were doing their business in a business way, it would save an ?immense amount of talk in the Coun- cil. (Hear, hear.) He thought the discussion partook of that character. The Gas Committee was composed of gentlemen of business capacity and habits, and they were , not at all likely to run into experiments indicated by Conn- cillors Dr. Mackie and John Pierpoint, and spend some £4,000— Councillor MACKIE said he bad mentioned no expense; Ile had given no cause for this gratuitous attack upon him. On the contrary, he urged the use of gas and the extension of it to a greater degree. If Councillor Monks was giving a lecture on good manners he would confine it to his own , side.

_ Councillor PIERPOINT : There was nothing experimental in my figures. The MAYOR remarked that he was sure Councillor Mackie did no; say anything about expense. ,It was, he thought, Councillor Pierpoiut. Uouncillor Momts, continuing his remarks, referred to. Dr. Mackie's suggestion to provide gas er.gines to turn mangles—(laughter)—and said he treated it seriously as a good suggestion; but he did not think the Corporation ought to find capital fcr people of the class of people men- tioned, who ought to find the capital and engine themselves. (Hear, hear.) They all knew that an engine might be so neglected in half an hour, that it would be se damaged as to cost a great deal more than any profit they were likely to get from it. With regard to the cooking stoves, he was in- clined to think.;;the ratepayers would be much benefited by the competition with the Gas Committee. He did not believe in the feeling that they should not sell stoves or anything to come into competition with the shopkeepers. He did not find that Warrington people would pay a penny more for iron because it was made in the town; they were all keen enough to buy it at the lowest possible price; and he did no See why shopkeepers should not be subjected to the same competition as manufacturers. It would be a good thing if the Gas Committee worked this thing as a matter of business, with a view of increasing

the consumption of gas' which, he thought, was one of the things looked to. It behoved them to take ad- advantage of every opportunity to increase the use- fulness, and what he termed, the day consumption of gas, in face of the competition they were going to have from the electric light. (Hear, hear.) Councillor PLATT observed that with the fact before them that the new gas works were practically closed, and that the electric light was making such rapid strides, he should like to urge upon the Gas Committee not to spend any sum of money in making fresh plant, if they could possibly avoid it, until they saw the ultimate effect of the electric light. With regard to encouraging the introduction of the use of gas in other directions than lighting, he thought the com- mittee might be safely left to their own discretion in the matter. (Hear, hear.) The Corporation, as a manufac- turer of gas would in future have to look more in other directions besides illuminating power, if they were to make the works more profitable. Alderman HOLMES, in replying, read the section in the Act of Parliament which empowered the Corporation to supply all kinds of apparatus. Councillor PIERPOINT : We are all aware you have the power, but I think it is an injustice. Alderman HOLMES went on to remark that the committee had mentioned previously in that chamber that they hoped, azd should endeavour to encourage the day consumption of gas, and with that view they were endeavouring to pro- mote the extension of gas cooking apparatus. (Hear, hear.) He might say that at various times they had spoken to the ironmongers, and asked them to push forward this trade. To one ironmonger they went so far as to offer to supply him with gas free, if he would put up ‘a series of gas cooking stoves in his premises, in order that the public might see them, and determine for themselves their useful- ness and efficiency. (Hear, hear, and a voice : " Quite right.") Of course the committee did not :wish to go into competition in any way with the ironmongers of the town; if they wished to supply gas cooking apparatus by all means let them do it. The committee had not finally settled the terms of the rent they should charge for the stoves, but they should hire them out on a certain percentage on their cost; such a percentage as would enable the borrower of the stove to become the owner in a certan time.

Councillor PIFRPOINT : Making the Corporation into a loan society. Alderman HOLMES (continuing) said as to the committee spending £5,000 or £lO,OOO upon plant, he thought they were sufficient men of business to suppose they should not do anything of the sort. Alderman Kean had rightly men- tioned the course they should pursue. If they spent £5O in purchasing stoves, and they were required to spend another £5O or £l5O they should do it, but by degrees, like b,:.siness men naturally did. Mr. Dixon had asked whether the new gas works were shut up. His answer was simply that for a short time the new gas works were closed, because the days were long. The gas was not probably lighted before nine o'clock, and the old gas works could produce sufficient gas for the requirements of the town, and they should probably not make any gas at the new works for—he did not know how long—until they required it. [Alderman Davies : September.] They would have to consider the question of gas engines carefully before they adopted any measure of hiring them out. The person entrusted with the manage- ment of the engine might smash it and leave the committee to pay for it. The thing had not been before the committee in any way, and he could not pretend to give any but his own particular views. Replying to a question, Alderman HOL3IES said they should charge no more for the stoves than was paid else- where, nor could they make two distinct charges for supply- ing the gas. The MAYOR: The real meaning of the Gas Committee re- commending this resolution is that it would lead to a greater consumption of gas. (" That's it," and hear, hear.) It appears to me, whether they or the tradesmen provide the cooking stoves the same thing will happen—the greater consumption of gas, which is their object. The amendment was then put, when there only voted for it Councillors Pierpoint, Dixon, and Taylor, nearly all the members voting against it. The motion was cafried.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

The minutes of the following committees were confirmed : —Watch, Markets, Street Improvement and Lighting, Finance (stating that at a meeting held on the 22nd May it was decided that after dae notice had been given for making an improvement rate, and also a general sewers rate, in accordance with estimates already approved by the Council, the Corporation acting by this committee hereby make the same accordingly, and directs that the common seal of the borough be affixed to the rates) ; Town Hall, Park and Baths (which recommended that the tender of Mr. Josiah Whittle for the painting of the outside of the Town Hall and buildings be accepted, and that the tender of Messrs. Clare and Ridgway for a flat bottomed boat be accepted, and showed that the income from the baths for the past four weeks was £27 143. 6d., and for the corresponding; period last year lie.); and General Purposes Com- mittees. The Council then adjourned.

div.head: WA RRINGTON POLICE COURT.
div.p: WA RRINGTON POLICE COURT.

SATURDAT.—Before Alderman Chandley and Councillor Fairclongh. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—John Maloney was brought up charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermar- ket-street on Friday morning.—Fined 5.s and costs, with the alternative of seven days' imprisonment. THEFT FROM THE PERSON.--A young man named James Welsh, as agrlcultnral labourer, of 9, Green's Court, was charged with stealing from the person of Wm. Price,. who resides at 3, Mersey-street, Runcorn, the sum of 3s. in silver and copper. It appeared that the prosecutor had been em- ployed during Friday cleaning the canal at Grappenhall, and had come into Warrington carrying his spade and other utensils, which he left at the British Workman Public-house whilst he looked about the town for a short time. About nine o'clock p.m. the complainant saw the prisoner near the Rain's Head, in Horsemarket-street, in company with three or four men, and he asked defendant to tell him where he could procure some refreshment. Prisoner at once con- ducted him to Mr. Buckle's dining rooms in Market-street, where prosecutor entered and ordered a bowl of soup. Prisoner also went in, sitting down next to Price, and telling him he was out of work. Price then paid for prisoner a bowl of soup. When prosecutor took his exit from Mr. Buckle's dining-rooms and was passing down Market- street, prisoner asked him if he would pay for a pint of ale. Prosecutor said he did not mind, and was in the act of sorting his money when prisoner snatched about 3s. out of his hand, at the same time running as fast as he could down Market-street. Prosecutor followed, but having lost sight of him he went to the police station, and gave a very minute description of Welsh, which resulted in his apprehension shortly afterwards.—Prisoner made a statement to the effect that he was drunk when he committed the theft, and did not know what he was doink.—The Bench considered the case proved, and sent W'elsk to gaol for one month with hard labour.
MONDAL—Before the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) and the

ex-Mayor (Councillor Fairclough). GOOD " CIISTOMEAS."—Thomas Fleming, a corner man, made his 17th appearance on a charge of being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-street, on Saturday night, and was fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days.—Daniel Crosby made his 32nd appearance on a similar charge, in reply to which Daniel had nothing to say except that he "come quiet." The Mayor: It is very expensive work for you, Crosby.— Daniel: Well, sir, I have not been here for this last five or six months.—The Mayor: Five or six months! You ought to say five or six years, not months. You have been here before this year.—Fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days' imprison- inent.

A DISORDERLY CASUAL SENT TO GAOL—John Quinn was charged with disorderly conduct at the workhouse, on Satur- day morning last, while a casual inmate of the workhouse; and further, with assaulting an inmate named John Hines. —Prisoner charged Hines with withholding his money, but Hines, who did not search the prisoner, denied that he had any money, whereupon Quinn became very disorderly, and bit the old man's arm very severely.—Prisoner was com- mitted to gaol for one month. AN ER-POLICEMAN COMMITTED FOR 14 DAYS.—John Gandy, an ex-policeman of the borough, was charged with having, on the Bth ult., run away from the borough, and left his wife and four children chargeable to the common fund of the union.—The prisoner pleaded "not guilty with intent to desert."—Mr. Garnett, relieving officer, stated that on the Bth ult. the prisoner's wife applied to him for relief. He visited the house and found she was without food, that her husband bad not been near her since the Saturday previous, and that she did not know where he was. He gave an order to the workhouse for the wife and four children, who had since been there, and until that morning he did not know where the prisoner was. He reported the case to the Guardians, who ordered him to prosecute. The prisoner was apprehended at Widnes by P.C. Wheatley.—The Mayor said this sort of thing was becoming very common, but as the prisoner had not a very comfortable home the Bench would inflict a light penalty.—The prisoner was committed for 14 days' imprisonment. A LODGING-HOUSE THlEF.—Elizabeth Basnett, a woman of loose character, was' charged with stealing 6,1 in copper from the person of Martin McLoughlin, at the lodging- house of Thomas Hines, Hill-street, between Sunday night and Monday morning.—Prosecutor, a farm labourer, arrived in town on Sunday night and went to line's house to lodge, and after paying for his bed he had 7d. left. He went to bed, and at seven o'clock the following morning he found his trousers had been removed and sixpence bad been taken. On looking round he saw the prisoner sleeping in another bed in the same room. Prisoner had is. Old. in her posses- sion when taken into custody, and as she had been previ- ously convicted of like offences she was now sentenced to three months' bard labour' the Bench regretting they could not send the case to the assizes, as the prosecutor was simply a wayfarer. NEGLECT OF FAMILY CASE.—Martin :Noon, a puddler, appeared in the dock under the following circumstances. On the Bth ult, he was summoned for neglecting to maintain his family, but the case was adjourned for a month. The prisoner took his wife and children but of the workhouse on the 20th ult., but the same day they were re-admitted, as the prisoner got drunk, with the result that he had spent the last 14 days in prison, whence he returned on Saturday last.—He was committed for one month's hard labour, the Bench remarking that the prisoner would not support his family. tRUNKEN WOMEN.—Elizabeth Townley, who, as the Mayor said, had a very "meek and mild appearance," was fined ss. and costs or seven days for being drunk in Win- wick-street on the 27th ult.—Eliza Smith was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Dallam-lane on the 28th ult. He may be consulted daily at his Private Consulting Rooms,

8, Charles—street, Macclesfield, 18th May, 1882. Dear Sir,—l beg to tell you that from a child I had been subjected to epileptic fits; and this last three years they have been so frequent and severe that I was obliged at times to give up work. Reading the numerous cases that had been successfully treated by your " llagnetaire " Appliances, I thought it worth trying. I am now pleased to say that since wearing your appliances I have had but one attack, and that was but very slight.—l am, dear sir, yours gratefully, Mr. R. Lonsdale. JOHN WM. RIDGWAY.
(Testimory from three of the same family.) 15, Lord-street, off Manchester-road,

Burnley, May 9th, 1.82. Dear 81r,—I, and two of my daughters, have received great benefit from the Magnetaire " Appliances we purchased from you on your last visit to Burnley. One of my daughters was suffering from indigestion, and the other daughter from great weakness, whilst I was very bad with bronchltts and difficulty in breathing. As the " Magcetaire" has proved beneficial in all the three clses. I don't see why the pubic should not have every confidence in your treatment, as I am sure sufferers will not regret ever haying tried your" Magoetaire " Appliances.— Yours truly. Mr. Lonsdale.
