div.p: RUNCORN 'SCHOOL BOARD. 'Matey. Canon Barclay presided at the monthly- meetingl of the above "Board held on Wednesday, at the offices, Bridgewater-street. -there were also present Messrs. John Simpson (vice-chairman), Thomas Norman, Jas. Pritchard, R. Lea, Peter Briscoe, and F. Rigby (clerk). HOU.: TRINITY MANAGER 3 AND THE ATTENDANCE OfIICER. The following letter, which was received at the last meet- ing and adjourned until Wednesday' last for consideration, was read : Holy Trinity Church School. Runcorn.—To the Chairman of the Runcorn School Board.—Rev. bk.—At a recent meeting of the managers of the above school. it was reported to them that the Board's off car, in making visitations, instructed par- ents whose children were suffering from any infectious or con- tagious disorder not to send such children toschool. Theinan- agers thought that the officer is not a competent person to form i an opinion respecting the nature of children's complaints, and that he was rathrr a.ssurning the functions of a medical gentle- I man by such action. ' I was directed to point out at the same time that providing your officer were as, diligent in weching the progress of the disorder upon which he based his recommendation, and urged attendance at school upon recovery, the managers would have no objection to his Interference, as it might tend to check the spread of infectious diseases in school; but they respectfully protest against his authorising and sanctioning absence from school without, as is apparently the case, afterwards enforcing regular attendance as soon as the cause for absenc3 has disappeared. I append three -cases that were hi ought under our notice, in each of which the original cause of absence was stated to be lever: John H. Pea- cock—absent from school from November Ist, 1881, to April 17th, 1882. His brother Alfred returned to Behold on Jan. 9. George Bkelding—re-admitted to school Oct. 5, 1881, through officer's pressure, attended three weeks, making 4,2, 6 atten- ' dances respectively. Has been absent since November 11, and is frequently seen in the streets. William Faulkner, residing in the district of Halton. Has been. absent since December 2, 1881.-4 remain, yours faithfully, W. H. ROGgRSON, hon. sec. May 2, 1882. TheCLEltit said Mr. Bowyer had prepared the following statsinent :—ln reply to the letter from the managers of the Trinity School, I beg to state that in the two first cases mentioned, I am not aware that there has been any con- tagious-disease at all in the families, but simply neglect on the part of the parents in not sending their children to school. To show that I have not neglected getting them to attend school, I beg to say, that after having frequently , seen them playing about the streets,' I visited both parents -several times, and cautioned them about it. The parents then alleged that the boys were in attendance at the Trinity Echool, and finding that they were still playing about dur- ing school hours, and not receiving sufficient reason for their absence, I served both parents with noticec on the 12th April last, ordering them to send their children regularly to school, and both are now in attendance. I may also farther state that one of the parents appaarer: before the Attendance Committee on t/Je ISth January last, and was then cautioned. With respect to the last-atentioned case of a boy living at Halton-within-Runcorn, I may say that I had reason to visit his parents on the 13th March last, respecting the boy's irregular attendance at the Mill Brow Board School. When I called, his parent informed -me that another of her boys who had been attending the Trinity School was suffering- from fever, and she also stated that the doctor was attending him and had ordered the children to be kept from school, she having received medical certificates to that effect, which she informs use have since been for- warded to the school.

The CHAIRMAN: He denies the stateoent. Mr. Simpsow: Have we anything to do with the childrerl living in Halton? The CLERK : We do use a little moral presure, but we have no legal ground. Mr. NORMAN: It is a great pity that the Trinity mana- gers cannot work comfortably with our inspector. How is it? I should like to get at the bottom of it. Mr. LEA s ticl;the schoolmaster thought that Bowyer hav- ing given them liberty to absent themselves on account of disease, had omitted to urge them to go to school after- wards.

Mr. NORMAN: He does not say that. He says it is so. He puts it in such a straightforward way. The CHAIRMAN said surely it was right on the part of Mr. Bowyer to tell parents not to send their children to school who were suffering from infectious disease. For his part he should feel very sorry if they were sent to his school, and should at once send them back again. Mr. SIMPSON thought the managers ought to be very much obliged to the officer for requesting parents not to send their children who are suffering from infectious disease to school. Mr. Rogerson puts it in the letter that they are suffering. Mr. LEA: But the rub was, that he did not arge them to go to school when they got over it. Mr. NORMAN: Our inspector has been ill for more than a month. The CLERIC: But this is really antecedent to his ill- ness. Mr. LEA: Mr. Kinnersle.y, the Government inspector,when here the other day, complained bitterly that he found 23 hove playing in the gutter in Regent-street. The CHAIRMAN said that was not the fault of the attend- ance officer. Mr. Kinnersley made the same complaint to the National School teachers, who showed him their books recording an attendance quite up to the average. This mat- ter very much concerned Mr. Simpson, for it turued out that on the very afternoon the Inspector was in Runcorn, the Wesleyan schools were closed for the Whitsuntide holidays. (Laughter.) Mr. PirTcHARD enquired whether the Board had not been relieved from all responsibility in regard to the Holy Trinity irregulars. He remembered that some months ago the schoolmasters undertook the duty and said they could do the work more efficiently. Mr. NORMAN said that was so. He wished Mr. Annett and the visitor could work together pleasantly. It made things very uncomfortable. Mr. LEA: He says it is the fault of the visitor. The Crux: All the complaints made respecting the visitor have been thoroughly sifted by the Board, Mr. Lea. The CHAIRMAN: Should we not have the visitor before us? I suppose this complaint arises out of the complaints made by Mr. Annett many months ago, which were proved to be misstatements. He cannot forgive his own mistake. Mr. BOWYER was then called before the Board, and ques- tioned respecting the attendance at school of the three boys mentioned in Mr. Rogerson's letter. He stated that the cases of irregular attendance had never been reported to him, and when he had seen them in the streets he had frequently cautioned them..
Mr. SIMPSON : That is the point. If the cases are not reported to the visitor, how is he to know anything about them?
The CLERK : Ai a matter of fact, be has got as much as he can do to get the children to scllcol who are reported to him.

Mr. BOWYER: That is one of the greatest difficulties under which I labour: Coi'dren will not go to school, unless the School Board is continually behind them. Mr. SIMPSON : Our position is this. Mr. Annett has refused to give us information with respect to his irregulars, and no notice can be taken of them unless Mr. Bowyer happens to see them. Mr. LEA: But the Department has said Mr. Bowyer must go to the school and get a list of the absentees. The CHAIRMAN: He has been, and they won't give him a list.

The CLIR% said he had never had such a letter from the Department. Mr. BOWYER, in reply to the Clerk, said between Novem- ber and April be had not received any intimation from the master of the Trinity School that the boy Peacock was not attending school, and be only discovered it by seeing the boy laying in the streets. Duting all that time he was not sup- plied with any returns. The CL-t• : And Mr. Annett is the only teacher who does not supply the returns?

Mr..lio;NY Ea : Yes. Mr. LEA said Mr. Annett argued that he had no right to give the officer a list of the abientees. The registers were open for the inspecier, and he could get the list. It was a waste of Mr. Annett'stitnn.

Mr. SIMPSON : But he puts it on a different ground to us. Mr. Annett maid he found he could do the visiting much more efficiently himself. . Mr. BOWYER said in some cases he did take the liberty of requesting pirents not to send their children who were suf- fering from any ir•Letions disease to school. He always mentioned this a, the teachers, and this course met with their approval. Therr vre many people who did not employ a medical man its eases of measles and scarlatina, and in these cases he had suggested that the children should not be sent to school. In the two cases first named he was not aware that there had been any disease, and the irregular at- tendance arose, through the neglect of the parents. Mr.Parretraun said the books showed that Mr. Bowyer had att. nded nine tier.es in respect of his child. Mr. BOWYEU asked whether he was justified in requesting parents whose children were suffering from infections disease to keep them at home. He referred more particu- larly to cases where the services of a medical man had not, been secured. The Board thought in a case like that referred to by the Attendance Officer the action he took was perfectly justi- fiable. Mr. NORMAN said if Mr. Annett would supply the returns as the ether teachers did, then the whole thing wouldbe in a nutshell. Mr. LEA : Mr. Annett has no right to do it. Mr. PRITCHARD: But the advantage would be great com- pared with the small amount of trouble to him. It was stated that from the schools supplying returns there was never any complaint. Mr. LEA remarked ttat he would lay the views of the Board before the managers at their next meeting. It was agreed that the Clerk should write to the managers of Holy Trinity School, stating that the Board had no reason to censure their officer, and that Mr. Annett must haveleen misinformed as to the facts. OFFICER'S REPORT. Mr. Bow B, school attendance officer, reported that the certified government accommodation was 2,323; the number of childrenlon the rolls was 2,858; with an average attend- ance of 1,931.8. The average attendance for April, 1881, was 1 958.8 ; and for the year 1874, 1,252. The accommo- dation in excess of average attendance was 391.2, and the number on the rolls in excess of accommodation 495. These figures showed a decrease in the average attendance as compared with the corresponding period of last year of 27, arid an increase as compared with 1874 (the year preceding the formation of the Board) of 679.8; total number inl attendance at private adventure schools under 9d. per week 75. In the returns of the past month the officer reported a decrease in tho average attendance as compared with the preceding month, and the correspondidg period of last year; this he attributed to the Wkitsuntide holidays, and this unavoidable absence through illness. The Board ordered the Clerk to prosecute 20 persons for not seDding their children to school regularly.

div.head: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
lONIDAY.—Before the Rev. E. A. P. Campbell (Gl:airman) - -
an/ Mr. Wm. Bankes.

ASSAULT ON THE LANDLORD OF A. BEERHOUSII—TWO young men, named John Fearnett, of Lower Cawdor-street, and Frederick Hulse, of Brick-kiln Houses, were charged withassaulting John Harding, landlord of the Lord Rodney beerhouse.—Complainant said that On the night of the 270 ult. the defendants came to his house between nine and ten o'clock. Shortly after, he heard Fearnett say he would loosen some man's teeth, and he ordered him out. He re- fused to go, on which he tried to put him out. In the struggle Fearnett twisted one of his arms in a savage man- ner, and knocked him down, on which Hulse hit him twice in the face. The latter then went away quietly, but Fear- nett had to be forced out of the house.—Kate Booth, servant at the Lord Rodney, gave evidence in support4fthis statement.—Wm. Woodward, a labourer, was called for the defence, and said that rearnett only struck the landlord after he had seized hint in a rough manner.—The Chairman said that the complainant was perfectly justified in putting defendants out, and landlords would be protected in the management of their houses, so long as they were con- ducted properly. Roughs like defendants well deserved punishment, and they would each be sent to gaol 14 days, with hard labour, in defaulL of paying 10s., and costs 12s. 6d. _

A FAMILY QUARREL.—E'ksa Billington and Jane Radley, both of Heath-road, were summoned for using threats to Mary Brown.—Complainant.said that on the night of the :31st ult. the defendants came lo her door with a large crowd. They made a great noise, and Billington, who is her daughter-in-law, threatened te.raurder her.—The defendants denied their guilt, and Billington said she merely went to the house to see her husband,who had caused her to have to apply to the Board of Guardians for relief.—The summons was,dismissed, on which the woman Brown said she lived in such terror as to the two women, that she dared not go home. FfiewrierG IN THE STREET.—Thomas Charles Jackson and John Davies were convicted, on the evidence of P.C. Mello:, of having, on the 20th ult., fought in Halton-road, and were each ordered to enter into sureties to keep the peace •Eiz months in £lO, and pay ICs. 6d. costs.: CHA-aciED WITH DISTURBINO THE SALTATION ARMY SER- yicEg.—A young working man named George Barnes was sumo:met.' for having, on the 14th ult., been guilty of riotous, violent, or indecent behaviour in a certain place of religious worship duly certified under the provisions of the 15 and 19tN:ic., cap. 81, called the Public Hall, during the celebration ak Divine service.—Mr. George Marshall (for- merly chairman of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners) gave evidencoto the effect that he had ju..t finished reading the Scripturee,.and was giving out a hymn in the hall,when a number of ynung men in the gallery caused a disturbance. They were askod to be quiet, but their only reply to this was to make a rush for the doors. The congregation became very much excited, but ultimately he conetrained them to commence singing, and sent for a policeman.—John Matthews, sparman, said he was looking after the hall door on the evening intuestion, and he let two men, who said they were flatmen, go out. Immediately afterwards the defendant, who had led the disturbance referred to by the last witness' asked to leave, but he told him he.could not do so.—ln reply to Mr. ,Johnson, deputy magistrates' clerk), witness said he declined to let defendant leave the hall because the meeting had not concluded.—William Dodd, a man wearing the uniform of the army, said defendant swore, and said he would force his way out if they did not permit him to pass.—Thomas Jones, of 10, Surrey-street, also gave evidence.—The Chairman .said it was quite evident that the defendant was not allowedp go out, and then became he spoke loudly he was charge,d with disturbing the service. The question arose of what right the people having charge of the hall had to prevent defendant's egress.—Shadrach Jones said that when defendaot rushed towards the door he stooped and touched the face a a young woman, as 1.7 he intended to kiss her, so that she screamed, and a great dis- turbance took place.—The Chairman wished to know upon what grounds the officers of theArrey refused to letdefendant leave the building.—The witness said there was a written order in the hall that no one was allawed to go out until the first meeting was closed, and defendant was well aware of this. If the doors were opened for one, generally 40 or 50 young men tried to obtain an entranee for the purpose of disturbing the service.—The Chairman said the Bench were exceedingly anxious that religious worship should not be interfered with; but the liberty of the subject must also be respected. If the defendant and others wished to leave the hall, the magistrates could not wonder at their objecting to remain inside; and if no further evidence could be brought firward the magistrates would be obliged to dismiss the case. —The Captain of the corps wished to make a few observa- tions but he was informed that the magistrates could go no further than listeninz to the evidence before the court.—As there was no further evidence forthcoming, the Chairman said that as the meeting was a public one people must have the right of going from it as they thought proper. Where was the evidence of riotous, violent, or indecent behaviour? —Mr. Marshall observed that the meeting was "quite upset" by the defendant's conduct. —The Chairman: We shall be very glad to assist you; but you must bring your evidence in a different form before we can deal with it. The summons will be dismissed.

MORE CHARGES OF DEFRAUDING TRU RAILWAY COM- PANY AGAINST FARMERS.—E. Gee, farmer, of Norton, was charged with having been the owner of certain milk at the station of that name, consigned to be carried from thence to Edgehill station, and on the 13th April, given to Mr. Pryce, the collector of tolls, a false account of the quantity so car- ried, with intent to avoid payment of the proper tolls. De- fendant was also charged with having committed a similar offence at Sutton Weaver station, on the 13th and 17th April.—Mr. Preston, who appeared for the Loudon and North-Western Railway Company, said that the exigencies of the present day had caused what were known as milk farms to spring up. With the object of encouraging the trade the company undertook to carry milk for a very small sum indeed, viz , for distances not ex- ceeding 20 miles, at a minimum rate of id. per imperial gallon, or 9d. per can. The cans varied in size, some hold- ing 14 gallons, and others 16. On the 13th April the quantity declared to he sent on was two gallons less than that actually forwarded. The quantity recorded on the ticket outside and the one inside the can varied to that ex. tent. In the second case, the milk sent from Sutton Weaver on the 13th April was stated to be 12 gallons, whereas the can contained 16. There was a somewhat similar difference as to the 17th April.—Defendant pleaded guilty, and no witnesses were, therefore, called.—Daniel Basnett, of Preston Brook, was summoned for committing a similar offence at Sutton Wearer, on the 2nd ult.—Mr. Preston said the quantity sent off by the defendant was 16 gallons, and his declaration was 14.—Defendant pleaded guilty.—Mr. Pres- ton observed that if a conviction was obtained in one of the cases against Gee, and he paid the fees in the other two, the company would be satisfied. The distance from Sutton Weaver was certainly only 15 miles, but by a special clause in the Act of Parliament, the distance across Runcorn rail- way bridge was measured as five miles.—The Chairman said there was no doubt that the defendants must have been quite aware they were committing an offence against the law. The matter was a serious one, but, in consideration of the remarks made by Mr. Preston, a moderate fine would only be imposed. Gee would have 20s. and costs to pay, making £3 15s. 6d., and Basnett a similar amount and costs (total, £3 145.) WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. J. Brundrit and S. B. Chadwick.

A FooLisn SAlLOR.—Elizabeth Ellen Bird, a woman of easy virtue, was charged with stealing 2s. from the person of Thomas Bartlett, a sailor, on the 7th inst.—The prosecu- ter, who is a sailor on the brigantine Emily, met the prisoner at the Blue Ball, in Fryer street, and afterwards went to her house with her, where he alleged she stole the money. He, however, admitted that he was drunk at the time, and the Bench, who said they did not consider there was sufficient evidence to convict, discharged the prisoner.

WIDNES POLIO E COURT. • MONDAY.—Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun. ANOTHER MEMBER OF THE ARMY OF BEGGARS.—A man who said he was a Frenchman, and gave the high-sounding name of Henri de Burgue, was convicted, on the evidence of P.C. Thompson, of having been guilty of begging in Victoria-road on Saturday—Prisoner, who was also credited with having been very abusive to several people, was sent to prison seven days. WEDNESDAY.—Before Ma. Edward Gibbon (chairman) and Mr. A. Fletcher.

THE SCHOOL BOARD AT WORK.—The following people were summoned by the Widnes School Board, for whom M!.. G. H. Danby, the clerk, appeared, for not sending their children to school, and were each ordered to pay 55., in- cluding costs :—William Bailey, Mary Ann Bowyer, John Riley, William Worthington (two cases), Sarah Williams, and William Dugan. RAID ON LICENSED VICTUALLERS. 1 Mr. Benjamin Holden, of Appleton, was summoned for 'permitting drunkenness, and also with selling drink to a couple of drunken men, named Hedge and Fletcher.—Ser- geant Strickland said that about a quarter-past ten on the night of the 27th ult. he, in company with Sergeant Mc- Gregor, visited the Albert Hotel, Albert-road, Widnes. They found four men in one compartment, and in another the two defendants, and all the men had drink before them. Hedge was holding on by the counter. They spoke to the landlady about having served defendants with drink, but she replied that she had not noticed they were so intoxi- cated. She added that she was very sorry, and hoped the police would look over the matter. She afterwards observed that she had heard that Fletcher had been in an asylum, and this, perhaps, accounted lier his somewhat excitable behaviour. Hedge gave is name as William Smith.— Sergeant McGregor offered cerr,borative evidence.—The defendant was not able to appear owing to illness, and his wife represented him. She maintained that the defendants were not drunk, and the action was merely "a little Spite" on the part cf the police.--Mr. John Holden, brother to the landlord, said he saw the two defendants at the house, and they were not inebriated.— John Dunn, signalman on the London and North-Western Railway, said that he was present when the officers entered the house, and Fletcher was not drunk.—The Chairman remarked that it had been stated that Fletcher had been in an asylum, and he had no doubt that his incarceration re- sulted from .taking intoxicants. If he were not decided to avoid drink an the future, he felt sure, speaking as the chair- man of sue of the county asylums, that he would end his days in such an institution. It was amazing that the past had not proved a warning to such a man as Fletcher. Both the men charged with having been drunk on the premises, would have ss..andsosts (89.) to pay, with the alternative of seven days' imprisonment—Fletcher: I will go for seven

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, JUNE 10, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, JUNE 10, 1882.

days rather than pay the money.--The- landlord would be fined 403. and costs (total £2 163.)—John Webb, landlord of the King's Arms, was also charged with permitting drunkenness on, his licensed premises.-P.C. Savery said that about four o'clock on the afternoon of the 22nd ultimo, he saw a woman named Catherine Coyne, in Anne-street, West, who was very much under the influence of drink. He ordered her home. Some short time afterwards, he was passing • the :King's Arms public house, when he heard a noise, and-ongoing into the bar, he found the same woman there, -.standing with five or six men, and partaking of drink. He asked the barman if he did not consider the woman to be drunk, and he replied she was.—Mr. Bartlett appeared for the defence, and objected to Superintendent •Barker examining the officer for the purpose of proving that the woman was afterwards brought before the Bench, and convicted of drunkenness.—The Chairman appealed to Mr. Lewin, deputy magistrates' clerk, who ruled thatnthe police ought to prove the conviction by a formal copy from-the court books. —Mr. Bartlett asked the police officer if he did not know it was his duty to lock the woman up, if he found her wander- ing up and down the streets in such a state as he had des- cribed ?—Witness: She could walk without help.—Mr. Bartlett: You let her wander about, I sv.ppose, in order that she might go into this public-house, and you might get a • case.—Superintendent Barker: I must object to such a remark on the part of Mr. Bartlett, as it is no advantage to this officer to get up a case.—The Chairman :'Let me say this, that the officer would not have been justified in taking her up, as she was going quietly along the street. ,He might have bean justified in summoning her, but not in appre- hending her.—P.C. Murdock gave corroborative evidence ; and Sergeant Strickland stated that on the woman being brought to the police office, she was drunk.—Mr. Bartlett said that the respectable firm for whom he appeared, had got special rules up in their houses, by which all their servants, including the barman, mere supposed to be guided, en pain of instant dismissal. The woman referred to entered the house with a child in her arms, and Ler conduct was quiet and decent when she asked for the glass .of ale. There was not the slightest sound of fighting, or dis- turbance, in the house.—George Withers, the barman, and .several other witnesses were called to ,prive the statement made by Mr. Bartlett.—Defendant was fined 40s. and costs 178.—Mr. Bartlett gave notice of appeal against the decision—The next case gone into was one in which Mr. McLoughland, licensed victual ler,was similarly charged. The men to.whom it was alleged the drink had been served were Cassidy and Tallon.—Sergeant McGregor said that about eleven o'clock on the night of the 27th ult,, be, in company with P.S. Strickland, visited the Star Inn, kept by McLoughland, in Elizabeth-street. On entering by the back door they found seven people there, of whom five were only from 14 to•IS years of age. The two men Cassidy and Talton were present, and were intoxicated. The landlady stated that the -drink in front of the two belonged to a couple of ,people who had just gone out, and whom she did not know. The landlord afterwards came into the bar, and witness asked him if he considered the two men sober or fit to be supplied with drink. The landlord turned round and said to another man named Caine, "that drink," pointing to the measures before•Caesidy and Talton, "belongs to you, don't it ?" Caine said" -Yes, it belongs to me and my mate." Witness then went to the compartment from which Caine had come, and there found two measures half filled with rum. Witness asked to whom the drink belonged, and Caine said "to me and my mate." He afterwards explained that they had the beer too, but had got tired of it and left it. Talton gave a false name, and be was locked up.—ln reply to Mr. Swift, junr., who appeared for the defence, wit- ness said he neither knew Talton nor Cassidy.—P.S. Strick- land gave evidence of a corroborative character.—Mr. Swift observed that his defence was that the two men were drunk, and his client's barman refused to serve them.—Mrs. Mc Loughland said she was sure neither of the men was served with drink.—Mrs. Kerry, barmaid at the house, said she did not serve either Cassidy or Tallon with beer.—Wm. Spelman having been called, Caine was put in the box, and then Caine gave evidence to the effect that the beer was his, and he left it because he was tired of it.—Patrick Mannien and the landlord were also examieed.—Defendant was fined 403. and costs, and Cassidy ss. and costs. The summons against Tallon was dismissed. SURETIES.—A person named Bushell was ordered to enter into sureties in £lO, and two in £5 each, to keep the peace, for having, on the 21st ult., been guilty of cursing and cacsing a disturbance in the public street.—Evidence was given, showing that Ellen Fairley was guilty of a like offence, at eleven o'clock on the night of the .30th ult., in Marsia-street, and that she also relieved her feelings by kicking several of the doors.—She was ordered to find similar sureties for one month. RESISTING A POLICE OFFICER. Matthew Barns was summoned for resisting P.C. Snowden.—The officer said that on the night of the 30th ult., he was apprehending a man for drunk and disorderly conduct, when defendant tried to rescue him, and threatened to kick him if he did not release the prisoner.—lnspector Barnett said there was no wish to press the case, and defendant was discharged on paying 7s. 61. costs. A CARELESS AND UNFEELING GREENGROCER. John Barton, greengrocer, was summoned for having, on the 30th ult., in Waterloo-road, been guilty of cruelty to a pony.—A police officer proved that he found the pony to be very lame and bleeding from wounds abaiit the fetlock.—Mr. Wall, veterinary surgeon, was called for the defence, and said the animal had been suffering from a dislocated joint, caused by contracted tendons. A piece of leather had been placed round the joint, so as to keep it in its place, and this had been so carelessly put on that, if the officer had not seen it, "it would have cut clean through." The pony bad now been placed under his care at Warrington.—The Bench said that under the circumstances, they would dismiss the summons.

A NEIGHBOURS' QUARREL.—Mary BrOWBIOW was Sum- moned for assaulting Mary Bratley.—Complainant said that on the 3rd inst. she went to the defendant's house for a small sum of money which she owed her. Defendant used most filthy language, and said she should not pay the money. Brownlow next seized her by the hair of her bead, and after giving it a good pulling, knocked her down. The husband encouraged her.—Defendant, who denied the state- ment of complainant, was fined ss. and costs. WARNING TO CARTERS—WiIIiam Yates was fined 2s 6d and costs, making 7s, for having, on the evidence of P.C. Ross, been proved guilty of allowing his horse to stray in Peelhouse-lane, Farnworth, on the 20th ult.

A SAD CASE.—A joinery named Thos. Sumner, of Wil- liam-street, was liroudt up on remand, charged with hav- ing on the evening of the previous Wednesday, attempted to commit a criminal assault on a girl aged five years, named Elizabeth Bennett, of Mill-brow. The particulars are not fit for publication. The case was heard in the magistrates' private room, and the prisoner was committed for trial at the Liverpool Quarter Sessions.

knew that they would do their duty as far as lay in their power. The Chairman briefly returned thanks on behalf of his wife, and in conclusion stated that on the following morn- ing the keel of a new ship larger than the last one would be laid, which he thought was a pleasant augury for the future. —Mr. Wilkinson proposed the health of Mr. John Davies, the designer of the vessel, and referred to the excellence of Mr. Davies' designs, and expressed a hope that he would for many years be spared to superintend the construction of other ships with the same skill and • success as he had done in the past.—ln responding Mr. John S. Davies thanked those pre- sent for the cordiality with which they had honoured the toast of his health. He had a desire that the vessel launched that day should be successful, for the reason that several gentle- men had been induced by his persuasion to take up shares. For this reason, among many others, he wished prosperity to the ship.—Other toasts followed, and the proceedings termin- ated.

RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.. TUESDAY.—Before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, Judge. CLAIM FOR GOODS DELINERED.—Mr. William 'Slather, grocer, sued Mr. William Jackson, of St. Helens, for £4 14s, goods sold and delivered.—Mr, Burton appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Riley (of St. Helens) for the defendant.— The plaintiff's books were examined, and as they were con- sidered rather unreliable, His Honour gave a verdict for the defendant.

ACTION FOR CLOTHING SCPPLIED.-Mr. Adam Thomp- son, draper, of Rusbolme road, Manchester, sued William Cooper, of Runcorn, for 12 lie, clothing supplied.—Mr. Burton appeared for the plaintiff, and the defendant was unrepresented.—Witnesses were celled to prove the case, and a verdict was given for the full amount claimed. The court only lasted about an hour, and the other cases tried were not of general public interest.

with the working of such Acts in Scotland and Ireland. Roman Catholic priests, Protestant clergy, ministers of all denominations, magistrates, and judges had borne their testi- mony in refutation of that statement. Again, it was said that drunkenness would prevail. Well, so far as their ex- perience had gone in Ireland that had not been the case. It did not prevail in any sense in which that term could be used, and therefore those very great objections fell to the ground. After quoting the opinion of Archbishop McCabe as to the good the Sunday closing measure had been in Ireland, he said it was for them to hold their views up and to write to their representatives in Parliament to bring that question to the front. He believed it was a foregone con- clusion; it was certain to come; it was simply a question of time. He asked them to have some of the credit of bring- ing about the solution of the question, and, to put the thing in a practical form, he would ask them to set about and make a canvass of Earlestown to see what were the wishes of the people, aud he was sure they would be encouraged by the result. (Applause.) , 'The Rev. R. CROZIER supported the resolution, which was then put to the meeting, and carried with acclamation. The Rev. W. C. TAYLER proposed the following resolu- tion:—" That the rapid ripening of public opinion throughout .England in favour of the Sunday closing of public-houses, and the recent carrying of the Act for Wales through Parliament by overwhelming majorities, are sub- jects for gratitude and hopefulness; and that as the testi- mony of Scotland in favour of Sunday closing, after 28 years' experience of the Act, is so remarkable (not a single petition having been presented against it for many years), and as the Sunday Closing Act of 1871 for Ireland has beea productive of such great and undoubted good that its ex- tention to the five exempted towns is now being loudly de- manded, this meeting authorises the chairman to sign on its behalf petitions to. both Houses of Parliament in favour of a measure which will bestow a similar boon upon the whole of England."

The-Rev..J. ALLATT, in seconding the resolution, said the Act had been operation in Scotland for a period of 28 years, and was unanimously approved of by the people. With re- gard to Ireland, there were five considerable towns exempted from the operation of the Sunday Closing Act, and such was the Opinion of the inhabitants of those towns, that in- stead of rejoicing in the rejection, they treated it as a grievance, and demanded that it should be extended to them. (Hear, hear.) Speaking of the Principality he said that, in consequence of a little bad grammar, the Act had not taken effect there, and the population had to bear up as well as they could. They had a very great grievance, and the privileges the places quoted claimed they also claimed. They had a positive right to look to the Government to for- ward the object in view. (Applause). Mr. P. M. CAMPBELL, who supported the resolution, thought it had been conclusively shown that public opinion was ripening on this question. He [remembered tbe time when the Scotch would not submit to their Sunday closing motion, but it had now been in operation for 28 years, and they saw that Ireland bad adopted it by a majority of nine to one, and there would be many a family thankful for it in this country, when it became law. (Hear, bear.) The sub- ject was one not to be treated lightly, but should be acted upon in a serious manner. (Applause.) The resolution was carried, and the proceedings closed with a vote of thanks to the Chairman.

div.head: LAUNCH OF A-SCHOJNER AT RUNCORN.
div.p: LAUNCH OF A-SCHOJNER AT RUNCORN.

On Monday, a launch took place at the ship building yard of Messrs. Brundrit and Co., Runcorn, in the presence of a large number of spectators. The vessel is a three-masted schooner of about 200 tons burden, and as she glided in the water, she was christened the "A. M. Brundrit," by Mrs. John Brundrit, of Brookfield, Higher Runcorn. The schooner measures 95 feet over all, with a breadth of beam of 22 feet 2 inches, and a depth of hold of 10 feet 2 inches. The frame of the vessel is of English oak, planked outside with American rock elm, bottom and bilges, the top sides being of oak, while the decks are of yellow pine. In fitting up the vessel 'are has been taken to secure good ventilation, and the appointments of the cabin and the crew's quaxters are of the best description. Mr. Davies is the designer of the vessel; Mr. Ravenscroft has supplied a complete set of sails; and Mr. Yarwood was entrusted with the painting and decorating. The schooner is now in the Bridgewater Navigation Company's docks, where she expected to receive her first load. In the evening the successful launch of the vessel was celebrat( d by a dinner to the employes in Wilson's Hotel. Mr. John Brundrit, J.P., presided, and was supported by the Rev. Cannon Barclay, Dr. McDougall, Mr. A. Green, Mr. G. H. Taylor, Mr. F. Fairhurst, Mr. Wilkinson, Mr. W. Mellor, Mr. R. Rigby, Mr. J. Unsworth, Mr. S. Ravenscroft, Mr. Mason, and others. The vice-chair was taken by Mr. J. Torkington.—The Chairman proposed the usual patriotic toasts, and in giving the "Bishop of the diocese, and clergy of all denominations," coupled with it the name of Canon Barclay.—The Vicar responded with a humorous speech, in which he expressed his pleasure in being at the launch that day. He trusted there was a long and prosperous career before the vessel, and that when she was so old and battered that she was not worth putting on the stocks, might she go down in shallow water with every sailor saved, and a good insurance to cover the whole business (Laughter and applause).— Dr. McDougall proposed the toast "Success to the A. M. Brundrit.'" They had seen successfully launched that day, he remarked, a vessel that in design and construction re- dounded to the skill of the management of Messrs. Brundrit and Company. (Applause.) It was a source of pleasure .to every one to have witnessed the growth of the shipbuilding trade in Runcorn. Some 12 or 13 years ago, the trade was at its lowest ebb; but the tide had now turned, and Runcorn once more had the advantage of a very prosperous ship- building trade, which kept the artizan class, who were the backbone of any community, fully employed. The new vessel had been built to the order of several gentlemen in the town, and he trusted that though it was their first order ,it would no be the last. Artizans should not forget that there was some advantage to be gained in ,encouraging tradesmen to become owners of ships; and what money they had to spend he hoped they would not fly away with it elsewhere, but spend it in the town in which they lived. By a co-operation of this kind, they would soon have one of the finest fleets of vessels belonging to the port. The toast having been honoured Mr. Wilkinson, of Liverpool, one of the owners, re- sponded. He complimented Mr. Davies on the clever design of the ship, and remarked en the former fine vessels which Messrs. Brundrit had built. —The Chairman next proposed "Success to the Lilly Heaps." a vessel launched a fortnight ago; and Mr. Fairhurst followed with the toast of" The Builders." The health of Mrs. Brundrit was proposed by Mr. G. H. Taylor, and the two toasts being honoured Mr. Brundrit replied. He said it had been their pride to build such vessels as could not be beaten, either as regarded material or workmanship. Many persons from different parts of the kingdom had seen the "A. M. Brundrit," and the general opinion was that no nicer vessel had ever been built at Runcorn. He liked above all things to see the yard full of men, with plenty of work for them to do. This plea- sant state of things could only be brought about by the co- operation of the men with the employers. He had every confidence in the men in the employ of the firm, and he

div.head: SUNDAY CLOSING QUESTION.
div.p: THE SUNDAY CLOSING QUESTION.

MEETING AT EARLESTOWN. •A meeting convened by the Central Association for Stop- ping the Sale of Intoxicating Liquors on Sunday, was held in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown, on Tuesday night. The chair was occupied by Mr. W. D. Stoba, Huyton ; and he was accompanied on the platform by the Rey. T. R. Matthews, Rev. J. Allatt, Rev. R. Crozier, Rev. M. Dicken- son,aey. W. C. Taylor, Rev. J.P. Rountree M.A. (vicar of Werneth, Oldham, who attended as a deputation), Mrae. F. Avelice, Mr. J. W. Emmett, Mr. P. M. Campbell, Mr. John Squires, ex. Letters of apology for non-attendance were read by the Chairman from the Rev. John Whitley, Rev. J. J. Lennon, and Mr. E. J. Weaver (town missionary). The CuAIRMAN, who was received with applause, after acknowledging the honour they had done him by placing ‘him in the chair that evening, said he should be glad to help forward the Sunday closing movement, a movement which had his whole sympathy-. The circular convening the meeting was very clear and distinct. It had no uncer- tain sound. It stated that a public meeting was to be called to advocate the necessity of stopping the sale of intoxicating liquors on Sunday. Their programme in the Sunday clos- ing movement was nothing less than a total suppression of the sale of intoxicating liquors on Sunday; and they did not mean to rest and be satisfied until the Bill for Sunday closing had been passed by Parliament, and had received the assent of the Queen. Other trades and businesses could not legally be pursued on the Lord's Day; and it was certainly unfair and wrong that the saleof drink should. be sanctioned, as at present, by Act of Par- liament. They were not satisfied with that state of things They had abundant evidence to show that drunkenness was eating out the life of the people. It was certainly impossible to estimate the amount of crime and misery which was brought about through the use of strong drink. Ireland had a Sunday Closing Bill, and he saw in a paper the other day that a town in Ireland which was not included la the operation of the Act had asked to come under its operation, a request which, it seemed to him, was a quite conclusive sign that the people in the large towns had seen that Sunday closing was a good thing, and they wanted it also. It was abundantly proved by figures that drunkenness and crime had decreased very materially in Scotland since the Sunday Closing Act was passed. He had been in Scotland many times, and had had opportunities on very many Sundays of seeing what was going on, feeling a little interested in the Sunday closing movement. The law was evaded in seine instances, and he had also been told that there was Sunday drinking carried on in Scotland; but during the whole of the Sundays he spent in Scotland he never saw a drunken man. He took the trouble to make enquiries in Scotland, from a few people whom he thought it worth while to ask, whether they would like to have the Act rescinded, and go back to the old system; and the reply he gnt in all the cases was "No." He believed that the pub- lic ins of Scotland, if they were polled, would acknowledge that the Sunday Closing Bill was a blessing to the people. In Liverpool they had 250 places of worship; but there were over 2,000 public-houses. He contended that was a very ugly item indeed. What could 250 churches and chapels do against 2,000 public-houses being open? He thought that was a fact all should concur in, and they ought all to say that it was not a right thing that the public-houses should be open on Sunday as well as the churches and chapels. Sunday closing was doing well for Wales and Scotland, and why should not England have it also? (Ap- plause.) The Rev. T. R. MarrnEws moved the first resolution, which was as follows :—" That this meeting is of opinion that the sale of intoxicating liquors on the Lord's Day is productive of a large amount of drunkenness, demoralisa- tion, domestic misery, pauperism, and crime; and that in- asmuch as other trades may not legally be pursued on that day, it is unfair and wrong that such sale should be sanctioned as at present by the laws of the realm." He said he knew from experience that very many of the publicans them- selves wished for Sunday closing. They felt it a great burden upon them to be obliged to remain at home certain parts of the Sunday; or as the next best thing, or the next worst thing, to leave some one in charge of their houses of business. He felt it his duty to help on that work of eman- cipation, for it was really after all a work of emancipation ; and, again, as a minister of the gospel, and as a professor of Christianity, it was his bounden duty to do everything he could to prevent or to put an end to the desecration of the Lord's Day. (Applause). The subject of the resolution put into his hand was not a new one. It was ag old subject well known to most temperance men, and he supposed that nothing very new could be said upOn it. At any rate he was not prepared to say anything new upon it. His ex- perience was much the same as it had been for many years, —that it was not a right thing that drink should be allowed to be sold on Sunday or the Lord's Day. He had heard that some of the publicans would very much like to see the day when they, like other people, could feel at liberty on the Lord's Day. There were others of different opinion, who were not so open and frank; but he did not know what their inmost thoughts and feelings were. He contended that it was their business and duty to go on with the agitation, and try with all tho means in their power to impress upon the Legislature the necessity of a Sunday Closing Bill. (Ap- plause). The Rev. J. P. ROUNTREE (Oldham), in seconding the resolution, said it gave him very great pleasure to come there that night. First of all because of the cause which he had to advocate. It was a cause dear to his heart as be thought it should be dear to the heart of every patriot. They all felt how much the drink question had to do with their condition as a nation ; and they, of course, must feel how important any branch of the subject, such as that specially before them that night, was connected with the well-being, spiritually and temporally, of the people. They were not there that night as total abstainers, though he dared say there were many in that room who would perhaps be pre- pared to array themselves on the side of total abstinence. They were simply there to advocate a very clear and definite thing, namely, the stopping the sale of drink on Sundays. They should not treat it too much sea question of policy, as a social question. Surely they were not prepared to give up their spiritual convictions ; surely they were not prepared to give up their convictions as regards the sanctity of the Lord's Day. Let them treat it to a certain extent as a religious question, But with regard to the question of the publicans themselves, the chairman, he thought it was, in his openini'y., remarks made allusion to what the wishes of the publicans were. There was no doubt that many publicans, even responsible publicans themselves, who were really bona pe owners of houses, felt that tgey would be glad of a time when they might have their weekly rest just as their neighbours had. But there was a large class of public• house assistants, who had no direct interest in the trade, who got their wages whether the public-houses were open six or seven days. He had been told by publicans themselves that a measure like the one they advocated should be passed by the Legislature. It was only natural, but many of them were very anxious, and it was from that keenness of competition that they were kept back from closing their houses on the Lord's Day. He dared say that there were many publicans, as there were people in other trades, who were so greedy of gain, so unscrupulous, so much without principle they would even sacrifice anything to add to their income, to add to the gain that they could suckle out of the people. But he ,was not blaming the publicans as a class in this. There were people in other professions who were just as much without principle. But in every trade there were some unprincipled people, and therefore there were some publicians who would tell them honestly and straightforwardly that they did not want Sun- day closing. The speaker then went on to give facts to prove that Sunday drinking was a frightful cause of im- morality, crime and pauperism. He stated they had great advantages over those who advocated this question some years ago. They had the advantage Of the experience of Scotchmen, and also of Irishmen; and the experience thus gained went very far towards establishing incontestably the position which was taken up by the resolution which they had heard read. He showed the decreased consumption of drink in Scotland since the passing of the Forbes Mac- kenzie Act, and said with regard to the Sunday Closing Act, he would just notice one or two objections to the pass- ing of it. There were many objections made to it, but when they were examined they were found to be without much foundation. It was objected that the measure was an attempt at class legislation; but after all had they not had class legislation before now with the very best results? What were the Factory Acts but class legislatio'n ? Then there was another objection made to it. Some said that the rich man could have his beer in his house, or he could go to his club and there get it on Sunday. The poor man could not do this. If they compared the two, and if there was the same feeling from one as the other then let them go in for suppressing the clubs on Sundays. 'They had heard it said that most fearful riots and disturbances would result if that Act were passed; but that had been confuted by the testimony of all those who have had to do

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
All the ships of the British squadron have left Alexan- dria eNeept the _Alexandra.

Sir Arehibald Campbell, of Blythwood, Renfrewshire, has granted 10 per cent reduction to his agricultural tenants. A Central News telegram from St. Petersburg states that the Government intends taking over those railways in Russia which are in financial difficulties.

Addressea were presented to Lord Fitzgerald in Dublin yesterday on his retirement from the Irish Bench by the Judges, the Bar, and the Incorporated Law Society. The Allerton Bywater collieries, near Leeds, were closed on Thursday night owing to the falling off in the demand for coals. All the men brought up their tools. According to intelligence received from San Domingo, via Havana, the Government have decided to make arrange- ments for immigrants when renewing expired treaties with European Governments.
Yesterday morning, an inquest was held at Ashton-under- Lyne, on the body of a female child found in a ditch. A verdict of wilful murder by some person unknown was re- turned.
Mark Purcell, who was brutally assaulted near Tralee a few days ago, died from the effect of his injuries to-day.wA man named Carlaghan, who is in custody, will be charged with the murder.

On Thursday evening a man named Patrick Stephens was walking along the Lancashire and Yorkshire line near Mag- hull, when he was overtaken by a train and run over. He was frightfully injured, and was conveyed to the Northern Hospital, where he died shortly after admission. He was a farm labourer.

Mr. William Henry Darby, colliery proprietor, ironmaster, of Brymbo, near Wrexham, died very suddenly yesterday morning. Mr. Darby was in Liverpool on Thursday on business, and seemed in his usual good health. Heart disease is supposed to be the cause of death. Mr. Darby, who was well known throughout the district, was a Congregationalist, and a staunch Liberal in politics,_ . . _

Yesterday morning, the Bolton'Coroner held an inquest on the body of Elizabeth Ellen Ireland, aged 4 years daughter of a widow residing in Church Court. Wharf road, Bolton. On Thursday night the child was seen playing in the yard, and in a few minutes afterwards the mother found it head foremost in a tnb of water in an outhouse. Life was quite extinct. The jury returned a verdict of accidental death. The Newcastle-on-Tyne Liberal Association have asked Mr. John Morley, London, to be their candidate in opposi- tion to Mr. Joseph Cowen, at the next election. Mr. Morley has written intimating that private arrangements preclude his giving any definite promise for a few months at least. As Mr. Morley's candidature is uncertain, the asssociation have determined to look for some other gentleman. At Blackburn Police Court, yesterday, two cases of over- crowding were heard. In one case a man and his wife and four children slept in one bed, while two young persons slept in another bed in the same room, which was only large enough for the accommodation of three persons. In an adjoining house ten persons slept in one room, which was only large enotrzh for four. The bench made an order against the defendants. _ _

• 'A demonstration of Lancashire fire brigades will take place at Bolton this afternoon. In addition to the local brigades there will be 31 brigades from other towns, who will form in procession in the Wholesale Market, and thence pass through the principal thoroughfares, accompanied by some half-dozen bands of music. Afterwards the firemen to the number of 400 will sit down to dinner, presided over by the Mayor. A meeting of the gentry residing in Dunham Massey was held on Thursday night at Bowdon, when it was unani- mously resolved to ad-opt the lighting act for the more populous part of the township. It is proposed to light 71 lamps, and the rate required for the first year will be 81d. in the pound. The,rateable value of the township is £15,000, and a 2d. rate will cover the expense after the first year. Twelve gentlemen were appointed as lighting inspectors. The South Staffordshire Coroner held an inquiry at Mount Pleasant yesterday respecting the death of a boy named Arthur Jones, who met with his death under the following circumstances. The deceased and a number of other children went into a field where a mare and her foal were grazing. When deceased was passing the mare she kicked him on the left temple, inflicting such injuries as to cause his death. A verdict of accidental death was returned. THE MURDERERS OF CAPTAIN SELBY.

The Porte havine, recognised the validity of Lord Dufferin's claim with regard to Captain Grenfell's immunity from prosecution before a Turkish tribune, for his share in the encounter with the Albanian shepherds at Artaki, the public prosecutor has had to prepare afresh indictment against the murderers of Captain Selby. The case will probably be brought before the Court of First Instance on Monday.

div.head: DOMESTIC TRAGEDY AT NOTTINGHAM.
div.p: DOMESTIC TRAGEDY AT NOTTINGHAM.

A respectable married woman named Ann Topl is, who has been missing from her home in Laurel-street, Nottingham, since Tuesday last, has been found drowned in the river Trent. When last seen the woman was carrying a child, and it is feared that the infant has shared its mother's fate. The woman's house contained only tradesmen's bills and pawn. tickets. The body awaits an inquest, and the police are making inquiries.

div.head: AN EXPLOSION IN THE MERSEY TUNNEL WORKS.
div.p: AN EXPLOSION IN THE MERSEY TUNNEL WORKS.

One of the workmen was terribly injured by an explosion, which took place in elle Mersey Tunnel Works late on Thurs- day night. The man, whose name is Brickley, was engaged in blasting operations, when a charge of gunpowder exploded, shattering his arm, awl partially blinding him. It is said the charge had been inserted in the here-hole without Brick- ley being made aware of it. The poor fellow is in the hos- pital in a precarious condition.
THE ALFRETON MAGISTRATES AND THE HOME
SECRETARY.

The Chairman of the Alfreton magistrates, yesterday, in reply to a memorial expressing confidence in their adminis- tration of justice, notwithstanding the case of Hannah Davies, said they treated the proceedings of the Home Secretary and his pompous interference with the most utter contempt. IMPORTANT STEEL MILKING EXPERIMENTS.

Yesterdays number of very successfu-le;PeTi.tneni;;:ere made at the Patent Shaft Works, Wedneshury, to test the process of converting Staffordshire common pig iron into steel under the Thomas Gilchrist patent. The trials were witnessed by the leading iron masters of the district. Steel ingots were rolled down into bars, sheets, and other descrip- tions, and withstood the enormous strain in doubling up without fracture. The cost is considerably below that of iron.

SHOOTING OUTRAGES ON FARMERS. On Thursday, at Ballyfarna, county Roscommon, a farmer named Henry Eas-t, of Coralereek, was attacked by three men armed with revolvers. He sestained no fewer than three wounds, one being in the leg, where the bultet still remains. He has for some time been'the subject of agrarian animosity. A Central News telegram says that Michael Brown, farmer, residing at Batbglass, six miles from Ballina, was shot in the leg on. Thursday night in his own house, six shoe, having been fired into the building. Brawn recently took a vacant grass farm, and received threatening notices for doing so. No arrests have been made.
On Thursday evening a farmer named Cornelius Hickey was shot at and seriously wounded in the leg, near Castle
Island. The motive is believed to be agrarian. Four arrests have been made.

SCENE IN THE HUNGARIAN DIET. A Central News telegram from Buda Pesth yesterday states that a remarkable scene occurred yesterday in the lobby of the Lower House during a debate on the Roman Jews. A Jew deputy named Watermann made an offending gesture towards deputy Isloczy. The latter followed Watermann into the lobby, where he publicly gave him a beating. MANSLAUGHTER IN LONDON. An inquest was held yesterday, at St. George's-in-the- East, concerning the death of Elizabeth Sullivan, wife of Timothy Sullivan, a waterside labourer. Deceased met her death by being struck by her husband with a poker, and the jury returned a verdict of manslaughter against Sul- livan.

div.head: MURDERS IN COUNTY '
div.p: THE MURDERS IN COUNTY '
GALWAY.

The Central News Dublin correspondent telegraphed yesterday :—The murder of Mr. Walter Bourke has created alarm here, but no surprise. Up to the present no intelli- gence has been received of any arrests. It is, however, stated that Mr. S. Taylor, of Castle Taylor, saw six men running away from the scene of the crime armed with seven guns, the extra gun being that belonging to the murdered escort. It may be mentioned in connection with the affair that recently a large firm in Dublin sent down a man to the locality to make estimates for some works that could not or would not be done in the neighbourhood. When, however, he arrived and saw Mr. Bourke armed with a rifle and the premises guarded by police he precipitately returned, refusing to have anything to do with the contract. Mr. Bourke lately received a communication from the authori- ties asking to keep them informed of hia movements. The Press Association says :—Special efforts are being made by the local police to discover the perpetrators of the deed, and some hope is entertained in official quarters that as the crime was committed in broad daylight, the murderers may be traced, but it is remembered that Mr. Bourke was by no means popular on his estate, he having been threatened with violence on many previous occasions. The assassina- tion of the soldier was probably accomplished to prevent the crime being traced. A Dublin telegram states that Mr. Burke left home a few days ago, it is supposed to visit Castle Naylor, a place over which he was agent, and was travelling along the fields when he was fired at. Mr. Burke's brother, who at present in London, on hearing a report of the terrible occurence, at once hurried to the lobby of the House of Commons to ask for official information. Mr. Trevelyan exhibited the foregoing message and other brief telegrams to the relative of the murdered man, and at the same time offered such consolation as he could under the circum- stances. Mr. Burke expressed an intense desire to go in- stantly to Ireland. to assist in tracking the assassins and protecting the family. It was explained to him that it would be impossible even by taking a special train to catch the mail steamer at Holyhead that night. After some further consultation Mr. Burke left, intending to proceed to Ireland at the enrliest moment. THE IRISH MEMBERS AND THE MURDER. Tho Central News says Messrs. Parnell and Dillon, as well as nearly every other member of the Irish Parliamen- tary party, expressed their regret at the assassination of Mr. Burke and his escort. They state that for the last six months the Land League organisation has ceased to exist in that district, and that wherever boycotting has been nut down agrarian outrages have multiplied. The crime, they think, is purely an agrarian one, and should not be looked upon as furnishing an argument in support of the new Coer- cion Bill, but rather as against the unwisdom of any attempt to utterly suppress the legitimate forms of agitation. A singular incident occurred on Thursday night whilst Mr. Burke's brother was walking down the lobby of the House of Commons towards the library with Mr. Trevelyan. Messrs. Parnell, Justin M‘Carthy, and Biggar wire walking in front of them, when seeing them Mr. Burke, who naturally was labouring under great excitement, said, "Parnell, this is your fault." No reply was made to this observation, the three Irish members walking on, whereupon Mr. Burke, looking at Mr. Biggar, made use of an observation which induced Mr. Trevelyan to take his arm and lead him aside. Mr. Biggar made no reply. During the time Mr. Forster was Irish Secretary gave.apprehensions were entertained for the safety of Mr. Burke's life, and special precautions were taken to ensure that gentleman against assassination. It was known that he was a marked man. Mr. Burke not long ago figured in an illustrated paper, in which he was shown acting as his own bailiff in serying writs upon the tenantry.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS. THE FLEET IN EGYPTIAN WATERS.—EarI GRANVILLE. replying to Lord Salisbury, stated he was quite sure that no portion of the fleet had been moved from Alexandria. TILE IRISH POLICE FORCE. Lord CARLINGFORD said there was no intention that the highest offices in him Irish police force should be filled by military men. THE MURDER OF MR. BIIRKE.—Lord CARLINGFORD, re- plying to Lord Oranmore, said three arrests had been made on account of the murder of Mr. Burke and his escort, who had been shot from behind a wall which had been loopholed for the purpose. There had been other outrages committed. Three farmers had been shot at and wonnded. Arrests had been made in one case but none in the ethers.
The Metropolis Management Building Acts Amendment Bill passed through Committee; and their Lordships ad- journed.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

REGENTS CITY AND DOCKS RAILWAY BILL.-011 the motion for the third reading of the Regents City and Docks Railway Bill, Mr. MoNK objected, as the transferring of canals to railway companies was in direct violation of the recom- mendations of the joint committee of both Houses on the subject. He moved that the Bill be read a third time that day six months.—A long discussion ensued, in which Sir J. Bailey, Mr. C. Ashley, Sir S. Waterlow, Mr. D. Jenkins, and Messrs. Watney, Anderson, Robertson, and others took part. On a division, there voted,for the third reading 220; against 74.

tartoxs IN IRELAND.—Mr. TREVELYAN, replying to Viscount Lymington, said the number of evictions in Con- nemara for the last two months were 233, mos tly for non- payment of rent. CETEWAYO.—Mr. EVELYN ASHLEY said no new restrictions had been placed on Cetewayo's correspondence, excepting that he should not be allowed to send messages into Zulu- land without the consent of Mr. H. Bulwer, special com- missioner for Zulu affairs at the Cape. EGYPT.—Sir C. DUBE said he could give no further in- formation than he had already done on Egyptian affairs. Replying to questions, Sir Charles said it was the opinion of the Government that the conduct of the Khedive had been straightforward and courageous, and was quite entitled to the full support of ourselves, Europe, and the Porte. He should be sorry to believe is the possibility of personal outrage to him, and we had no apprehension of that sort. THE MURDERS IN IRELAND.—Mr. TREVELYAN, replying to Sir S. Northcote, said three arrests had been made for the murder of Mr. Burke and the soldier who accompanied him.. Four more agrarian outrages had been reported from different parts of Ireland. In each case a farmer had been shot in the legs from revolvers. No arrests had been made. PREVENTION OF CRIME (IRELAND) BILL. The con- sideration of Mr. Bryce's proposal to omit the last paragraph of the clause which defined intimidation was resumed.—Mr. DILLON insisted that it was most important that a clear de- finition should be contained in the Bill.—Sir W. HARCOURT said when Mr. Bryce's proposal was disposed of they could move further definition of intimidation if that contained in the Bill was not sufficient, but until Mr. Bryce's 'proposal was disposed of they could do nothing.—Mr. SYNAN wanted it clearly set out that exclusive dealing was not intimida- tion. Colonel COLTHURST supported the clause as it stood, believing it would put down boycotting.— Mr. C. RUSSELL asked the Government if they intended to *make any alteration in the clause, to state their intentions at once. He strongly objected to the clause as IL stood. Sir W. HARCOURT said the . Govern- ment had done their best to define intimidation. It was not for them to amend their own clauses.— A long discussion ensued.—Mr. COWEN stiggested an amend- ment to the clause, so as to pro% ide that it should not be used to prevent political agitation. The Government had stated that was their desire; let them then introduce words to carry that desire into effect —The committee divided : For Mr. Bryce's amendment, 49; against, 130.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

SUDDEN DEATEL—Another case of sudden death occurred at Go!borne on Wednesday evening, May 31st, the victim being a strong-looking man named Henry Bate, aged 49 years. He resided at the house of John Bate, Bank Heath. He went to work as usual on Wednesday morning, and was in good health apparently. He returned about five o'clock in the evening, had tea, and afterwards went out, joining some of his acquaintances near to his home. About nine o'clock he was heard to complain that he did not feel well, and said he would go home and go to bed. He did so immediately, and was followed soon after by Joseph Pennington, a man with whom he slept. When Pennington got upstairs he heard Bate breathing heavily, he shook him, but got no reply. William Page, who slept in the same room, and Pennington's mother, who was downstairs, were both called, when they got into the room Bate was dead. Dr. Worsley and Police Constable Whiting were sent for, but life was extinct. An inquest was held on the body a day or two after, when a verdict was given iii>f " Ditd from natural causes."

FATAL ACCIDENT TO A BRIDGEWATER NAVIGATION ENGINEER, AT LIVERPOOL.—On Saturday night, as a man named Richard Banks, engineer on board the Bridgewater Navigation Company's tug "Helen," was getting on board the steamer by means of a ladder reared from the paddle-box to the pier wall, he missed his footing. In falling, his head struck some part of the craft, and he fell into the water. The accident was seen by these on board, and Banks was got out, but he had sustained serious injuries, and in a few minutes died.—An inquest on the body was held on Tuesday by Mr. Clarke Aspinall. The evidence adduced howed that the vessel was moored alongside the wall of the Albert Dock on Saturday afternoon from half-past four till half-past ten. At a quarter to ten the second engineer, George Bate, heard a splash in the water, and he found the deceased bad gone overboard, and was holding to one of the floats under the paddle-box. He was immediately got out, but only survived about seventeen minutes. A verdict to the effect that the deceased had fallen into the river and received a concussion of the brain, from the effects of which he had succumbed, was returned. Deceased, who was a married man, was well known in Runcorn.
